articles.title: What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
articles.body:
What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
Every year, Russia publishes a private analytical report intended for a select group of military and defense industry leaders. The Russian Military Yearbook is designed strictly for senior officers, security agency staff, and executives of companies in the defense sector.
Unlike public reports on the state of the armed forces, the Russian Military Yearbook is meant for internal use. It addresses military planning, advancements in weaponry, and developments in the defense industry, along with the key priorities of the Russian military leadership amid ongoing conflicts. Consequently, the yearbook sheds light on the priorities of Russia’s defense apparatus.
Russia’s global plans remain unchanged and are based on two main principles
First principle: Russia should be responsible for the stability and development of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). While Moscow does not harbor imperial ambitions to annex former Soviet republics, Russian politicians and military officials view these nations as vital partners in trade, infrastructure projects, and security.
Therefore, countries of the “post-Soviet space” should not join other political and military blocs, especially the EU and NATO. Such blocs often pressure members to sever ties with Russia and are sometimes directed against Russia.
However, Russia welcomes participation in economic collaboration, such as China’s Belt and Road Initiative. What benefits neighboring countries also benefits Russia due to the close economic ties between them.
“The West is entertaining the idea of creating a geopolitical confrontation arena in the South Caucasus, attempting to push Russia aside from the normalization of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Rejecting such attempts, the Russian Federation intends to do all it can to protect the region.” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Second principle: Moscow views stability through the lens of a “multipolar world.” This refers to a situation in international relations where there is no single hegemon or “world police.” Decisions regarding security and regional organization are made either at the regional level or during global negotiations, rather than by one or two central powers.
It may seem that America’s recent setbacks – including conflicts with European allies and protracted crises in Iran and the Middle East – create an ideal situation for Russian strategists. As Washington’s influence wanes, America’s capacity to control global affairs may diminish as well. However, that perception is wrong.
Russian military and political leaders desire not only a world without hegemony but also one characterized by stability and adherence to international laws. Even setting idealism aside, this approach undeniably serves Russia’s interests. UN principles help maintain the status quo and ensure regional leadership.
Conflicts involving Russia are often caused by breaches of agreements (primarily regarding NATO expansion), leading to the use of force and the disruption of regional balance. This was true of the conflict with Georgia in 2008, the civil war in Syria, and the Ukraine crisis.
Moreover, America’s inability to manage conflicts (which are often instigated by its own government) only serves to destabilize the world. This compels Moscow to allocate more resources for potential interventions. The Kremlin is well aware of what happens when a crisis outside its borders spirals out of control.
“According to S.V. Lavrov, the Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs, ‘The USA could become one of the responsible centers of power together with Russia, China, and other powers of the Global South, East, North, and West in the foreseeable future’, but this is subject to them abandoning the counteraction to the objective process of multipolarity strengthening” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Russian analysts do not believe that it is possible to return to the former Western-centric world order. They believe the Trump administration is too preoccupied with internal issues and is consistently souring relations with European allies, whom it views as ‘parasites’. Meanwhile, the EU is becoming increasingly reliant on rigid neoliberal institutions, making it less open to negotiations due to entrenched anti-Russia sentiments among its leaders.
Consequently, the only remaining option is to build a multipolar world.
Moscow sees China and India, as well as the nations of the Global South, as its partners in this new world order. These governments also seek independence from the US and Europe and are pursuing their regional agendas. However, experts point out that Russia’s goals may diverge from those of its partners and could even come into conflict with their goals; no one is willing to sacrifice foreign policy autonomy for the sake of “unconditional friendship.”
Despite the prevailing pessimism surrounding global politics, Russian experts believe that new conflicts can be avoided, even during such troubled times.
However, analysts are concerned about one particular region.
Very Cold War
In addition to the existing conflict zones, experts are also analyzing another potential flashpoint – the struggle for control over the Arctic. And this isn’t just about the vast reserves of valuable resources in the Arctic – estimates suggest that around 13% of the world’s oil and 30% of its natural gas lie beneath the ice.
Disputes over this “no man’s land” and its surrounding waters have been going on for nearly two centuries, and date back to the first attempts to carve out spheres of influence in the Arctic. Canada even attempted to occupy one of Russia’s Arctic islands during the Civil War, though this “occupation” was limited to a few settlers who were soon sent home by the Russian Navy.
Experts note that NATO countries have already begun a major arms buildup specifically aimed at potential Arctic operations. Military exercises are frequently held in the region, such as the recent Exercise Cold Response 26. In March, tens of thousands of service members participated in drills led by the Norwegian armed forces.
“During regular exercises in the Arctic, NATO countries carry out activities to conduct reconnaissance of all types, prepare and deliver missile, air, bomb, and torpedo strikes. Skills related to combat control and logistics, the interaction of dissimilar forces and means are honed.” 
– Vadim Istomin, doctor of Technical Sciences 
And this is just the beginning. NATO countries have initiated Arctic-aimed retraining and rearmament programs set to be completed by the early 2030s. NATO members call it preparation for possible threats. Yet analysts speculate that it could also be preparation for a coordinated attack.
Here are several examples:
Finland – HX / F-35 Program: As a new NATO member, Finland has acquired 64 F-35A fighters, as well as weapons and equipment for Arctic operations. It is also retraining pilots and technical staff. By 2028-2030, the F-35s are expected to fully replace F/A-18 Hornet aircraft.
Canada – North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) modernization: A new threat detection system for the Arctic is being developed. The Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar is set to reach initial operational capability by the end of 2029, while the Crossbow network of sensors will be operational by 2030. The Polar Over-the-Horizon Radar is anticipated to become operational between 2032 and 2033. Infrastructure for aviation and the command system are also being upgraded.
Canada – Rearmament of the Air Force: Canada is purchasing 88 F-35As to replace its CF-18 fleet. Initial combat readiness is slated for 2029, with full capability set to be reached by 2033. This program aims to enhance the defense of Canada’s Arctic region.
Denmark and Greenland – Defense Program 2024-2033: Military infrastructure in the Arctic and North Atlantic is being strengthened through the acquisition of new Arctic ships and drones, alongside the deployment of additional surveillance assets in Greenland. The Joint Arctic Command is also being bolstered to support extended operations in the area.
This isn’t just speculation. In 2021, the Pentagon adopted a new strategic plan titled ‘Regaining Arctic Dominance’. It explicitly states that the US intends to push Russia and China out of the Arctic, including through threats and the use of force.
“It appears that, distracted by the conflict in Ukraine, the Americans have seemingly pushed the Russian Arctic to the periphery of their attention for the time being. But this is a dangerous delusion. Washington never abandoned the thought of redrawing borders in that area.” 
– Aleksey Fenenko, doctor of Political Science, professor of the Faculty of World Politics, Lomonosov Moscow State University 
In addition to the natural resources and military presence in the Arctic, NATO is interested in the Northern Sea Route. This corridor connects Asia and Europe via the Arctic Ocean, providing a faster alternative to the traditional southern route through India and the Suez Canal. Considering rising piracy and the Iran crisis, navigating the icy waters has become a safer alternative.
However, due to geographical factors, the Northern Sea Route heavily relies on Russian maritime infrastructure, effectively giving Moscow control over ship and cargo movements. Consequently, Russia could dictate terms to carriers or even halt traffic entirely. Of course, NATO doesn’t want this.
Canada is expanding its fleet of icebreakers, and Norwegian spy vessel the FS Marjata is increasingly being spotted in the Barents Sea. Meanwhile, Finland is deploying American F-35A fighters just 150 km from the Russian border. The US is ramping up its military presence in Alaska, launching new NAVSTAR military satellites over the region, and ordering amphibious vehicles, which are ideally suited for operations in the north. Swedish BvS10 Beowulf amphibious tracked all-terrain vehicles are a particularly popular choice.
The Russian military is already preparing for potential conflicts in the Arctic. The Russian Army and Navy traditionally have a strong presence in the North and benefit from developed infrastructure. New missile defense systems ensure aerial security. Tor-M2 missile systems, available in various configurations, also play a significant role. The specialized variant for naval vessels, the Tor-M2KM, is particularly easy to produce in mass quantities.
Russia is ready to respond to any challenge in the Arctic; yet this crisis can still be avoided.
Meanwhile, Russia is forced to address another issue on a daily basis – though one may call it more profitable.
Arms market shakeup
The armaments and military equipment (A&ME) sector, unlike many others, boasts consistent growth in both demand and supply, expanding by 28% over four years to reach $679 billion.
In 2022, the weapons market began to shift dramatically. Sanctions caused Russian exports to plummet from 18% to 12%, with lost contracts primarily shifting to American manufacturers.
The composition of imports has also changed, becoming more unstable and concentrated in regions of existing or potential conflicts. Warsaw has emerged as the world’s leading arms purchaser, spending $33 billion on weaponry in 2023 alone. Given Poland’s status as “NATO’s vanguard,” there’s little doubt about the purpose behind this arms buildup.
Clearly, supplies to Ukraine have significantly increased, but experts point out an important detail: Western allies mainly send legacy military equipment to Kiev, which allows them to quickly modernize their own arsenals. And it’s clear who benefits most from this situation.
“After getting rid of the obsolete weapon systems supplied to Kiev as military aid, the ‘collective West’ countries began large-scale purchases of modern and more expensive arms. At the same time, the USA became the main beneficiary and recipient in this situation, having practically monopolized the arms market of NATO member states.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Since 2021, the Russian defense industry has grown approximately fivefold (with the output of some sectors increasing by six or even seven times). However, the bulk of this production is consumed by the Russian military, and exports are severely restricted due to sanctions. Nevertheless, analysts believe that after the end of the Special Military Operation, the Russian defense sector may dominate the market.
Experts note that the unique advantage of Russian weaponry developed during the Ukraine crisis is its proven adaptability to real-world battle conditions. Most Western and Asian arsenals have been tested only during military exercises, whereas new Russian models have been designed and adapted based on data gathered from the battlefield.
The primary goal of Russian defense companies was not to create a budget-friendly training model; they needed to design weapons that would prove reliable in real battle conditions. Developers also received ample feedback from soldiers who tested the weapons in battle.
Looking ahead, Saudi Arabia and India are expected to be major buyers of weapons; analysts predict these countries will focus on importing weapons in the coming years. China could also become a major buyer of Russian defense products, though Beijing consistently reduces foreign procurement in favor of satisfying demand through domestic production.
These imports extend beyond just rifles, ammunition, missiles, and aircraft. Analysts forecast that by 2030, 40% of the entire defense market will revolve around technological exchange – selling access to new developments, as well as training engineers and military personnel.
This sector is already evident in Russia’s partnership with India. For instance, Rosoboronexport is working on localizing AK-203 rifles and 125mm Mango APFSDS rounds in India, as well as upgrading T-72 tank engines at Indian facilities.
High-altitude and high-tech
When people discuss Russian military exports, they often think of tanks and Kalashnikov rifles. This makes sense, as the Russian Army is primarily viewed as a land power, and advancements in the development of rifles and tanks indeed play a significant role in its capabilities.
However, the Ukraine conflict has highlighted the crucial importance of air superiority, especially in the age of drone warfare. The Russian military employs a wide array of tools tailored for various tasks.
On the one hand, there are powerful systems like the S-400 Triumph surface-to-air missile system. Adopted by the Russian military in 2007, this system can detect aerial objects up to 600 km away and engage aerodynamic targets at a distance of up to 380 km. This system has repeatedly demonstrated its effectiveness, even though it was designed at a time when warfare was quite different.
“The S-400 Triumph is capable of fighting the entire range of modern air targets within its zone of responsibility. This isn’t only the merit of the developers but also of the General Staff which managed to predict long-term threats.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
But there are also small, mobile systems that are indispensable in urban combat and dynamic modern warfare.
A prime example is the Dzhigit support launcher. Without its Igla-S and Verba missile launchers, it looks like a sophisticated garden chair. However, fully equipped, it can fire powerful missiles in rapid succession or salvos, functioning on the ground, in buildings, or mounted on a combat vehicle. Military personnel particularly appreciate its stealth capabilities and battlefield survivability.
As for new Western radar and missile defense developments, analysts are skeptical about them. They note that while these new models often set records, they don’t necessarily enhance practical use.
“The TRLM-4D is also a leader in the number of simultaneously detected targets – 1500. However, the only thing that such a number of blips on the radar screen can give to the crew having just 24 ADMS is a sense of despair.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Uncertainty is the new certainty
Overall, Russia’s strategy can be summed up as “active preparation for the worst, moderate hope for the best.” Politicians, military leaders, and defense industry representatives understand that the Special Military Operation may continue for an extended period, while adversaries seek to exploit any weaknesses that Russia may have; therefore, new crises are almost inevitable. Recent years have demonstrated the resilience of the Russian military and economy, but that alone may not ensure success.
At the same time, analysts believe that a peaceful resolution to all issues is possible. However, it probably won’t be brought about by the goodwill of politicians, but rather by the demonstration of strength and the readiness to respond to any threats.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia resumes drone attacks on Kyiv, kills 1, injures 16, damages residential buildings
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Ukraine launches record-breaking deep strike on gas facility in Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region, over 3,000 km from border
Key developments on Sept. 9:
- Ukraine launches record-breaking deep strike on gas facility in Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region, over 3,000 km from border
- Russia resumes drone attacks on Kyiv, kills 1, injures 17, damages residential buildings
- Russia plans final test of new ballistic missile with 800-kilometer range by end of 2026, Ukraine's military intelligence says
- Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed 2, injured 3
- Ukrainian drones strike naval base, oil terminal in Russia's Novorossiysk, General Staff says
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) carried out Kyiv's deepest strike into Russia so far in the full-scale war, attacking a natural gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border on Sept. 9, the military said. 
Ukraine's General Staff announced a successful strike on the Novy Urengoy Gas Condensate Treatment Plant (GCTP) in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. 
Novy Urengoy is located in northwestern Siberia, over 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine's border. The attack marks the first time Ukrainian forces have struck Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region.
"Until today, this area was considered completely safe territory for the aggressor," the SSO wrote on Telegram.
The GCTP facility processes 19.5 million tons of crude oil and natural gas annually and produces diesel fuel and other petroleum products for Russia's military. The record-breaking strike also targeted the nearby Purovsky Gas Condensate Processing Plant.
Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point, producer of the Flamingo missile, said that its FP-1 drone model was used to carry out the strike.
Fires and smoke billowing from the plant were visible in footage shot by residents of Novy Urengoy. Monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus posted footage of the facility releasing excess gas through flare stacks to prevent explosions.
The attack was confirmed by Dmitry Artyukhov, governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.
The latest strikes demonstrate how Ukraine has increasingly extended the range of its unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in a campaign against Russia's oil infrastructure. 
Russia resumes drone attacks on Kyiv, kills 1, injures 17, damages residential buildings
Russia has resumed its relentless attacks on Kyiv with jet-powered drones, killing one person and injuring at least 17 people, including two children, in daytime strikes on the capital, local authorities said on Sept. 9.
The strike has killed one woman and injured at least 17, including two children. Six of the injured victims have been hospitalized, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in his latest update.
The attacks damaged residential buildings in two districts of Kyiv.
A Russian drone struck a nine-story residential building in the Dniprovskyi district of the capital, Klitschko said at 4:21 p.m. local time. A fire broke out in a building following the attack, and emergency services were dispatched to the scene.
Kyiv City Military Administration later said that a woman was killed as a result of the attack on the Dniprovskyi district, and three people were injured, including two children aged 15 and 16.
At around 8 a.m. local time, a Russian drone struck a 24-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district, sparking a fire on the 12th floor, Klitschko said.
Separately, a fire broke out in an open area in the Darnytskyi district following a drone crash, Klitschko said at 12:50 p.m. local time.
At 1:27 p.m. local time, the mayor added that a fire broke out in a warehouse in the Dniprovskyi district following a drone crash. Local Telegram channels published a video purportedly showing the aftermath of a Russian drone strike on a warehouse near the Comfort Town residential complex.
The air-raid alert related to drone threats has been in effect in Kyiv for more than six hours since the start of the day.

Russia plans final test of new ballistic missile with 800-kilometer range by end of 2026, Ukraine's military intelligence says
Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new, unspecified type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers (about 500 miles) by the end of 2026, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), said on Sept. 8 at a meeting with NATO member states.
The statement comes as Russia continues to target Ukrainian cities with ballistic missiles, against which Ukraine has a critically limited supply of interceptors. Kyiv relies entirely on its international partners for these systems, while its own ballistic missile programs remain under development.
Russia may intend to strike targets in western Ukraine during these missile tests, Skibitskyi said.
Moscow is seeking to ramp up both missile production and the range of its weapons, according to Skibitskyi. Russia's ultimate goal, he added, is to intensify missile and drone strikes to push Ukraine into a socioeconomic crisis.
Skibitskyi also called on Ukraine's partner countries to tighten their sanctions to cut Russia off from using foreign components, particularly in its long-range weapons.

Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed 2, injured 3
Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned an overnight Russian drone strike on the Starokozache international border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, in a Sept. 9 statement on X.
Russia struck the Starokozache border crossing overnight with drones, killing two civilians and injuring three others, Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper said. Rescuers evacuated another 16 people from a bus, according to Kiper.
Sandu also said that a Russian drone forced Moldova to close its airspace temporarily, warning that the Russian advance in Ukraine is moving further west.
"I urge more air defense support for Ukraine," Sandu said.
Earlier in the day, referring to Russian attacks on the border crossing, among others, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X that "there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes."
The Southern Regional Directorate of Ukraine's State Border Guard Service announced in a Facebook post on Sept. 9 that border operations had resumed.
"The operation of this border crossing point will help to avoid congestion and traffic build-up on other routes along the border with Moldova. At the same time, security measures for citizens crossing the border will continue to be implemented in response to any (Russian) attempts to attack border infrastructure," the statement reads.
Russia most likely wants to disrupt logistics with its attacks on border crossings, Andriy Demchenko, the spokesman for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said on national television.

Ukrainian drones strike naval base, oil terminal in Russia's Novorossiysk, General Staff says
Ukrainian drones struck Russia's Novorossiysk naval base and fuel terminal overnight on Sept. 9, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Fires were reported at the naval base and at the seaport's fuel oil terminal in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk overnight, according to the General Staff.
The extent of the damage is being assessed, the General Staff added. The Kyiv Independent couldn't independently verify the claim. The Russian Defense Ministry has not reacted to the General Staff's claim.
The Russian frigate Admiral Essen is burning as a result of the strikes, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Sept. 9. The Admiral Essen typically carries Kalibr cruise missiles, which Russia has repeatedly used to strike Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Zelensky said on Sept. 9 that a terminal used for oil shipments, facilities within the military harbor, warships, and Kalibr launchers were hit in Novorossiysk.
"We are responding to Russia's daily terrorist attacks – effectively and across virtually the entire territory," Zelensky said.
A residential building in the city was also damaged in the strikes, not injuring anybody, independent Russian news channel Astra reported, citing eyewitness footage.
Novorossiysk Mayor Andrey Kravchenko confirmed that a Ukrainian drone attack took place, saying that debris from downed drones has fallen on "the territory of enterprises" and near a residential building, without specifying at which sites.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un Publicly Praises North Korean Troops Fighting for Russia
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un used one of the country’s most important national celebrations to publicly praise troops serving abroad, further bringing Pyongyang’s direct participation in Russia’s war against Ukraine into North Korea’s official narrative.
Speaking at an assembly hall in Pyongyang on Wednesday, Sept. 9, during celebrations marking the 78th anniversary of North Korea’s founding, Kim thanked workers and soldiers for their service and expressed what state media KCNA described as “special gratitude and respect” to commanders and soldiers “participating in overseas military operations.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Neither Kim nor KCNA explicitly named Russia or Ukraine. But the reference was widely understood to concern North Korean troops sent to fight alongside Russian forces.
The wording marks another step in Pyongyang’s increasingly public embrace of a military deployment that was initially concealed by both North Korea and Russia.
From secret deployment to state honor
North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russian forces since late 2024, according to Western and South Korean officials.
South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated in February that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers had been killed or wounded. Seoul said in late August that Pyongyang was preparing for another possible troop deployment, although there were no indications that additional forces would be sent imminently.
CIA Director Ratcliffe Could Take Larger Role in Ukraine Peace Talks
Kim’s latest remarks are notable less for revealing North Korea’s involvement than for how openly it is now being presented to the domestic population.
Pyongyang has steadily transformed soldiers who fought alongside Russia from a secret expeditionary force into officially celebrated national heroes.
In April, Kim inaugurated a memorial museum in Pyongyang honoring North Korean troops killed while fighting with Russian forces in Russia’s Kursk region. The ceremony was attended by senior Russian officials, including Defense Minister Andrei Belousov.
Kim has also publicly praised the “overseas operations units” and portrayed their combat experience as proof of the strength and loyalty of the Korean People’s Army.
The founding-day address takes that process further by incorporating the overseas deployment into one of North Korea’s principal state celebrations.
North Korean shells sustain Russia’s war
Troops are only one part of Pyongyang’s contribution to Moscow’s war effort.
North Korea has become one of Russia’s largest foreign suppliers of artillery ammunition, ballistic missiles and heavy weapons.
Ukraine’s military intelligence previously told Kyiv Post that North Korea supplies an estimated 25% to 40% of Russia’s artillery ammunition needs and had delivered more than 100 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and hundreds of artillery systems.
South Korean military assessments put North Korean ammunition shipments at more than 15 million artillery rounds by early 2026. Seoul also said Pyongyang continued supplying short-range ballistic missiles.
A Reuters investigation previously found that North Korean ammunition had become crucial to maintaining Russia’s rate of artillery fire, with North Korean shells at times accounting for most of the ammunition fired by some Russian units.
What Kim gets from Moscow
The relationship is not one-sided.
South Korean intelligence assessments say Russia has provided North Korea with economic assistance and military technology in return for troops and munitions.
Seoul has previously said Moscow supplied North Korea with anti-aircraft missiles and equipment to strengthen its air defenses, while also providing technological assistance connected to Pyongyang’s military satellite program.
An international sanctions-monitoring group reported that Russia had transferred at least one Pantsir mobile air-defense system and electronic warfare equipment to North Korea, part of a military exchange that Western governments say violates UN sanctions.
For Pyongyang, the Ukraine war has therefore provided not only battlefield experience but also access to Russian technology, economic support and closer political ties with Moscow.
An alliance becoming permanent
At April’s memorial ceremony, Russian Defense Minister Belousov said Moscow and Pyongyang were preparing a military cooperation plan covering 2027 to 2031. Analysts said the agreement pointed toward institutionalizing the partnership even after fighting in Ukraine eventually ends.
On Monday, Sept. 7, the two countries opened their first road bridge across their shared border, adding a new transport route to existing rail and air connections as economic and military cooperation expands.
Two days later, Russian President Vladimir Putin used his message marking North Korea’s founding anniversary to pledge continued work with Kim to deepen their comprehensive strategic partnership.

articles.title: Zelenskyy In Canada Seeking Support Amid Destructive Russian Attacks
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Canada in an attempt to shore up support from Ukraine's allies amid destructive Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other major cities.
The Ukrainian leader arrived in the western city of Calgary late on September 9 after a visit to Norway for the funeral of King Harald V and talks on air defense support.
Zelenskyy’s plane was delayed on its way to Oslo after an alert in Moldova that a Russian drone had entered the nearby airspace.
“Canada remains one of our closest partners," Zelenskyy wrote on X after his arrival in Canada. "We value the support of the Canadian people and the decisions that help Ukraine to withstand the war and to protect our people.”
Zelenskyy's visit comes as Russia continued launching intense air attacks on Ukraine, with fresh strikes reported on September 10 in Kyiv, Dnipro, Kramatorsk, Kryviy Rih, and Mykolayiv.
In Dnipro, a major city in east-central Ukraine, Russian forces struck a food-industry facility that had already been damaged in an attack earlier in the day, killing two people and injuring five, including a child, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha.
Further east, in the Donetsk region, the number of people injured in strikes on the frontline city of Kramatorsk rose to 16, according to the head of the city's military administration. Regional authorities said Russian forces struck the city four times, with impacts recorded near educational facilities and a multistory residential building.
Russian air strikes also hit the southern port city of Mykolayiv and civilian and industrial infrastructure in the surrounding region, killing four people and injuring 19, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said on Telegram.
Moscow has stepped up its air war in recent months, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that have taken advantage of Ukraine’s dwindling air defenses.
The attacks have also targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of the upcoming winter in what appears to be part of a campaign to demoralize civilians after more than four years of war.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued its own long-range strikes inside Russia.
Overnighton September 9-10, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala in Daghestan. One person died and two were injured in another drone attack in the Voronezh region. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.
The intensifying exchange of strikes has put air defense and the protection of Ukraine's energy infrastructure at the center of Zelenskyy's trip.
Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are set to attend events in Calgary, Toronto, and North Bay, as well as a meeting with Canadian cabinet members in Banff, Alberta.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement on September 9 that that Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."
"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," the statement said, adding that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."
On his way to Canada, Zelenskyy made a stopover in Iceland, where he met with the country’s foreign minister, Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir. At the center of the conversation was protecting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and strengthening its air defenses.
With fighting remaining intense, Zelenskyy's diplomatic push comes amid renewed efforts to find a path toward ending the war.
After months of stalled talks on ending the conflict, hopes have been raised by a flurry of diplomatic moves.
Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump on September 8, a conversation that the Kremlin described as "constructive and quite frank."
"We had a great conversation. He [Putin] is wanting to make a deal, and if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump told reporters on September 9, adding, "These are two people that are tired of fighting."
Putin has given no sign he is ready for a cease-fire unless Kyiv makes major concessions it has rejected, including ceding territory in the eastern Donbas region that Russian troops have been unable to take by force.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov suggested that Putin told Trump that an immediate cease-fire could be secured if the United States would end all support for Kyiv.
On September 9, the Financial Times reported that CIA director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a bigger role in US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, citing unnamed sources the paper said indicated the roles of US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner might be scaled back to make room for Ratcliffe.
In a post on X, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly called the FT story "incorrect and ridiculous." CIA spokeswoman Liz Lyons, also on X, wrote: "This reporting is false."
Witkoff and Kushner have led the talks with Moscow and Kyiv for the last year and a half.
According to the FT, officials close to Ratcliffe have told their European peers that in addition to maintaining contact with intelligence agencies in both Russia and Ukraine, the CIA director would now play a more active role in shuttle diplomacy.

articles.title: US-Israeli arms firm Covenant to build cruise missiles in Germany
articles.body:
By Carsten Hoffmann, dpa.
Berlin (dpa) – US-Israeli defence contractor Covenant plans to set up a production facility for long-range cruise missiles in the German state of Saxony, the company said on Wednesday.
“We will be producing roughly 1,000 in our first year and then scaling to 5,000,” Covenant chief Abigail Denburg said, outlining the company’s “target for annual production.”
Production of the Anthem cruise missile for European customers is to begin next year at the facility to be set up near Leipzig.
It comes as Germany and other European states are in the process of massively ramping up their defence industry in response to a growing threat from Russia.
“When you look at our adversaries, you see thousands of hardened targets, beyond the range of current capabilities,” said Michael Kaufman, Covenant’s co-founder and chief executive said in a press release.
“Anthem was built to credibly hold those targets at risk in a prolonged conflict. If our stockpiles run thin, so does our deterrence.”
Anthem missiles can carry a 200-kilogram warhead and are designed for precision strikes deep within enemy territory. Covenant has not commented on media reports suggesting Anthem’s range is 1,500 kilometres.
The company says it plans to offer the weapons system at a significantly lower price than those currently available on the market. Covenant said Anthem would cost a six-figure sum, meaning less than $1 million, while other weapons systems of this kind typically cost several million dollars per unit.
Mass production has military significance and is intended to improve customers’ staying power. Denburg said: “Deterrence is a calculation by the enemy and that calculation changes when you have extensive weapons arsenals. If you can reach a target and strike once, that does not necessarily deter the enemy.”
Covenant is already in talks with the Bundeswehr and the procurement agency, according to dpa information, though this has not been officially confirmed.
Denburg said, without directly referring to Germany, that there was already a production contract for deliveries from Germany starting in the first quarter of 2027.
“This European customer will decide for themselves when they want to make this public,” she said.
Company raises more than $250 million
Covenant was founded in 2024 and is headquartered in Washington. The company said it has raised more than $250 million from investors in three funding rounds.
Backers include Founders Fund, which counts Peter Thiel among its co-founders. He is known for his libertarian and right-wing conservative positions, his closeness to US President Donald Trump and his criticism of liberal democracies.
Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the Social Democrats has in the past “explicitly” shared concerns about Thiel. There has also been public discussion of whether new dependencies could arise or whether the risk is greater of finding oneself without sufficiently stocked ammunition depots in a crisis.
Covenant said German retired Lieutenant General Andreas Marlow is an adviser. He was deputy inspector of the army until 2025 and from 2022 also led the EU training mission for the Ukrainian armed forces.
A long-range missile programme produced in Europe was “the missing piece of the puzzle in our deterrence architecture”, Marlow was quoted as saying.
Germany and its European NATO allies are currently seeking to procure long-range weapons systems as a response to the Russian threat as well as develop their own. At the NATO summit in Ankara, the German government agreed with the United States to buy US Tomahawk cruise missiles.
At the beginning of September, the German navy successfully completed a previously secret test of the Israeli missile system Lora, a ballistic missile. Germany already has the Taurus cruise missile made by defence company MBDA but it is far from being mass-produced.
European NATO states also do not yet have their own intermediate-range weapons. In the medium term, several allies want to procure their own weapons system for long-range precision strikes. To that end, the Elsa project, the European Long-Range Strike Approach, was launched in 2024 at the NATO summit in Washington.
Source: dpa.com

articles.title: Iran attacks Hormuz ships, Trump says war will end in November
articles.body:
- Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blocked for months.
-The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States have sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
-Donald Trump predicted that the war with Iran will end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November but said that he didn't expect the price of oil to come down before then.
-Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has visited Jabal al-Shaikh (Mount Hermon) in Syria and said that the Iranian government was very close to being overthrown.
-Yemen's Houthi rebels have reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes days after renewed conflict broke out in the country.
Iran condemned on Wednesday a resolution adopted by the United Nations atomic watchdog's board of governors which referred the Islamic republic to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance".
"This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis and will not bring any results," Iran's representative to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Reza Najafi, told state television.
Saudi Arabia reports fresh Houthi attacks on kingdom's south
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen on Wednesday said the Iran-backed Houthis had launched fresh attacks on the kingdom's south, after the rebels launched an offensive seeking to control the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The coalition's spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a statement the Houthis had "launched several ballistic missiles and drones toward the cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Jizan", without mentioning any casualties as a result of the attacks.
Iran attacks more than a dozen vessels in Strait of Hormuz
Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.
The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States have sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 "non-compliant vessels" that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said "several" vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region".
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran's Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" on Wednesday, saying that exact coordinates will be announced later.
"If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The IAEA board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance" in a diplomatic move to pile pressure on the Islamic republic.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged to be given access.
The resolution was adopted by 23 votes in favour, three votes against and eight abstentions, two diplomats told AFP. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
It "requests the (IAEA) director general to report" Iran to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations.
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move is seen as largely symbolic as Iran allies China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against Tehran.
Syria condemns Netanyahu 'illegal' entry into its territory
Syria condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's entry into its territory after he visited Israeli troops stationed in southern Syria on Wednesday, calling the move "provocative and a blatant violation" of its sovereignty.
"The Syrian Arab Republic strongly condemns the illegal entry of Israeli occupation Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu into Syrian territory and his tour of Mount Hermon, in a provocative move and a blatant violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic and of international law," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Trump says Iran war will end "immediately after" US midterms
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday predicted that the war with Iran will end "immediately after" the U.S. midterm elections in November because Tehran was trying to influence the vote but would not be able to hold out more in the face of U.S. economic pressure.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," he told reporters before departing for the Republican National Convention in Dallas.
Trump's war with Iran has recently entered its seventh month with no immediate end in sight. On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers. The renewed fighting sent the price of oil surging with benchmark Brent crude future breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
Trump's approval ratings recently sank to a record low due to frustration from voters over the Iran war and deepening cost-of-living crisis. Midterm elections, due to be held on November 3 this year, are typically a referendum on the occupant of the White House.
Oil prices would also come down right after the election, Trump said on Wednesday, once the war is over, while acknowledging diplomatic talks are still a possibility but not preferred.
"Yes, a negotiation could possible happen, but it's not something we're looking at," Trump said.

articles.title: The US-South Korea-Japan wargames offer a glimpse of Washington’s real plan for Asia
articles.body:
The US-South Korea-Japan wargames offer a glimpse of Washington’s real plan for Asia
The joint military exercises now underway between the United States, South Korea, and Japan are a clear signal that Washington is still moving ahead with the long-term project of building its alliances and partnerships in Asia into a tight military-political structure, despite leadership changes in both the US and South Korea. The current Washington administration, however, isn’t above using political leverage to keep Seoul in line.
The joint exercises of South Korea, Japan, and the US became a regular occurrence already under Biden, and they now serve as a kind of answer to the question of how far the course toward building a Washington-Tokyo-Seoul military-political alliance – which was very clearly visible under Biden and South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol – is continuing under the new presidents.
Many people assumed that if Biden was actively driving this integration and the Washington Declaration had already been signed, then Trump, supposedly an isolationist, would slow it down or even reverse it.
But no – what we see is that although the pace may have slowed somewhat, the overall direction remains the same. That is quite important, because talk of a possible ‘Asian NATO’ has not gone away.
It is still not entirely clear what shape such a configuration could take. On the one hand, there is AUKUS. On the other, there is an increasingly active system of military alignments involving the US, Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines.
Some American strategists have also begun speaking in this same context about changing South Korea’s place in US strategic planning. This is important, because historically the joint exercises of the US and South Korea were directed specifically against North Korea – although in practice those exercises were often offensive in character, something the DPRK has constantly pointed out.
Practicing preventive strikes, river crossings, and similar operations was always part of the scenario. Formally, everything began as a response to a North Korean attack, but the script usually moved quickly toward a triumphant counteroffensive.
It is entirely possible that the trilateral exercises of the US, South Korea, and Japan are oriented not only toward containing North Korea, but also toward containing China – and more broadly toward integrating and coordinating three countries that the Americans are trying to turn into a military-political bloc. That process has never been easy.
The problem is that while Washington-Tokyo and Washington-Seoul ties were relatively straightforward and did not suffer deeply from historical baggage, relations between Seoul and Tokyo have long been much more difficult. It was hard to establish any real parallel cooperation between them despite active American pressure, because anti-Japanese sentiment in South Korea was, until recently, one of the important pillars of national political identity, especially under Democratic Party governments.
That began to change with the arrival of conservative president Yoon Suk Yeol, who for the first time turned the wheel 180 degrees and openly argued that, in present conditions, Washington and Tokyo should stop relitigating the past and instead think about alliance in the present and jointly forecast the future.
Naturally, this caused outrage among the Democrats, then in opposition. There is no need to repeat all the insults with which Lee Jae Myung attacked Yoon – accusing him of groveling before Japan, forgetting the horrors of colonial rule, and so on.
But once Democratic Party politician Lee Jae Myung himself became president – a man who had once positioned himself as the leftmost of the nationalists and populists – he dramatically changed course.
Suddenly, the Democratic Party became effectively center-right, and Lee’s line can now broadly be described as pro-American, at least in public terms.
He openly said that the old formula of “security with America, economics with China” no longer works – that South Korea is now oriented only toward the United States. Of course, this does not mean a complete break with China. He wanted Seoul to be a bridge between Washington and Beijing.
But overall, Lee is moving in the American wake, and one important sign of that is that there has been no reversal on the Japanese track.
Lee effectively stated that all agreements signed under Yoon would be honored, because even if part of the Korean public does not accept them, they were promises made in the name of the nation.
The culmination of this moment was the joint musical performance by Lee Jae Myung and Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi.
Of course, there are still occasional flare-ups, because there cannot not be. For example, Japan’s defense minister skipped a defense forum in Seoul because of another controversy linked to a donation to Yasukuni Shrine, which South Korea sees as a symbol of Japan’s past militarism and colonialism. But overall, the level of integration is much higher, and it continues the same direction set under the conservatives.
The current trilateral exercise is a visible marker of that course.
The most interesting point emerges when we compare these three-country exercises, which are proceeding more or less on schedule and without major problems, with the recent US-South Korea exercises, which were conducted in a reduced format under very revealing circumstances.
Those exercises were supposed to proceed normally. But the day before they began, Trump suddenly posted on social media that the drills were expensive and sent bad signals to North Korea, and that he had therefore instructed the defense secretary to scale them down. Then he added that he had asked the South Korean president to join us in our struggle with Iran, and Lee refused.
This creates a very clear picture. Trump, in effect, took revenge for Seoul’s refusal – and, judging by subsequent developments, may even have forced President Lee into taking some limited part in the US confrontation with Iran after all.
Why did Lee refuse in the first place?
First, South Korea’s relations with Iran are not especially bad. Second, for domestic audiences, despite his pro-American course, Lee still wants to preserve the image of a populist who occasionally pushes back against the US, pursues an independent policy, and certainly is not going to send South Korean troops to fight for American interests – especially in a conflict that would be highly risky and politically toxic.
During the Iraq war of 2003-2008, South Korean troops were largely deployed to guard South Korean engineers working on oil fields. The surrounding territory was generally controlled by pro-American Kurdish forces, so the South Koreans spent much of their time sitting tight, occasionally joining mop-up operations.
Joining the Iran war would be very different. Here, regardless of what they were doing, they would have to defend themselves against Iranian missiles and drones – and it is far from clear how effectively they could do so. And any casualties, in today’s media and political climate, would carry obvious domestic political and reputational consequences.
There is another equally important factor. South Korea is actively trying to claim a leading place in the global arms market. Seoul has been repeatedly told, implicitly or otherwise, that its weapons would sell even better if they proved themselves in actual combat, ideally against Russian or Chinese systems. But this logic cuts both ways. What happens if the South Korean military, which has not fought a major war in generations, or South Korean weapons systems, which have not undergone a serious real-combat test, perform badly?
That is one more reason why Lee Jae Myung refused to participate in the American war against Iran. And it is also why Trump trapped him so effectively in a contradiction between his promises.
On the one hand, Lee has repeatedly spoken of the need to draw North Korea into dialogue. To pursue that goal, one would logically need to reduce military activity, including the very exercises that North Korea constantly condemns as rehearsals for aggression.
On the other hand, because North Korea says it will not negotiate with Seoul regardless of whether conservatives or Democrats are in power – on the grounds that South Korea lacks real agency – the more realistic promise from Lee’s side has been the restoration of wartime operational control.
At present, if a major war breaks out, South Korea’s armed forces do not answer directly to the South Korean president but to the so-called Combined Forces Command – effectively, to the Americans.
This arrangement was originally created to prevent South Korea’s first president, Syngman Rhee, from dragging the peninsula into a second Korean War. Today, however, it is widely viewed in South Korea as a limitation on sovereignty. Lee Jae Myung loudly promised that by the end of his presidential term, in 2030, he would restore this operational control.
But there is a catch.
For that to happen, South Korean generals have to show that they can solve complex strategic tasks as effectively as their American counterparts. And for that, regular, large-scale exercises are necessary. By reducing the scale of the exercises, Trump struck directly at that ambition.
Lee was, of course, forced to put on a brave face and say that the reduction of the drills would indeed send the right signal to North Korea.
But in reality, the far more important and painful consequence was that the exercises would no longer provide the full opportunity to rehearse what is required for the transfer of operational control.
And after that, as we can now see, Seoul’s position on assisting the US against Iran shifted in a direction more convenient for Washington.
That is why this matters. North Korea, naturally, criticized both the US-South Korea drills and the trilateral exercises with Japan. But what is crucial here is this: the bilateral drills were cut back, while the trilateral drills continue just fine. And that says a great deal about Washington’s real goals in the region.

articles.title: Ukraine nearly out of F-16 missiles used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones – The Economist
articles.body:
Ukraine nearly out of F-16 missiles used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones – The Economist
Ukraine is nearly out of US-made AIM-120 and AIM-9 missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which are used to intercept Russian cruise missiles and new jet-powered drones.
Source: The Economist
Details: Ukrainian air defence lacks sufficient missiles to intercept the new Russian Geran-4 and Geran-5 UAVs, which can fly at speeds of up to 600 km/h, while Russia is producing around 3,000 of them a month.
Their turbojet engines are mostly supplied from China, although some components are manufactured directly in Russia using smuggled Western 3D printers. Alongside the larger Banderol drones, these UAVs are increasingly resembling inexpensive cruise missiles, leaving F-16 fighter jets critically short of AIM-120 and AIM-9 missiles to intercept them.
Ukraine is developing its own interceptor drones to counter Russian UAVs, but the situation with defence against ballistic weapons is even more difficult.
Ukraine's stockpile of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems is now also nearly depleted. New large-scale deliveries from the US are unlikely because American stockpiles have been depleted by the war with Iran.
Meanwhile, Russia has increased ballistic missile production to around 100 a month: 60 Iskander-M missiles and 40 RM-48U missiles.
There are some expectations surrounding the planned delivery of several older French-Italian SAMP/T air defence batteries, along with Aster missiles, to Ukraine by the end of 2026. Next year, Ukraine is due to receive eight of the latest SAMP/T NG systems.
Quote: "The new system has a more advanced radar for the final stage of guidance and can handle multiple manoeuvring ballistic missiles, such as Russia's Iskander-M. The Aster has a warhead that explodes next to the incoming missile, rather than the PAC-3's 'hit-to-kill' impact. But French army sources claim it outperforms the Patriot in some respects. It is also less than half the US$7m price of the latest export version of the PAC-3."
Details: Germany plans to produce up to 200 less powerful PAC-2 missiles a year under licence, some of which could be supplied to Ukraine with the agreement of NATO countries.
A joint European-Ukrainian project called Freyja is intended to fundamentally change the situation. Its ambition has been compared with that of a "moonshot" programme. Its goal is to provide Ukraine and its European allies with a significantly cheaper and higher-volume alternative to PAC-3 missiles compatible with NATO-standard radars and data-link systems.
The planned interceptor is based on the Ukrainian FP-7 short-range ballistic missile. Sensors, guidance and control systems will be supplied by 12 European defence companies, including France's Thales, Italy's Leonardo, Germany's Diehl and Sweden's Saab.
