articles.title: Trump was warned: Iran war could last until end of his term in 2029
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump made an intriguing statement Wednesday night, saying the war with Iran would end “immediately” after the midterm elections, which will be held November 3. But The Wall Street Journal reported overnight between Wednesday and Thursday that senior officials had warned him the conflict could instead continue until the end of his term in 2029.
U.S. officials who spoke with the newspaper said the warning had also been voiced by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who cautioned in closed-door discussions that Tehran could withstand U.S. pressure, both from the blockade and from “other military tactics” — a scenario that could prolong the confrontation beyond the inauguration of the next president in January 2029.
The report was published hours after Trump’s surprising declaration, which came after he was asked about the surge in oil prices following the renewed escalation with the Islamic Republic, as crude oil prices crossed the $100-a-barrel mark Wednesday. Trump said the price would fall — but only after the midterms.
His remarks came against the backdrop of assessments previously voiced by commentators and Israeli officials that after the elections — once the political pressure on Trump to avoid price increases that could hurt Republicans’ chances of preserving their narrow majorities in both houses of Congress has eased — the president may resume intensive military action against Iran.
Speaking with reporters before departing for a Republican conference in Dallas ahead of the elections, in which control of Congress is at stake, Trump was asked why he believed the war would end immediately afterward. In response, he attacked Democrats hoping to regain control of the House and Senate.
“Because they [the Iranians] can’t hold on anymore. They’re desperate to try to influence the election, so that we get a nice, weak group of people in there [meaning the Democrats], who will leave them alone and allow them to get their nuclear weapon. All they want is a nuclear weapon, and if they get a nuclear weapon, the whole world will be in very serious trouble.”
Before boarding his new Air Force One — the aircraft he received as a gift from Qatar — Trump was forced to wait about 10 minutes while the plane’s emergency slide was inspected after it deployed in front of photographers covering the president.
Trump was asked about it and said “they were just doing a check.”
“They checked it earlier, and they wanted to make sure. I assume they’ve already put it back up, they wanted to see that everything works perfectly,” he said.
Asked whether it was safe for him to board the aircraft — against the backdrop of the unusual incident in July in which he was secretly transferred by truck from the Qatari aircraft to an alternate plane in Turkey, out of concern over an Iranian attack — he replied: “Yes, otherwise I wouldn’t be on it.”
Oil prices climbed about 3% Thursday following the renewed escalation with Iran, which is believed to be seeking to intensify the confrontation in an effort to raise the price Trump pays for the blockade he is imposing on it, as he tries to force Tehran into submission by worsening its economic distress.
Iran has escalated its recent actions and, according to reports, is now trying, unlike in its previous attacks during the war, to hit U.S. warships as much as possible. In recent days it has fired ballistic missiles at them several times, so far without success.
The United States has vowed to respond to each such attack by destroying Iranian oil tankers in retaliation and on Wednesday struck five such tankers, disabling them, after attacking three more tankers on Saturday.
Iran responded by launching 20 missiles at U.S. targets in Jordan, and the interceptions over Jordan were visible from Israel.
The Jordanian military said it intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles, and U.S. officials told The New York Times on Thursday evening that “minimal” damage had been caused to U.S. military equipment at a base in the kingdom. The officials added that there were no known casualties, though soldiers could report injuries in the coming days.
Historic move at IAEA, with Putin and China providing protective umbrella
Meanwhile, for the first time in 20 years, the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) voted Thursday evening to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council after determining that Tehran was violating its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
The move is not expected to have practical consequences such as new sanctions, because any such proposal would almost certainly be blocked by Iran’s allies China and Russia, which hold veto power on the Security Council. But referring the issue to the U.N.’s highest body is viewed as a diplomatic escalation by the West, and Tehran has threatened to respond.
The proposal to refer Iran to the Security Council was led by the United States, Britain, France and Germany and was approved by 23 of the IAEA Board of Governors’ 35 member states.
According to reports, only three countries — Russia, China and Niger — voted against the measure at IAEA headquarters in Vienna. Eight abstained and one did not participate in the vote.
The move is a direct continuation of a previous IAEA resolution from June 12, 2025 — one day before Israel launched Operation Rising Lion against Iran, at the end of which the United States bombed Iran’s main nuclear facilities — which determined that Iran was violating its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Those violations relate to IAEA investigations that have been underway for years into traces of uranium found at several undeclared nuclear sites in Iran. The investigations began following the Mossad’s exposure of Iran’s “nuclear archive” in 2018, and the suspicion is that the sites were previously used for Iran’s military nuclear program, a program Tehran officially denies ever having operated.
It was previously reported that the program was shut down in 2003, but Israel has accused Iran of continuing it afterward.
Iran has previously expressed anger over IAEA resolutions against it, claiming they effectively provided Israel with a pretext to attack, and dramatically curtailed cooperation with nuclear inspectors, who have not been permitted to visit the nuclear sites since they were bombed last June.
Iran’s refusal to cooperate with the IAEA and allow its inspectors access to nuclear facilities has now become a new focal point of friction, leading to another resolution against the Islamic Republic in June this year, in which the Board of Governors demanded that Iran reveal what happened to its enriched uranium stockpile.
Before Operation Rising Lion, Iran had 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% — very close to the 90% level required for nuclear weapons — an amount estimated to be sufficient for at least 10 nuclear bombs.
It was previously reported that a large portion of the enriched material had been buried deep underground near the nuclear facility struck in Isfahan. But Iran has not allowed the IAEA to access that site or the other facilities attacked, Natanz and Fordow, where enriched uranium may also have been buried.
The question of the enriched uranium has remained a central issue since the outbreak of Operation Lion’s Roar at the end of February this year, and the fact that it remains deep underground in Iran is seen as a significant failure to achieve one of the war’s main objectives — destroying the Iranian nuclear threat.
The concern is that Iran could retrieve the material from underground and, relatively simply and quickly, enrich it to weapons-grade levels at a secret location — perhaps the facility at “Pickaxe Mountain,” which has been dug to great depth and may therefore be protected from bunker-busting bombs.
Although the referral to the Security Council is not expected to have practical consequences, Iran threatened Monday to retaliate against such a decision.
So far, the ayatollah regime has not announced any concrete response, but Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi criticized the move.
“They attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, which are under safeguards, disrupt the proper verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution at the Board of Governors. Through such maneuvers, you will not be able to compensate for the failure of your policies and actions, nor achieve any results at the Security Council.”
A statement issued Thursday evening by Iran’s mission to the IAEA also made no mention of any retaliatory action.
“Once again, a political resolution concerning Iran has been adopted by the IAEA Board of Governors without consensus,” the Iranian delegation to the international nuclear agency said.
“The current situation was created solely by the criminal acts of aggression of the United States and the Israeli regime. The delusional goal of the United States, to force the great Iranian people into ‘surrender’ and plunder its oil, will never be realized,” the statement added.

articles.title: North Korean leader salutes ‘overseas’ troops
articles.body:
This picture taken on February 25, 2026 and released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on February 26, 2026 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un (R) and his daughter Kim Ju Ae attending the military parade to commemorate the 9th Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea at Kim Il-sung Square in Pyongyang. (AFP Photo/KCNA via KNS )
Leader Kim Jong Un praised troops in “overseas military operations” during a speech marking North Korea’s founding anniversary, state media reported on Sept. 10, an apparent nod to Pyongyang’s assistance in Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, North Korea has become a key ally of the Kremlin, sending troops to support Moscow’s war effort in return for economic benefits and military technology, analysts say.
During comments marking North Korea’s Sept. 9, 1948 founding, Kim hailed overseas compatriots but paid special tribute to troops deployed abroad, the official Korean Central News Agency reported on Sept. 10.
“I also extend my special gratitude and profound respect to the commanders and soldiers of our military participating in overseas military operations,” said Kim on the nation’s the 78th anniversary.
“Our ideal is being realized rapidly thanks to patriotism, voluntary service and devoted contributions by all citizens praying for the country’s prosperity,” he added.
According to South Korea, some 2,000 North Korean troops have been killed in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine claimed that Moscow had launched North Korean ballistic missiles in a strike that killed at least nine people and wounded dozens.
Kiev has also said that up to 50,000 North Korean troops are due to deploy to Russia, although it has provided no evidence to back the claim or a timeframe for the deployment.
In making the claim, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky asked Seoul to supply air defense systems to protect against Russian missiles, a request that has gone unanswered by the South.

articles.title: Timeline: How a Russian drone nearly hit Zelenskyy's plane in Moldova
articles.body:
Russia’s latest drone incursion into Moldova and NATO airspace comes as Moscow increasingly deploys jet-powered attack drones, blurring the line between traditional UAVs and low-cost cruise missiles and making them much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was preparing to leave Chișinău for Oslo on Tuesday afternoon when Moldova’s military detected an unmanned aerial vehicle in the country’s airspace.
What initially appeared to be another Russian drone incursion took on greater significance the following day, when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre revealed that Zelenskyy’s plane had almost been hit by a drone.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in,” Støre told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
The timeline shows how the events unfolded.
Moldovan military first detected an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle at 4:20 pm EEST (3:20 CEST).
Moldovan officials confirmed to Euronews that the country’s airspace was closed shortly after 4:30 pm.
“The airspace was closed to protect the aircraft flying over Moldova at the time - three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result.”
By 4:37 pm, Romania’s Defence Ministry said the drone crossed into Romanian — and therefore NATO — airspace.
Two minutes later two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced Air Policing mission took off to monitor it.
The jets did not intercept the drone. Romanian radar continued to track it until 5:02 pm, when contact was lost.
Five minutes later at 5:07 pm the drone was detected again over Moldova, where it later crashed about 25 km east of the Romanian border.
According to Moldovan officials, the flight restrictions were lifted after 5:20 pm, when authorities confirmed the drone had come down and exploded near Mihăilenii Vechi, in the Râșcani district, about 160 km from Chișinău International Airport.
“For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took off from Chișinău International Airport later than scheduled," officials said.
According to monitoring channels, Zelenskyy’s plane took off from Chișinău around 5:57 pm.
For much of Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine that began in early 2022, Zelenskyy has travelled abroad primarily through Poland, with Rzeszów serving as a regular departure point.
In recent months, however, his presidential aircraft has also begun using Chișinău more frequently for foreign trips.
What type of drone was it?
The exact model of the drone involved in Moldova and Romania has not been officially established.
Ukrainian open-source monitoring channels identified it as a Geran-4, one of Russia’s newer jet-powered attack drones.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 are among the newest additions to Russia’s expanding Geran family, although they differ significantly in design and capabilities.
The Geran-4 has a wingspan of about three metres and is roughly 3.5 metres long. Its maximum take-off weight is around 450 kilograms.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Geran-4 can reach speeds of up to 500 km/h and carry a warhead weighing between 50 and 90 kilograms.
Russia has recently stepped up its use of jet-powered drones, including in complex barrages alongside ballistic and cruise missiles designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.
Their speed makes them much harder to intercept than conventional Shahed-type drones, particularly for the mobile fire groups and other relatively inexpensive systems Ukraine has relied on to counter slower-moving UAVs.
Ukraine is instead forced to use scarce and considerably more expensive air-defence missiles against the faster threats, putting additional pressure on already limited interceptor stocks.
Several Ukrainian companies have reportedly begun testing missiles specifically designed to shoot down the new jet-powered Geran models.

articles.title: Timeline: How a Russian drone nearly hit Zelenskyy's plane in Moldova
articles.body:
Russia’s latest drone incursion into Moldova and NATO airspace comes as Moscow increasingly deploys jet-powered attack drones, blurring the line between traditional UAVs and low-cost cruise missiles and making them much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was preparing to leave Chișinău for Oslo on Tuesday afternoon when Moldova’s military detected an unmanned aerial vehicle in the country’s airspace.
What initially appeared to be another Russian drone incursion took on greater significance the following day, when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre revealed that Zelenskyy’s plane had almost been hit by a drone.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in,” Støre told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
The timeline shows how the events unfolded.
Moldovan military first detected an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle at 4:20 pm EEST (3:20 CEST).
Moldovan officials confirmed to Euronews that the country’s airspace was closed shortly after 4:30 pm.
“The airspace was closed to protect the aircraft flying over Moldova at the time - three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result.”
By 4:37 pm, Romania’s Defence Ministry said the drone crossed into Romanian — and therefore NATO — airspace.
Two minutes later two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced Air Policing mission took off to monitor it.
The jets did not intercept the drone. Romanian radar continued to track it until 5:02 pm, when contact was lost.
Five minutes later at 5:07 pm the drone was detected again over Moldova, where it later crashed about 25 km east of the Romanian border.
According to Moldovan officials, the flight restrictions were lifted after 5:20 pm, when authorities confirmed the drone had come down and exploded near Mihăilenii Vechi, in the Râșcani district, about 160 km from Chișinău International Airport.
“For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took off from Chișinău International Airport later than scheduled," officials said.
According to monitoring channels, Zelenskyy’s plane took off from Chișinău around 5:57 pm.
For much of Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine that began in early 2022, Zelenskyy has travelled abroad primarily through Poland, with Rzeszów serving as a regular departure point.
In recent months, however, his presidential aircraft has also begun using Chișinău more frequently for foreign trips.
What type of drone was it?
The exact model of the drone involved in Moldova and Romania has not been officially established.
Ukrainian open-source monitoring channels identified it as a Geran-4, one of Russia’s newer jet-powered attack drones.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 are among the newest additions to Russia’s expanding Geran family, although they differ significantly in design and capabilities.
The Geran-4 has a wingspan of about three metres and is roughly 3.5 metres long. Its maximum take-off weight is around 450 kilograms.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Geran-4 can reach speeds of up to 500 km/h and carry a warhead weighing between 50 and 90 kilograms.
Russia has recently stepped up its use of jet-powered drones, including in complex barrages alongside ballistic and cruise missiles designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.
Their speed makes them much harder to intercept than conventional Shahed-type drones, particularly for the mobile fire groups and other relatively inexpensive systems Ukraine has relied on to counter slower-moving UAVs.
Ukraine is instead forced to use scarce and considerably more expensive air-defence missiles against the faster threats, putting additional pressure on already limited interceptor stocks.
Several Ukrainian companies have reportedly begun testing missiles specifically designed to shoot down the new jet-powered Geran models.

articles.title: Zelenskyy’s big bet: Ukraine can outlast Russia
articles.body:
A helicopter flies past smoke billowing from a Russian e-commerce warehouse near St. Petersburg after a Ukrainian drone strike on July 24, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is gambling that taking the fight deeper into Russia will put enough pressure on Vladimir Putin to force him to get serious about peace talks.
For much of the war, the Russian president has been able to shield ordinary Russians from the worst of the conflict. The Ukrainian leader is now trying to break that insulation — disrupting air travel and striking refineries, factories, warehouses and other targets deep inside Russia.
The logic is brutal but simple: Raise the economic and political cost of the war for Russians faster than Putin can raise the military and civilian costs for Ukrainians with his escalating air assaults.
Advertisement
With that aim in mind, Ukraine mounted in August one of its heaviest waves of strikes on Russia since the war started more than four years ago.
The campaign expanded quickly to target not just conventional military facilities but also oil refineries, factories, and the vast warehouses of Russia’s online retail behemoths, Wildberries and Ozon. And ordinary Russians have expressed frustration at the domestic fuel shortages, the disruption of air travel and the upending of Russian e-commerce. Ukraine has scaled up domestic production of its attack drones as it tries to make the war unsustainable for Moscow.
But there is little evidence yet that the disruption poses any serious threat to Putin’s hold on power. Coups have been forecast before. European spymasters, Ukrainian officials and Russian exiles have issued numerous predictions that Putin’s days are numbered, that Russians will turn on him or he’ll be ousted in a Kremlin uprising by oligarchs and Russia’s elite.
Nonetheless, Putin has endured.
What Ukraine’s air campaign does appear to have done is make the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore. That’s significant given how the Kremlin has succeeded largely in silencing public dissent and has Russian-based media on a tight leash.
“I don’t think the authorities’ approval rating can fail to decline when people go outside and see a huge column of smoke rising over the city, or when they arrive to a gas station and there’s no fuel, while on television they’re being told that Russia is a great oil power,” said Ian Matveev, a Russian political analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny.
Advertisement
Matveev added that Zelenskyy’s air campaign has exposed how the Russian military can’t fully protect the country.
That was underscored in May when the Kremlin reluctantly pared back the Victory Day jamboree celebrating the Red Army’s defeat of Nazi Germany.
Shortly after, in June, Ukraine repeatedly struck Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, including around Moscow. In July, Ukrainian drones reached the Omsk refinery in Siberia, Russia’s largest, about 2,700 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory, reportedly using an upgraded drone.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrives to attend the pared-back Victory Day military parade at Red Square in Moscow on May 9, 2026. | Pool photo by Alexander Kazakov via AFP/Getty Images
By then, Ukrainian strikes had hit many of Russia’s major refineries, oil terminals and fuel-storage facilities. At the same time, Ukraine launched an operation against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black and Azov seas, targeting more than 200 vessels, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Russian media has reported on the impact of the strikes at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses on small businesses, with sellers of clothing and electronics lamenting that they’ve lost years of work, even their livelihoods. Pro-war military bloggers have not held back on their criticism, faulting the Russian armed forces for ineffectiveness.
But are these complaints enough to alarm Putin and prompt him to stop the war?
Advertisement
The strikes are clearly embarrassing the Russian autocrat, said John Lough, a former NATO official who is now at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a think tank founded by exiled Russian businessman and prominent opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
“These attacks are damaging for Putin — more in terms of his credibility with the elites than with the population at large,” Lough said. “They can see increasingly that the war is not winnable on the terms advertised and that he has damaged rather than improved Russia’s security.”
Lough said he doesn’t see a revolution or coup around the corner. “But if the fuel problems continue and more warehouses burn down, there will be more questions from the population about how long this is all going to last and why it started in the first place,” he added.
To ramp up the pressure, Zelenskyy and his tacticians are now eager to make Russia’s commercial airspace increasingly difficult to use.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” the Ukrainian leader said last week. He warned foreign airlines to stay clear as the skies over Russia would become increasingly unsafe because of Ukraine’s drone operations. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he added.
Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat, described Ukraine’s air campaign as “ very, very successful.” But Ukraine’s position as it enters into another wartime winter is more desperate than Russia’s, he feared.
Advertisement
“I think Kyiv is terrified about going into another winter, and this time without any means to defend itself against ramped up Russia’s ballistic missile attacks,” he said.
Putin is unlikely to have missed that vulnerability. Nor have Ukraine’s allies.
During a meeting with Zelenskyy and top security officials from Britain, Germany and France last week, much of the focus was not on the peace deal recently proposed by a U.S. delegation fresh from a visit to Moscow.
It was, according to a senior Ukrainian official who spoke to the AP, on “how to get through the winter.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Arctic attack extends Kyiv’s strike reach into Russian gas heartland
articles.body:
- 
  Ukraine’s special forces said they attacked two crucial natural gas plants in the Arctic about 3,000km (1,800 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border. Both lie in the heartland of Russian gas production: Novy Urengoy is Russia’s unofficial gas capital, located in the Yamal-Nenets region in north-western Siberia. The other plant is in the Purovsky district of Yamal-Nenets. A Ukrainian statement described the two plants as “crucial for the gas condensate industry … Previously, this was considered an absolutely safe area away from the front for the aggressor.”
- 
  Fire Point, a Ukrainian company that makes deep-strike weapons including the Flamingo cruise missile, posted: “Guess who just travelled over 3,300km and successfully hit the target?” Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, praised the strikes for their effect on the Russian economy. The Russian regional governor confirmed the attack and said the damage was being assessed. About 80% of all natural gas in Russia is extracted in the Yamalo-Nenets region, according to the Interfax news agency.
- 
  Ukrainian forces also targeted Novorossiysk, a Black Sea port in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The attack hit the Russian naval base, including a terminal used to load oil, military port facilities, and warships carrying cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said.
- 
  Ukraine and neighbouring Moldova played down reports that a plane carrying Volodymyr Zelenskyy was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo. In fact, Zelenskyy’s departure for Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldovan airspace due to a drone alert, a Moldovan government spokesperson said. The president’s plane was cleared for take-off from Moldova on Tuesday once it was established that the drone had come down. In all, three departures and four arrivals were delayed. Norway’s prime minister was among those who thought Zelenskyy’s plane had been attacked.
- 
  The Moldovan president, Maia Sandu, denounced the drone intrusions as a “serious threat to people’s lives” and condemned an earlier Russian drone attack on a border crossing with Ukraine that killed two people. Three other people were injured in the strike on the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova. One person was killed and at least four people injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Kyiv, while more strikes were reported in Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr. A Russian drone strike on a shopping centre in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy killed two people and injured 20, four of them seriously, said the regional governor.
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared “there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes”. He added: “A response is needed – Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences. The aggression must be stopped here and now, before it spreads any further.” He called for “effective” sanctions against Russia and support for Ukraine, saying “the partners who can help know exactly what is needed every day”.
- 
  A Ukrainian couple got married anyway after a Russian air raid on the eve of their wedding wrecked their Kyiv apartment. Before going to bed, Liudmyla Ryzhak had hung on the bedroom door her dress, white skirt and her soldier fiance Leonid’s traditionally patterned shirt. As they slept a Russian strike hit a warehouse across the street from their building. They fled with Liudmyla’s six-year-old daughter and two guinea pigs to a bomb shelter – but soon returned to dig their wedding clothes out of the rubble of their ruined apartment. In the morning, amid more air raids, they forged ahead with the ceremony – only possible after Leonid had been able to make it back from the frontlines in eastern Ukraine. “If God gave me a continuation of life, then why should I put it off?” the bride said. “At least for now, I have the right to be happy. Both him and me.” – Associated Press
- 
  Russia’s arms production poses a future threat that goes beyond the war in Ukraine, the German defence minister, Boris Pistorius, warned on Wednesday. “Moscow uses large parts of its budget … to fill its inventories for future conflicts, not to deploy weapons to the frontline in Ukraine,” he told the German parliament. “On average, only 80 of the 150 short and medium-range missiles that Russia can produce per month are being deployed to Ukraine.”
- 
  In the UK, a man has been charged after allegedly assisting Russian spy services in planning a sabotage operation, Raphael Boyd writes. Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested in Swindon on Friday 4 September. Scotland Yard said it relates to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that has been accused of engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies. Cammidge would appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday, police said.
- 
  Moscow wants peace talks to take place in Abu Dhabi, the UAE capital, said a Kremlin aide, Yuri Ushakov. Ushakov also said the US should halt aid to Kyiv if the fighting is to stop. Moscow has been indignant throughout the war about Ukraine being able to defend itself with military aid from its allies. Another Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, cited a “confirmed political will” for the talks and suggested prisoner exchanges between the US and Russia might be part of the picture. Peskov was responding to a comment by the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, about a possible roadmap to restart talks. There have been no talks between Russia and Ukraine since February.

articles.title: Zelensky arrives in Canada to discuss Ukraine's air defense needs
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky stands with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during the G7 Leaders' Summit in Kananaskis, Alberta, on June 17, 2025. (Suzanne Plunkett-Pool/Getty Images)
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Canada on Sept. 9 as he seeks support for Ukraine's air defenses and preparations for the winter.
Zelensky is expected to hold "important meetings" aimed at strengthening the countries' strategic partnership for years to come. He is expected to meet with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney later in the day.
"We will discuss how to strengthen our resilience, support people, and ensure that Ukraine has the capabilities it needs to defend itself," the president said in a social media post on Sept. 10.
According to Zelensky, First Lady Olena Zelenska plans to meet with Canadian philanthropists who support Ukraine.
The visit follows Zelensky's trip to Norway, where he and the first lady attended the Sept. 9 funeral of King Harald V.
In Oslo, Zelensky also met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store to discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and advancing the Freyja anti-ballistic missile program.
Ukraine aims to have a working prototype of Freyja ready in the first half of 2027. The project brings together Ukraine and nine European countries, including Norway, as well as several European defense manufacturers.
Kateryna Denisova is the reporter for the Kyiv Independent, specializing in Ukrainian politics. Based in Kyiv, she focuses on domestic affairs, parliament, social and war-related issues. Kateryna began her career in journalism in 2020 and holds a bachelor's degree in journalism from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. She also studied at journalism schools in the Czech Republic and Germany.
Three of the tankers, the Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco, have direct links to Russia's shadow fleet and have been involved in transporting Russian oil, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
U.S. officials have reportedly told their European counterparts about the proposed diplomatic shift, with Trump considering downsizing current special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner's role in negotiations.
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) carried out Kyiv's deepest strike into Russia so far in the full-scale war, attacking a natural gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Russian officials said a fire broke out on a port embankment in Sochi as a result of a Ukrainian unmanned surface vessel (USV) strike. The attack reportedly disrupted a nearby concert.
The Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the EU has thrown out Orban's attempt to block military aid for Ukraine as "it does not fall within the jurisdiction" of the court.

articles.title: One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
articles.body:
Moldova closed its airspace on the afternoon of 8 September and delayed the plane carrying Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Norway after a Russian drone crossed into the country, its government said in a statement to Reuters. The aircraft was cleared for takeoff once officials established that it had come down on Moldovan territory. Norway's prime minister described the episode as a near-miss, and neither government has said how close the drone came.
Russia runs three things at once along the EU's eastern frontier—mass drone attacks on Ukraine, drones crossing into Moldovan and Romanian airspace almost weekly, and strikes on the border checkpoints tying the three countries together—and states without interceptors can answer only by closing their skies.
What happened, and when
Moldova's National Army detected a Shahed-type drone entering from Ukraine at 16:20, the country's Defense Ministry reported. It flew toward Bender, a city in the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria, then turned toward the capital, Chișinău, by 16:32. At 16:37, it left the country over western Moldova and headed into eastern Romania, across the Prut river border.
Controllers restricted the airspace over central Moldova at 16:30. The same drone came back from the Romanian side, crossed the north of the country, and came down outside a village in the northwest, near the Romanian border, setting dry vegetation alight, according to the log. Nobody was hurt, and the airspace reopened at 17:39, more than an hour after it closed. The BBC's Ukrainian service placed the crash near a different northern village, without naming a source, so the exact spot is unsettled.
The violation fell in the window when Zelenskyy's aircraft was preparing to take off, Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The civilian airport he was leaving from suspended operations and the border service closed the nearby crossings, the outlet added. Three departures and four arrivals were delayed in all, Reuters said.
A drone nearly hit Zelenskyy’s plane taking off from Moldova on his way to a king’s funeral, Norway’s PM says
How the plane and the drone crossed paths
Zelenskyy flies an Airbus A319 corporate jet, and the threat to it probably came from a jet-powered Geran drone that crossed Romanian and then Moldovan airspace at around 17:00 that day, Militarnyi wrote, publishing the drone's track from the monitoring channel Oko Hora. That fits the return leg in the army's log, though no authority has tied a specific aircraft to the delay.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told the broadcaster NRK the plane was almost hit as it prepared to leave, without naming his source. His office later described a danger recorded in Moldovan airspace that forced the delay. Norway's Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said Zelenskyy recounted the details himself at a closed meeting in Oslo.
Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska attended the farewell ceremony for King Harald V, who died on 28 August. Around it, the president worked on air defense, meeting Støre and then executives of defense companies from partner countries about the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, which Norway's government casts as a cheaper alternative to the Patriot.
Trending Now
The next night, the border crossing
Overnight on 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing on Ukraine's border with Moldova, killing two people and injuring three. The dead were Ukrainians, and a Moldovan citizen was among the injured, Moldova's Foreign Ministry told the broadcaster TV8. Border guards reopened the crossing that afternoon.
Russia claimed it had struck the crossing because it was used for military logistics. Moldova's Foreign Ministry rejected that outright, saying no weapons move through its territory, and that the people crossing there are families, children with their mothers, and the elderly. It is one of the working crossings on the Odesa Oblast stretch of the Ukrainian-Moldovan border, where the heaviest traffic runs through Palanca and Giurgiulești.
Moldova's President Maia Sandu condemned both the strike and the Geran-type drone that had forced her country to close its airspace the day before, and said the events show Ukraine needs more air defense.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it
The pattern, and Moldova's empty sky
Russia has hit at least five checkpoints on Ukraine's western borders since late August, four of them facing Moldova and one facing Romania, and the drone that struck the Kotlovyna crossing on 20 August flew in through Moldovan airspace. Euromaidan Press has covered part of that campaign, including burned food cargo near the Giurgiulești crossing in August. The State Border Guard Service has called such strikes an act of terrorism, because people are present at the crossings when they are hit.
In the air, Moldova can do little. It is still buying its first serious air defenses, so it restricts airspace and waits while Romania scrambles jets against the drones that reach its side. It logged three airspace breaches in nine days in August, and more than 100 drones were detected near Romania in four days that month.

articles.title: General Atomics Offers First Glimpse of Wildfire Drone, Eyed as MQ-9 Successor
articles.body:
General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft.
Wildfire was unveiled in a sizzle reel-type video General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. posted on social media Sept. 9. The video touts more than three decades of the company’s unmanned aerial vehicle development, starting with the Gnat and Predator drones flown in the 1990s up to and including its latest FQ-42A Dark Merlin, before revealing the first three images of Wildfire in short succession.
The images provide hints of the drone’s expected capabilities. One image shows Wildfire carrying four Joint Strike Missiles, which are stealthy cruise missiles, and another shows it with two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, or LRASMs.
“The whole point of a flying weapons truck is to come heavy,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in response to Air & Space Forces Magazine questions. “Wildfire will be able to carry a minimum of two LRASMs, four JSMs, or some similar configuration of heavy stand-off weapons, across meaningful combat distances.”
Brinkley said the MQ-9A is not be able to carry those payloads, and that they’re twice as much as the Pentagon originally envisioned for MMA. Brinkley said it’s too soon to sat how many Hellfire missiles—which the MQ-9A frequently employs—the Wildfire drone will be able to carry.
A third image shows a swarm of nearly a dozen Wildfire drones bearing down on a group of enemy ships and firing a barrage of missiles at them.
The Air Force envisions Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA, as a low-cost drone to take on missions now done by General Atomics’ MQ-9A, and wants MMA to be semi-autonomous and able to be sent in groups to overwhelm enemy defenses.
Top Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that they want the MMA’s air vehicle—not counting sensors or other capabilities—to cost no more than $10 million apiece. This would allow MMA to be “attritable,” meaning they would be inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.
The Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit, when unveiling the MMA concept in July, said losing $30 million drones in battle against an enemy would be unsustainable in a large-scale conflict, and a less expensive option is needed.
The conflict with Iran has cost the Air Force about 45 of its MQ-9 drones. In the Sept. 3 briefing, Air Force officials said the MQ-9 losses were concerning enough to push the service to accelerate its MMA effort. The Air Force and DIU want to have a prototype MMA a year after is contract is awarded and to start fielding it at scale within three years, or as early as 2029.
General Atomics created Wildfire as a clean-sheet design, and said it will be able to achieve all the Air Force’s MMA requirements at a high quality and an affordable price.
Brinkley said Wildfire will be able to exceed the Air Force and DIU’s 8,000 nautical mile ferry range requirement for MMA.
It will be modular, which will allow the Air Force to rapidly add or swap out different capabilities. When asked about Wildfire’s sensing capabilities, Brinkley said it will have “certain features available right out of the box,” but it will be up to the Air Force to decide what modular capabilities it wants to add.
“Modularity is key,” Brinkley said. “We’re showing that now with our Gambit series of uncrewed jets, which includes the XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station and FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft. One design, seamlessly pivoting to various missions. Wildfire will be able to do much the same from an [intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance]/strike lane.”
Brinkley said General Atomics will use its experience on autonomy, artificial intelligence, and machine learning from its work on programs like CCA and the MQ-20 Avenger, “to network dozens of Wildfires together on Day One.”
Brinkley said General Atomics has more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing space it could leverage to build Wildfire, and that the company has produced up to 100 aircraft per year, including MQ-9s.
“We have said from the beginning that we can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the [Air Force and DIU’s original] fiscal 2031 timeline,” Brinkley said. “We can deliver more than twice as many aircraft as originally asked for in the same amount of time. We’re not worried about scaling at all.”

articles.title: Iran Damages US A-10, F-15s with Missile Attack on Air Base in Jordan
articles.body:
A U.S. Air Force A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft flies in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Aug. 30, 2026. U.S. Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Tiffany A. Emery
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
An Iranian ballistic missile attack on a key U.S. air base in Jordan damaged multiple U.S. warplanes, people familiar with the matter confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
One A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft suffered a severely damaged wing and about eight F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were lightly damaged but are considered serviceable after Iran attacked Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on Sept. 8 Eastern Time.
The damage to U.S. aircraft was first reported by CBS News.
A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The attack on the base, known as MSAB, came after the U.S. struck five Iranian tankers Sept. 8, and Iran retaliated by lobbing scores of ballistic missiles at the installation. U.S. and Jordanian forces launched dozens of interceptors at the Iranian missiles. U.S. officials said no American personnel were killed. But Iran was able to harm American materiel. In the hours after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it damaged U.S. aircraft at the base.
The U.S. has dozens of warplanes operating from the base, which acts as a key airpower hub for operations against Iran. Tehran has targeted the facility, near the Jordanian town of Azraq, numerous times since the conflict began in February. Three Army Soldiers were killed in a missile attack on the base in July.
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft.
In the small world of Air Force weather specialists, combat weather specialists are a niche unto themselves, deploying with Army ground units to provide forecasts and, if need be, fight alongside those Soldiers. For Staff Sgt. Francisco Estrada, the hardest part of the job isn’t the possibility of ground combat,…
Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force.
In a dramatic flare-up in the hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan.
After months of delays, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to…
The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.
The U.S. is rotating fresh fighter squadrons to the Middle East to support the Trump administration’s open-ended campaign of economic and military pressure against Iran.
An F-16 Air National Guard unit’s six-month deployment to Kadena Air Base, Japan, this year illustrated the capabilities the Guard’s oldest fighter units can still offer—but also the challenges they face, officials told reporters this week.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Intel Hacks Russia’s Institute Behind Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M and Oreshnik Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Intel Hacks Russia’s Institute Behind Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M and Oreshnik Missiles
Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) has breached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology (MIT), Russia's chief designer of intercontinental ballistic missiles, and identified 2,648 of its employees who it links to the killing of Ukrainians.
The operation was announced in a statement on HUR's official Telegram channel on September 9. The agency described a unique cyberspace operation inside Russia through which its specialists obtained an array of data on the corporation's structure, leadership, and current and prospective developments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, engineers at the institute's facilities in Moscow and other Russian regions produce the drawings, software, engines, and control units for several of Russia's core strategic systems:
- the Yars (RS-24) intercontinental ballistic missile, a central component of Russia's nuclear forces;
- the mobile Topol-M (RT-2PM2) intercontinental missile system;
- the Bulava (R-30), a three-stage missile designed for submarines;
- the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile complex;
- the Kedr, also known as the Oreshnik, Russia's newest hypersonic ballistic system.
HUR added that the institute also develops satellite communications for the Russian army, including a system for rapidly deploying military satellites into low orbit to provide Russian forces with a resilient, protected command-and-control network.
The agency noted work on the Start-1M conversion launch vehicle, which could let Moscow deploy low-orbit satellite constellations for optical-electronic and radar reconnaissance, alongside a scalable space platform designated Typoryad.
The Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology is at the center of Russia's strategic missile industry, with subordinate enterprises including the Prozhektor design bureau, the Vympel machine-building plant, the Votkinsk Plant, and the Iskra enterprise.
Among the people identified, HUR named the corporation's director general, reserve Lieutenant General Sergey Ponomarev, along with his deputies Yuri Kirillov, Yuri Solomonov, Andrey Bashirov, Artyom Khrebin, and Sergey Solonichkin.
HUR stated that the material would be used to weaken Russia's capacity to wage its war against Ukraine and to hold those tied to war crimes accountable.
The corporation has surfaced before as the endpoint of sanctioned supply chains. Computer-controlled machine tools traced through Chinese intermediaries—including controllers built by Germany's Siemens and Heidenhain and Japan's Fanuc—reached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology despite export bans intended to deny Moscow access to the technology.
Roughly 70% of the CNC machines operating in Russia are imported, and as much as 80% of that equipment goes to the military.
The machinery has sharpened the accuracy and lethality of missiles such as the nuclear-capable Oreshnik, first fired at Ukraine on November 21, 2024.

articles.title: Trump Promises End to Iran War After Midterms
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said he expects the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran to end “immediately after” the midterm elections.
Trump suggested that Iran is on the verge of collapse, but that its government is holding out in hopes of hurting Republican political prospects in November.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he headed to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday.
But “they can’t hold out any longer,” he said.
Trump added that “it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm” for gas prices to come down, but that they would fall once Iran soon seeks an end to the war, which is now in its seventh month.
Trump’s comments come as renewed fighting, including a barrage of tit-for-tat strikes in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, has driven up energy prices to their highest levels since late May. The global benchmark oil price topped $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
The national average for gasoline in the U.S. climbed 7.3 cents to $4.22 a gallon on Wednesday, the largest single day increase since May, according to AAA. Diesel reached a record $5.94 a gallon on Wednesday.
The Trump Administration has sought to tamp down rising energy prices amid growing affordability concerns among Americans. Last month, the Administration extended the Jones Act Waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to transport oil and other commodities between U.S. ports.
U.S. and Iran exchange biggest attack on shipping
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the U.S. and Iran exchanged the largest wave of attacks on shipping since the war began. Iran said it attacked 10 ships, including two U.S. vessels, near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. destroyed five Iranian oil tankers. Iran also launched missiles at a base hosting U.S. forces in Jordan, which U.S. officials reportedly said resulted in limited damage and no casualties.
The U.S. said its tanker strikes were retaliation for two Iranian attempts to hit a U.S. Navy warship.
The latest exchange came after days of escalating attacks. U.S. forces struck Iranian military sites on Sept. 1 in retaliation for attempted Iranian attacks on commercial vessels and U.S. personnel, CENTCOM said. One U.S. strike hit a wedding party in southern Iran, killing at least five people and injuring more than 60 others, according to Iranian officials, and prompting an internal investigation by the U.S. military. On Saturday, Iran fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer. In response, the U.S. destroyed three Iranian oil tankers.
Trump officials have downplayed the nature of the conflict, despite the continued fighting. Last week, Vice President J.D. Vance said he would not call the recent flare up “a war.”
When will the war end?
Trump and his officials initially estimated that the war would last four to six weeks, and have repeatedly said that energy costs will fall quickly once the war is over. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested in July that gas prices could return to $3 a gallon by Labor Day.
But Iran’s hold on the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery in the Persian Gulf through which a fifth of the world’s oil trade flowed before the war, has proved an enduring strategy to disrupt the global economy. Iran militarized the Strait at the start of the war in retaliation against U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28. Iranian leaders have used the Strait as a key point of leverage in now-stalled talks with the U.S., and restarted strikes on ships in the waterway in an attempt to force the U.S. to agree to its demands.
Trump, however, has maintained that he is under no pressure from the economic pain or its potential impact on the midterm elections to strike a deal with Iran, especially one that would be unfavorable to the U.S.
“A negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at,” Trump said on Wednesday.
Trump has insisted that Americans understand the need to continue the war until the U.S. eliminates the possibility of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon.
“I think it’s very easy to explain to America, all you have to do is say: ‘Will you let Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ And the answer is no,” Trump said.
Nevertheless, the public has grown increasingly weary of the war. Just 31% of Americans said they supported U.S. strikes on Iran in a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, while 63% opposed it. And 83% of those polled said they expect U.S. military involvement in Iran to continue for an extended period of time. Americans also appear to be concerned with the economic consequences of the war, with 61% of respondents believing the conflict has made life more expensive for their families, according to a Politico poll in August.
Last month, the Treasury Department launched an economic pressure campaign on Iran in an effort to force its capitulation. Its measures have included a slate of new sanctions on Iran, the ongoing U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports, and the threat of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners.
Iran’s economy has been hit hard by the measures, as well as disruptions and damage from the war. Its already weak currency has spiraled to record lows, while inflation, unemployment, and shortages of essential goods have substantially worsened.
Nevertheless, recent intelligence assessments reportedly indicate that Tehran is prepared to continue fighting for months despite severe economic pressure. Iranian leaders have also signaled a willingness to escalate the war by intensifying attacks on U.S. warships, targeting commercial vessels, and expanding shipping restrictions beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
Analysts have argued that Iran’s leadership might be hoping to inflict greater political and economic costs on the U.S. Administration in an effort to increase its leverage over Washington. Trump advisers, including Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have reportedly discussed with Trump the prospect that the war continues through the remainder of his presidential term.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Key Russia-Iran Shipping Hub on Caspian Sea in First Makhachkala Port Strike
Ukrainian drones struck the Makhachkala International Commercial Seaport on Russia’s Caspian coast overnight on September 10, hitting a strategically important transport hub linked to maritime traffic with Iran roughly 1,000 kilometers from Ukraine’s border, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed.
The Ukrainian OSINT community Exilenova+ published footage of the operation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Residents of Makhachkala reported explosions around the port during the overnight raid, marking the first known Ukrainian strike on port infrastructure in the city.
The target is particularly significant because Makhachkala serves as one of Russia’s principal maritime gateways on the Caspian Sea and maintains extensive shipping links with Iran.
The port has been used by vessels traveling between Russia and Iranian ports, including routes associated with the movement of military cargo and components for Iranian-designed drones supplied to Moscow.
Cargo arriving through Makhachkala can then move farther into Russia by road, rail and air, making the port part of a broader logistics network connecting Iranian suppliers with Russian military infrastructure.
Makhachkala is also Russia’s only ice-free deepwater commercial port on the Caspian Sea, allowing it to operate year-round.
The facility handles both liquid and dry cargo, with oil and petroleum products playing an increasingly important role in its operations.
Cargo volumes have surged during Russia’s war against Ukraine. During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, an increase of 42.5% compared with the same period last year.
Oil accounted for more than 2.08 million tons of that total, rising nearly 50% year over year.
The acceleration was already evident earlier in 2026. Cargo turnover reached 1.4 million metric tons during the first four months of the year and climbed to 2.11 million tons by the end of June, roughly 50% above the same period in 2025.
Liquid cargo drove most of that expansion. During the first half of the year alone, the port handled nearly 1.57 million metric tons of oil and other liquid cargo.
Previously, Ukraine’s Security Service used long-range drones to strike multiple military and logistical targets across Russia overnight on July 25, including maritime targets in the Caspian Sea.
Ukrainian drones struck several targets in the Caspian Sea, including the Filanovsky offshore oil platform, the sanctioned cargo vessel Port Olya 2, the dry cargo ship Begey, and a Russian Project 12418 Molniya missile boat.
Ukrainian military intelligence further reported that Begey had been used to transport ammunition, artillery shells, body armor, and helmets from Iran across the Caspian Sea. During voyages between Iranian and Russian ports, the vessel’s crew allegedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to Ukrainian authorities.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine carried out a drone attack against a sanctioned Russian cargo ship in the Mediterranean Sea, striking the vessel 12 times as it allegedly transported Iranian weapons and armored vehicles to Russia.
