articles.title: Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The Houthis have seized the strategic Yemeni port city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, government sources said on Thursday, marking a major development in the renewed fighting as tens of thousands have been displaced across the country.
Three Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi forces had entered Mocha and taken control of the coastal city, while local sources told The New Arab that large numbers of residents were fleeing towards the southern city of Aden.
The takeover comes after weeks of escalating Houthi attacks on Mocha and its port and amid a broader offensive by the Iran-backed group across western Yemen.
Mocha is strategically important because of its location on Yemen's western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The city's capture could therefore have wider implications for security around the strait and commercial shipping through the Red Sea, as fighting intensifies across Yemen's western coast.
The Houthis launched a major offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces last week aimed at advancing towards Bab al-Mandab, prompting government-aligned forces to mount counterattacks and expand operations elsewhere in the country.
Mocha had already come under repeated Houthi missile, drone and explosive-laden boat attacks in recent weeks.
The city's port suspended all commercial and maritime operations in mid-August after it was struck by more than 25 Houthi missiles, according to information provided by sources.
The attacks caused civilian casualties and damaged facilities and property, with material losses estimated at around $16 million.
The takeover coincides with an escalation in fighting along Yemen's western coast, particularly in southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, where government and allied forces have been carrying out military movements and withdrawing from several positions.
Yemeni government forces withdrew overnight from Hays district in southern Hodeidah as military units operating around Hays and western Taiz began a process of reorganisation and redeployment, military and local sources said.
It remains unclear how many troops withdrew from Hays and Al-Wazi'iyah or where they have been redeployed. Military sources said the movements were part of preparations for a coordinated field operation.
Tareq Saleh orders western coast forces to regroup
Tareq Saleh, deputy chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said on Thursday that government forces on the western coast had suffered heavy losses in recent days while confronting the Houthi offensive.
Saleh said forces had been ordered to regroup and establish an alternative command centre in a secure location in consultation with the Saudi-led coalition and the Presidential Leadership Council.
Military media affiliated with Saleh's National Resistance said the joint forces had established a command centre south of Mocha following Houthi breakthroughs on several fronts under heavy fire.
The forces involved in the western coast fighting include the National Resistance, the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield forces, alongside units from the Taiz military axis.
Saleh accused Iran of planning, supporting and participating in the Houthi offensive through what he described as its "various tools", without providing further details about Tehran's alleged involvement.
Iran has rejected accusations that it is interfering in Yemen, saying this week that it supports the country's unity and territorial integrity and a Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.
Meanwhile, military media sources reported air strikes on Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah province.
The National Resistance's military media also said the Houthis had targeted Zuqar Island with two ballistic missiles.
The latest developments come amid the most significant escalation on several Yemeni fronts following years of relative calm. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but clashes resumed in July and have since widened.
Fighting has also spilled across the border into Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh accusing the Houthis of targeting Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities said this week that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.

articles.title: North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says
articles.body:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has voiced “serious concern” over evidence that North Korea has built a facility capable of enriching weapons-grade uranium to bolster its nuclear arsenal.
The new building, located at the the country’s main Yongbyon nuclear facility, can house up to 28 centrifuge cascades – machinery commonly used to enrich uranium – according to a report by the nuclear watchdog released this week.
The regime has also expanded operations at an enrichment site in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, according to the report, which was based on analysis of satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by the country’s state media.
The IAEA, whose inspectors were expelled from North Korea in 2009, identified the Yongbyon building as the site’s second uranium enrichment facility after comparing satellite images taken during its construction with media photographs of a visit in early June by the country’s leader, Kim Jong-un.
During his visit, Kim claimed the North’s capacity to produce weapons-grade nuclear material had more than doubled over the past five years, according to state media, promising “vast future plans to exponentially strengthen the country’s nuclear forces”.
Citing a 2025 analysis by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in the US, South Korea’s Chosun Daily said the potential 28 cascades comprising 4,592 centrifuges at the Yongbyon facility could yield about 85 kg of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year – enough to build three or four additional warheads.
In a statement released this week, the IAEA’s director general, Rafael Grossi, said: “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of [North Korea’s] production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.”
“The continuation and further development” of North Korea’s nuclear programme are “clear violations of relevant UN security council resolutions and are deeply regrettable”, he added.
South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, said in August that the North possessed between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads – a much higher number than the 57 cited by Donald Trump the same month. The South Korean figure was based on estimates by private research organisations, Ahn told lawmakers, adding that the country’s military could not confirm the numbers.
North Korea has made rapid progress in its ballistic missile and nuclear programmes in recent years, as it demands international recognition as a legitimate nuclear state.
North Korea has conducted multiple long-range missile tests since 2017, the year it last tested a nuclear weapon. In a report submitted to the UN security council in 2020, international experts said the North had “probably developed nuclear devices to fit into the warheads of its ballistic missiles”.

articles.title: Iran strikes ships, expands no-go zone outside Hormuz strait
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran strikes ships, expands no-go zone outside Hormuz strait
Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.
The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Brent oil closed at $101.21.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 "non-compliant vessels" that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said "several" vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region".
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran's Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" on Wednesday, saying exact coordinates will be announced later.
"If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The Guards also said they struck a US military base in Jordan in response to US forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers a day earlier.
Jordan's army shot down 18 missiles fired at the kingdom, it said.
Iran's foreign ministry condemned the attack on its oil tankers as "an overt threat to regional and international peace and security," saying the strikes "increase the dangers of tensions in the region".
It said the targeting of US military facilities in the region was "self-defence".
The US military for its part had said it was responding to an Iranian attack targeting an American warship, the second such incident in less than a week.
Nuclear referral
Iran's Guards, the ideological arm of the military, said the war could be brought to an end if Washington met its conditions, which included demands on the wars in Lebanon and Yemen.
"It must... refrain from renewed threats, withdraw the Israeli regime's army from Lebanon, end the blockade of Yemen, release $24 billion in Iran's frozen assets and refrain from any interference in the country's nuclear and missile capabilities," Mohebi said, according to Fars news agency.
Donald Trump, an unpopular president eager to end an unpopular war, asserted Wednesday the conflict will conclude right after the mid-term US elections in November. Polls show his Republican Party could face a drubbing and lose control of one or both houses of Congress.
"I think the war will end immediately after the election" because Iran "can't hold out any longer," Trump told journalists, accusing Tehran of being "desperate to try and affect" the vote.
But as Washington tries to choke off Iran economically, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance", in a diplomatic move that piles pressure on Tehran.
The resolution was adopted by a 23-3 vote with eight abstentions, they said. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
Iran's representative to the UN nuclear watchdog said the resolution was passed under US pressure, saying it "has no basis and will not bring any results".
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also repeated his claim Iran was on the verge of collapse.
"The main task is to bring down the terror regime in Iran. We are very close to that," he said Wednesday on a troop visit in southern Syria, where Israel has occupied what it calls a "security zone".
The latest round of US-Iran fighting was triggered after American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday, with the US military saying it "directed the crews to abandon ship" before hitting the vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers, and I think you'll see that again today," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.
Iran has asserted control of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli strikes began the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.
Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the strait.

articles.title: Sybiha, amid new Russian attacks, urges partners to boost air defense, weapons and sanctions
articles.body:
Following another round of Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on international partners to strengthen Ukraine's air defense, increase weapons deliveries, and step up sanctions pressure on Russia.
"Russia should enter this winter knowing that the sky over Ukraine is getting harder to penetrate, that the missiles and drones it produces will be intercepted more and more often, and that the industry, technology, revenues and supply chains sustaining its attacks will face growing disruption and cost," Sybiha wrote on X.
He said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight, targeting cities and communities across the country with missiles and drones, with the attacks continuing into the morning.
"This is exactly what Russia does when it sees that repeated attacks carry too few consequences. It widens the geography and increases the frequency of strikes, testing how far it can go," the foreign minister said.
According to Sybiha, international partners need to make decisions now, including on additional air defense systems and interceptors, particularly to counter ballistic missiles.
Sybiha also called for providing more missiles for F-16s and additional aircraft to bolster Ukraine's ability to defend its skies, as well as for imposing tougher sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex and sanctions-evasion networks.
"The world cannot stand idly by while Russia treats Ukrainians as targets on a shooting range," Sybiha said.
He stressed that closing Ukraine's skies should no longer be a matter of reacting to individual Russian attacks, but must instead involve depriving Russia of the confidence that it can keep terrorizing Ukraine indefinitely at an acceptable cost.
"The longer Moscow sees hesitation, the more it will try. The task is to change that calculation," the foreign minister concluded.

articles.title: US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
articles.body:
US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers, 3 linked to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukrainian official says
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Sept. 8, three of which have ties to Russia's shadow fleet, Ukraine's sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said in a comment shared with the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) on Sept. 9 said its forces struck the five vessels in response to attempts by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to target a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
The five vessels were the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, as well as the Derya near Iran's Kharg Island. U.S. forces instructed the crews to abandon the vessels before striking them, CENTCOM said.
Three of the tankers, the Kaviz, Charminar, and Riesco, have direct links to Russia's shadow fleet and have been involved in transporting Russian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The Kaviz had called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk and transported Russian oil, according to Vlasiuk. He added that the vessel had repeatedly switched off its Automatic Identification System (AIS), which ships use to broadcast information including their location and identity.
According to Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), the Kaviz was previously affiliated with Fractal Marine DMCC, a company sanctioned by the U.K. for servicing Russia's energy sector and identified by HUR as a key operator of Russia's shadow fleet. HUR also lists the tanker as sanctioned by the U.S., Ukraine, the EU, Switzerland, the U.K. and Canada.
The Charminar had previously called at the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Primorsk, Vysotsk and St. Petersburg, Vlasiuk said.
HUR lists the Charminar as having been involved in exports of Russian crude and petroleum products and links the vessel to Fractal Marine DMCC. The vessel has also been linked to a shipping network associated with Iranian oil trader Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, who trades in both Russian and Iranian oil, Vlasiuk said.
The third vessel, the Riesco, has likewise transported Russian and Iranian crude and petroleum products, including through ship-to-ship transfers with sanctioned vessels, according to HUR. The tanker has been under U.S. sanctions since November 2025 and Ukrainian sanctions since February 2026.
CENTCOM published footage showing the Riesco sinking in the Gulf of Oman following the strike.
Russia's shadow fleet is a network of vessels used to move sanctioned Russian oil around the world, at the same time obscuring ownership to avoid Western restrictions. HUR's register had identified more than 1,400 such vessels as of May 2026, many of them aging ships sailing under third-country flags.
The fleet has become a crucial source of revenue for Moscow, with estimates suggesting it carries about 75% of Russia's sanctioned oil and helps generate income used to fund the Kremlin's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: How China and Iran used barter system to dodge US sanctions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How China and Iran used barter-like system to circumvent US sanctions
Iran has used a barter-like arrangement to bypass sanctions on its oil sales and buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods from China, including military gear, two senior Iranian sources and three other people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The secretive trade mechanism, in which Iranian oil is exchanged for credits for Chinese imports, has provided a financial lifeline for Tehran in recent years as the United States stepped up economic and military pressure over its nuclear program, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
It has also helped China, the world's biggest crude importer, retain access to discounted Iranian oil while shielding banks and companies that export to the Islamic Republic from international scrutiny or penalties, they said.
The US has imposed sanctions on some smaller Chinese entities that buy or facilitate shipments of Iranian oil but has stopped short of the most punishing measures that could have repercussions on the global economy.
Washington has intensified the pressure as it tries to resolve its war with Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. In August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or risk being forced out of the dollar-based financial system.
Reuters could not determine the impact on the barter-like arrangement of the US naval blockade imposed on Iran as part of the six-month war. No Iranian crude cargoes have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz to China since the blockade was reinstated on 14 July, the news agency reported last week.
China and Iran have repeatedly denounced what they regard as illegal unilateral Western sanctions and have vowed to protect their interests. The countries are longstanding economic and political partners but have said little publicly about how they keep trade flowing despite international restrictions.
Iran has used the arrangement to buy medicines, vehicles and communication equipment from China, all the sources said. The manufacturers were not dealing directly with Iran, and there is no indication they were in breach of sanctions.
The mechanism was also used at least once in the past year in connection with contracts to supply Iran with air defense equipment worth millions of dollars, the sources said.
They did not provide details about any of the alleged transactions with Chinese manufacturers, and Reuters could not independently verify that they took place.
A UN embargo on the export of most major conventional weapons to Iran was reinstated with other sanctions in September 2025 after the US withdrew from a 2015 nuclear accord between Iran and world powers during President Donald Trump's first term, and Tehran stopped complying with some of its provisions.
Iran and China said the move by European countries to automatically restore the sanctions through a "snapback" mechanism was "legally and procedurally flawed."
Responding to Reuters questions about the barter-like trade, China’s foreign ministry said it was "not familiar with the situation you describe."
"China has consistently opposed unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law and have not been authorized by the United Nations Security Council," it said.
Iran's UN missions in New York and Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.
In response to questions to the White House, a US official said the Trump administration works with economic partners including the European Union to "deprive Iran of the material means of furthering its nuclear ambitions." The official did not comment on the arrangement described to Reuters.
Avoiding banking channels
Decades of US sanctions have left Iran with few oil customers. China is the main buyer, accounting for more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil in 2025, or an average 1.4 million barrels per day, according to commodities data and analytics firm Kpler.
In 2021, the two countries signed a 25-year strategic partnership accord covering sectors such as energy and infrastructure, but public details remain scarce.
The arrangement described to Reuters is one of a number of mechanisms through which Iran purchases goods and services from China without paying Chinese companies directly through international banking channels, three of the sources said.
A Western official and two other people familiar with the matter said a buyer acting on behalf of Chinese state-owned oil trader Zhuhai Zhenrong was at least until this year depositing hundreds of millions of dollars a month with an obscure, China-based financial entity known as ChuXin.
The deposits covered purchases agreed with a Hong Kong-registered company linked to Iran’s national oil company, the people said, citing material gathered by intelligence agencies. ChuXin would then send funds to Chinese exporters and companies that build infrastructure in Iran, likely via other Chinese financial institutions.
Roughly 70% of the Iranian oil proceeds handled by ChuXin are allocated to infrastructure projects, the three sources said, an arrangement first reported by the Wall Street Journal last October. The rest go into accounts belonging to a special purpose vehicle (SPV) used to pay companies that supply goods to Iran.
The Iranian sources, who are close to the country’s decision-making circle, confirmed the existence of the SPV, which has not previously been reported.
All five sources said funds in the SPV are managed by two entities: a firm acting on behalf of China's Ministry of Commerce and one linked to Iran’s central bank. The Iran-linked firm notifies the Chinese one when Iran's central bank authorizes importers to access funds in the SPV so payments can be sent to the suppliers, three said.
Reuters could find no record of a financial institution called ChuXin in Chinese company registries or of the firms said to be acting on behalf of China's commerce ministry and Iran's central bank. One source said ChuXin might only exist on a spreadsheet.
Companies with the same names as those said to be acting on behalf of the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) and Zhuhai Zhenrong are listed in the Hong Kong companies registry, but Reuters could find no public records of their ownership structure or business dealings. Neither responded to questions delivered to their registered addresses, which are in offices belonging to secretarial services companies.
Plausible deniability
Zhuhai Zhenrong has been a target of US sanctions over its alleged dealings with Iran. One source shared what appeared to be a 22 July 2025, letter from NIOC to the Chinese oil trader requesting confirmation of an outstanding balance—evidence, the person said, of a business relationship.
Reuters could not independently authenticate the document. NIOC and Zhuhai Zhenrong did not respond to questions about it or their alleged roles in the trade mechanism.
Iran’s central bank and China’s commerce ministry also did not respond to requests for comment.
The mechanism described to Reuters has been in place since at least 2021 and was first used to supply medicines and COVID-19 vaccines to Iran, three sources said.
As Washington has stepped up pressure on companies that do business with Iran, it has become increasingly important for trade, they said. They estimated that between $2 billion and $2.5 billion flowed through the SPV over the last year.
China is using such arrangements to push back against the US and show it cannot be coerced with the threat of secondary sanctions, said Andrea Ghiselli, an international politics lecturer at the University of Exeter who studies Beijing’s relations with the Middle East.
But he said China's leaders do not want their banks or companies excluded from the international financial system. "They want plausible deniability."

articles.title: Nuclear agency board refers Iran to UN Security Council for first time in 20 years
articles.body:
Nuclear agency board refers Iran to UN Security Council for first time in 20 years
IAEA remains blocked from key sites damaged during June 2025 military strikes by the US and Israel
The UN atomic watchdog’s board on Wednesday reported Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, citing it for failure to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.
Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons programme until 2003. Iran says that it is not pursuing nuclear weapons, and that its programme is entirely peaceful.
Reporting Iran to the Security Council opens the country to possible sanctions and asset freezes, though such punitive measures are unlikely because Iran’s allies Russia and China hold veto power on the panel.
Twenty-three countries on the International Atomic Energy Agency’s 35-member board of governors voted for Wednesday’s resolution at IAEA headquarters in Vienna.
China, Russia and Niger opposed it, while eight countries abstained and one did not vote as it was in arrears, according to diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the outcome of the closed-door vote.
The resolution was put forward by the United States, Britain, France and Germany.

articles.title: Russians abroad are losing access to passport renewals and other consular services. Belarusians know what comes next.
articles.body:
Russians abroad are losing access to passport renewals and other consular services. Belarusians know what comes next.
In the summer of 2026, Russian authorities banned Russians abroad who have been convicted in absentia from receiving any consular services. The ban applies to anyone convicted under any article of the Criminal Code, as well as anyone with an administrative fine for “discrediting the army,” failing to label themselves a “foreign agent,” or working with an “undesirable organization.” In effect, many will face an illusory choice: return to Russia and serve their sentence, or live in another country without a foreign passport, since it can no longer be renewed. Because of this, the law has already been dubbed the law on “stripping citizenship.” Belarusian citizens who have left the country have been in a similar situation for three years already. In 2023, Alexander Lukashenko banned them from obtaining passports at embassies and consulates. Meduza spoke with them about life without a passport.
Sergei, 38, lives in Poland
My wife and I left Minsk in late 2021 to start a business in Poland. When the [full-scale] war began, we decided not to go back. In Belarus, we’d manufactured and sold electric scooters, kick scooters, and bicycles, and we wanted to expand that business into Europe — but the laws here turned out to be completely different: in Poland, you need a license to operate that kind of vehicle. So we switched fields. We’d always worked with Chinese factories, and we still do, but now we import household goods.
I live in Gdansk because we originally planned to work through sea shipments — there’s a port here — and because we wanted to live closer to nature. We lived in Warsaw for a while but didn’t like it; it’s a big, noisy city.
My passport expired at the end of 2023. In theory, I could go back to Belarus and get a new one — that would mean going to the consulate for special permission to return without a valid passport. I don’t want to risk it: there are many stories about people being pulled off buses, interrogated, and detained.
My residence permit made everything easier, but it expired a month ago, and a new one takes a long time to process. Wait times vary by region, and Gdansk is the slowest. A work-based residence permit takes about two to two and a half years; a business-based one takes even longer, about three years. Poland has handled this well, though: it issues a podróży document valid for one year that can be used for travel, and Belarusians get it free of charge through a simplified process. But it’s only valid together with a residence permit, so right now I can’t leave the country.
The expired passport hasn’t caused major problems so far. Once, a leasing company turned us down when our business tried to rent a car — we just put the contract in my wife’s name instead, and everything went fine. This year we took out another lease, and they didn’t even ask for my passport; all the contracts were handled using the residence permit.
We’re renting an apartment now. We wanted to take out a mortgage on a house but were turned down because of the expired residence permit — the bank was willing to accept two local documents instead of a Belarusian passport: the residence permit and the podróży document.
Another problem: I can’t get a power of attorney. We still own property in Belarus and would like to sell it rather than let it sit there as dead weight.
I’ve gotten used to living without a passport, but living without a residence permit is hard. I’m grateful to the Belarusian opposition in exile — thanks to their efforts, it’s now possible to get the podróży document through a simplified process and to replace an expired driver’s license.
I can’t really offer Russians advice, except to hope they’ll be treated the same way as Belarusians and given the chance to get, say, the podróży document through a simplified process if they live in Poland. And I’d wish them faster residence permit processing — not a three-year wait.
My wife’s documents are in order — her passport is valid until 2031. She has no plans to go to Belarus; nothing ties her there anymore, and her parents have died. My own mother and I don’t see each other. She lives in a village and doesn’t want to deal with getting a visa. She’s fine with my having left. She watches television, but she basically understands what’s really going on.
I miss Svietlahorsk, the town where I was born. I don’t much want to go back to Minsk, especially given what happened there after 2020. We lived in the Novaya Borovaya neighborhood, home to a lot of programmers and businessmen who supported political change. At the time, [the authorities] came down hard on our neighborhood — you’d walk out of your building and find riot police there, constantly asking where you were going, when you’d be back, checking your documents. What stuck with me was the total control, the constant threat of getting locked up for a few days. People grew scared, unhappy, withdrawn. Even though I never went to the protests, I remember that constant fear of being detained for no reason.
I don’t think I’ll ever be able to go back, because I don’t really believe things will change for the better.
Dmitry, 46, lives in France
I left Belarus in June 2021, partly for political reasons — but overall, I’d long stopped seeing a future there for myself and my family. I went to France alone at first. I already had a residence permit, since I’d spent a lot of time in the country before moving there, and I started looking for work. My wife joined me six months later.
In Minsk, I worked at a tattoo studio, but when COVID hit, I had to find a different line of work and spent a while in forestry. Now I’ve gone back to tattooing — I’m registered as a sole proprietor and work for myself.
My Belarusian passport expired in April 2025. I could go back to Belarus to renew it, but there’s no guarantee I’d be able to leave again — no guarantee I wouldn’t be detained over my correspondence. I don’t have any critical problems in everyday life right now, since I have a 10-year residence permit valid until 2035; I actually got it after my passport had already expired. It all depends on the prefecture. In some regions, people wait years for a decision and end up suing the prefecture — and then there are cases like mine. After [the authorities] asked for a copy of a valid passport, I wrote back saying I had no way of getting one and asked them to process everything without it. They approved my request.
The main problem is that I can’t really travel normally by plane — I can’t just get up and fly somewhere for vacation or personal reasons. For now, we mostly drive to neighboring European countries, so [not having a passport] isn’t as noticeable day to day. It could obviously create more problems down the road.
I like France; the quality of life here is high. But this country hasn’t replaced Belarus — it’s just a different part of my life. What I miss most is Belarusian nature, the forests and rivers. France has beautiful nature too, but it’s different.
Nikolai, 35, lives in Poland
My wife, our child, and I left in December 2021. We sat down, talked it over, and decided Belarus wouldn’t offer our child anything good, and that my wife didn’t see room to grow there professionally. So we decided to move to Europe. Since my wife and I both have Polish roots, we quickly got Karta Polaka cards [which grant the right to obtain a residence permit in Poland] and later got residence permits.
My passport expired in January 2025, and I applied for a podróży document. Last year they issued these quickly, but now I’ve been waiting nine months with no word at all. I have pobyt stały status, but banks require a passport, so all my online accounts got blocked once mine expired. The only thing saving me is Revolut, where I passed verification using my pobyt stały status.
Just two months before Lukashenko’s decree [barring people from renewing documents abroad], I wrote to the consulate asking whether I could get my passport replaced. They told me to come to Belarus, where they’d issue a new one. I think they already knew the decree was coming and had stopped renewing anyone’s passport.
Recently, I tried to get them to confirm I hold a Belarusian [driver’s] license so I could replace it. They refused because my passport is expired. The only thing I got out of them was an official written refusal stating the reason. As I understand it, they can’t process any administrative request for me except issuing permission to return to Belarus.
My wife and I have never had any contact with the [Belarusian KGB], though she went to rallies a few times in Ashmyany, our hometown. She traveled home in 2025 and had no problems at the border. I don’t want to go, because I’ve already received summonses from the local draft office, and there’s no way to check whether I’m on a list of people barred from leaving the country.
My mother has visited me in Poland once. I avoid political topics with her, because she thinks that since Belarus isn’t at war with anyone, Lukashenko must be relatively good. I don’t want to bring it up, because it’s [easy] to end up in an argument.
My child is 10 and adapted very quickly. When we arrived, he went straight into kindergarten and then school; he picked up Polish fast and now speaks two languages. My own social circle is mostly Russian-speaking. Interestingly, some Poles now in their 40s studied Russian in school and still remember it — surprisingly.
In Belarus, I worked at Beltelecom, an internet provider. After we moved, I retrained as a web developer and now work freelance in that field. I like Poland better than Belarus — everything is more accessible, and you can go away for the weekend somewhere in Europe without a second thought. But that’s only when your documents are in order. Right now, I can’t leave Poland at all.
Viktor, 52, lives in Ukraine
I was born in Belarus, in the Gomel region, and worked as a welder my whole life. My mother moved to Ukraine in the ‘90s, and my younger brother was born there. I moved to Ukraine myself in 2018 and remarried. My ex-wife and our two children stayed behind in Belarus.
My Belarusian passport expired in 2022. I could have renewed it, but I didn’t know that could be done through the embassy. I wanted to go to Belarus, but prices had risen during COVID: a one-way bus ticket cost around 5,000 hryvnias, and I couldn’t afford the round trip. Then my work-based residence permit expired too, and I became an undocumented resident. There’s a war going on now, and I can’t leave — the police would immediately take me in for questioning — but I can’t get legal status either, because my passport is expired. So I’m stuck in limbo.
A TRC (territorial recruitment center) drafted my younger brother into the war in 2025. He’s 35 and holds a Ukrainian passport. Everyone back in Belarus assumes I’m fighting too. I once got in touch with my cousin, who’s retired now. I told him, “I’m at work.” He asked, “What, on the front line?” I asked if he was laughing at me. What kind of soldier am I?
When I went to the migration service, they told me, “Go home, get a new passport, and then we can legalize your status.” I said, “How do you imagine that, when my brother is fighting?” They said that if I were caught [by the Belarusian authorities], the least they’d do is exchange me for prisoners of war. In other words, if I ended up there now, whether in Russia or in Belarus, I might not even make it to a prison or a camp. They’d simply tear me apart, because I fully and completely support Ukraine and consider Lukashenko a tyrant, just like Putin.
Crossing the border is science fiction for me right now. I live in Kharkiv and rent an apartment; the most I can do is get to the nearest checkpoint within the region, where they check documents and that’s it. The police and the SBU would take me in and interrogate me, even though I have no incriminating material — not on my phone, not anywhere. With this mobilization going on, TRCs are everywhere, and I run from them. Once, they [TRC officers] took my bicycle after I got away — spite, for not catching me.
I see the bombing, I see people dying. There are constant strikes here now, day and night — drones and missiles. Just today [August 12, 2026], there were already two strikes. We don’t go to shelters; we just go down to the first floor of our building each time. And how is that supposed to work anyway, when the all-clear on an air raid siren sounds and then a minute later it’s announced again? Am I supposed to run down from the fourth floor every single time?
I’d gladly take my wife and leave — the Netherlands, Germany, France, Canada, anywhere I could live in peace and keep working. My wife is Ukrainian, from Donbas, and works in retail. Her documents are in order, but she won’t leave without me. And if our roles were reversed, I wouldn’t leave without her either.
I don’t use banks — I pay for everything in cash and get paid in cash. My salary, as you can imagine, isn’t much, just pennies. It covers rent and the gas and electric bills.
I don’t know how to get legal status. I’ve tried consulting lawyers, but it’s all just a way to drain your money, with no meaningful results — one consultation costs 3,000 hryvnias, and I simply can’t afford that. There are scammers and con artists everywhere, and I don’t trust them. I live in constant fear, just waiting for some kind of change for people like me. I know other people here in Kharkiv in the same situation, with expired documents.
I have two children in Belarus, a 16-year-old son and a 28-year-old daughter. My cousin and aunt are there too, but I don’t talk to them — they support Russia and Belarus, get everything from television, and don’t see what’s really happening. Of course it’s hard without my children, but I can’t force my way into their heads and explain what’s actually going on.
I love Ukraine, despite the madhouse and the bombing here. Why not consider it my homeland if I’m comfortable here? Home, if you’ll excuse the expression, is wherever your ass is warm. Besides, my mother is buried here, and my brother and nephews are here too. I don’t miss Belarus at all. As long as Lukashenko’s regime is in power, I don’t want to go back.
Ilya, 46, lives in Poland
I’m from Minsk. My wife, our son, and I left in February 2022 — I was afraid Belarus would get pulled into the war too. We went to Georgia first, for three months, to see how things were, then went back to Belarus and got visas for Poland. I work in IT, so getting a work visa wasn’t hard, since Poland had a program for attracting highly skilled specialists.
There was a lot of back-and-forth over whether to stay. Then mobilization began in Russia, rumors spread that it would happen in Belarus too, and I’m a reserve officer. We decided to go temporarily — but that “temporarily” turned into three and a half years.
I face risks in Belarus because I donated to organizations designated as extremist there, including the ”BYSOL Solidarity Fund.” Cooperating with that organization carries the risk of a criminal case and up to five years in prison.
After the 2020 protests, a lot of things were criminalized — it got almost absurd, with people detained over social media comments, over participating in neighborhood chat groups. Then things quieted down somehow; it seemed like the protests had been broken up and things had calmed down. But apparently the authorities decided to go after everyone. They started identifying people through photos, Facebook comments, and donations. It became clear these weren’t one-off actions meant to scare people — they genuinely wanted to reach every dissenter and participant in any kind of activity in 2020. Now, if you’ve spent a long time abroad, you’re guaranteed an interview with a KGB officer at the border. I don’t want to find out.
My Belarusian passport expired in the fall of 2024. I don’t expect anything good from Lukashenko, and I’m glad he can no longer harm me, that he can’t reach me. But not having a passport is very inconvenient — banking, travel, any contract you might need to sign are all at risk. Santander and Crédit Agricole told me they don’t open accounts without a passport. I went to several branches of the Polish bank PKO, and only the third one accepted my podróży document.
Credit to the Polish government for understanding the situation well. The podróży document replaces a passport in many cases — you can travel abroad with it, and visas can be put in it — and mine was renewed even though my passport had already expired. The Belarusian opposition in exile does a lot to help the diaspora and political refugees. They meet with heads of state, explain the situation, and push for specific laws and regulations. It’s largely thanks to them that local politicians distinguish between Belarus’s official authorities and the Belarusians who have left the country.
My wife and I are glad we got our son out. He’ll turn 18 soon, and the war still hasn’t ended; here, he definitely won’t be drafted or sent to the front. He finished eighth grade in Poland, learned Polish within a year, and enrolled in a technical college to study programming. The move was hard on him — he didn’t even get to say goodbye to his friends — and the first year was full of sadness and depression. Now he’s grown up and understands what’s happening in the world and why we left. He doesn’t have much desire to go back.
Our elderly parents stayed behind in Belarus. It’s depressing that I can’t go, but I hope it’s not forever — not for decades. The war needs to end, and then some kind of change will start. Or our leaders’ health will fail them.
In Poland, there’s no feeling of home, of certainty, of any real sense of your future, and at my age that’s not very comfortable anymore. On the plus side, you’re not afraid they’ll come for you, lock you up, or beat you with a baton. You don’t realize you’d been living in constant fear until you move abroad. Here there’s none of that — you can speak your mind freely, you don’t delete your message history or photos from your phone. You don’t have to choose between putting up with injustice and fighting it. You just live a normal life.
My advice to Russians: prepare for emigration in advance. Renew all your documents for the maximum possible term while you still can, make copies of everything, and get powers of attorney for relatives in case you need to handle things remotely. Choose a country that’s more accommodating toward emigrants and Russians and more understanding of the situation — Spain, for example, decided in 2026 to recognize expired Belarusian passports as valid.
Another piece of advice: stick together, and act collectively wherever possible.
It’s a shame the Russian opposition hasn’t managed to build any authoritative, centralized structures that could represent Russian émigrés, help solve their problems, and influence the policies of Western countries. That would help a great deal.

articles.title: Russian drones kill at least nine in strikes targeting warehouses and ports in Ukraine – Europe live
articles.body:
Russia's actions are 'reckless, dangerous and a threat to life,' Nato's Rutte warns, but says they only strengthen resolve to help Ukraine
In his speech, Rutte repeatedly praises Germany’s role within Nato, and then eventually gets to his stark assessment of the situation in Ukraine – and Europe.
He says:
“Russia’s brutal attacks against Ukraine are unrelenting. Russia is suffering enormous losses, now estimated at more than 40,000 killed or seriously wounded every month. Think about it for a moment. Over 40,000 every month.
Despite those heavy losses, Putin shows no willingness to bring the war to an end.
Instead, Russia repeatedly strikes Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, often targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and at the same time, the list of Russia’s malign hybrid activities across Europe grows longer and longer: cyber-attacks, sabotage, arson, airspace violations, drone incidents.
…
The latest hostile actions by Russia are reckless, dangerous and a threat to life. But we are not intimidated. We know these are the tactics of a desperate regime that is failing to meet its objectives in Ukraine. Putin thinks he can divide us, destabilise us and weaken our support for Ukraine. But he will fail. These malicious actions are having the opposite effect.”
Malta warned of corruption crisis after Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict sends ‘chill down the spine’
Juliette Garside
Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.
At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.”
“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.
Macron meets Stubb for talks on Ukraine, European security
Over in France, it looks like Emmanuel Macron is focusing not only on future space endeavours, but also on very down-to-earth issues of European security.
Aside from his space conference (11:01), he met for talks with Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb on “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, European security, and ways to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy.”
“Finland and France are closer than ever before. France is an important partner for Ukraine and the whole of Europe,” Stubb said.
Despite its low-key format, the meeting is worth noting given Stubb’s central role to all diplomatic efforts on Ukraine, as he is one of the few European leaders that have a genuinely good rapport with the US president, Donald Trump, and so is closely involved in all relevant discussions on Ukraine, Russia and European security.
By the way, we will be liveblogging the Swedish election night for you here on Europe Live, straight from Stockholm, so make sure to join us on Sunday night.
Swedish Muslims challenge far right ahead of key election this weekend
Swedes will vote on Sunday in a tight election that will be another litmus test of whether far-right parties should join the government, as the Sweden Democrats, with roots in the neo-Nazi fringe, poll at around 19% of the vote and could join the ruling centre-right coalition led by Ulf Kristersson.
The Guardian’s Ashifa Kassam visited Sweden recently to take stock of the atmosphere in the country ahead of the vote, and look at how migration and religion are being weaponised for political purposes.
“Not far from one of Scandinavia’s biggest shopping malls, Kashif Virk stood on the pavement, handing out flyers and smiling at those who passed by. On a cloudy Tuesday afternoon, the Swedish-born imam had taken to the street to invite people to ask him anything they had ever wanted to know about Islam.
For years, Sweden’s far right has peddled its own, distorted view of Islam, portraying it as being at odds with Swedish values. The Ask-a-Muslim – or Fråga en Muslim – campaign, conceived by Virk in 2017, was his way of fighting back.”
Rutte’s visit is not the only show in town in Berlin today, as the leader of the United Arab Emirates is paying a state visit to Germany, and is expected to sign off on multi-billion deals on energy, technology, and transport.
Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is getting the full treatment and was welcomed with military honours by president Frank-Walter Steinmeier this morning, before meeting chancellor Friedrich Merz later today.
AFP noted that the UAE is Germany’s largest trading partner in the Gulf, with bilateral trade topping $15bn last year, and many big German companies have a presence there including BMW, Siemens, ThyssenKrupp and rail operator Deutsche Bahn.
The UAE meanwhile has made major investments in Germany, including in the chemical industry and offshore wind power.
Inexplicably, there is no joint press conference scheduled as part of the visit.
Just as Rutte and Wadephul talk about the role played by the US in today’s Nato, German chancellor Friedrich Merz gets in early with his comments on tomorrow’s 9/11 anniversary in the US.
“That the 25th anniversary of 9/11 is approaching soon touches us deeply. We Germans felt back then just how much connects us with our American friends. We knew: the terrorist attacks were also aimed at our way of life.
Germany is also today determined, together with the USA, to stand up for the values that define and unite us: freedom, democracy, and respect.
But that doesn’t change the underlying tensions between the administrations in Germany and the US – after all, only yesterday Merz cancelled his planned phone call with Trump, with media speculating about a possible link with the US president’s public show of support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (Europe Live, Wednesday).
Wadephul and Rutte get asked if they are sure the US would still defend Europe.
Rutte says “absolutely” and that he has “no doubt.”
He then goes on his usual spiel about “a big irritant” in the US’s relationship with Nato on spending, and how it needs to be resolved and how Europe is “finally addressing it.”
He says there are sometimes some answers or social media posts that “are hard to understand” – a likely swipe at Trump’s recent comments on the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt – but generally “we really have no doubt that the United States are ready to defend us and will be staying with us.”
Germany needs to 'show we have learned our lesson' from Weimar Republic, foreign minister says
Wadephul also makes a very strong point there, as he says:
“We have to defend our democracy. And, Germany knows from the Weimar Republic, what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system? And now I think we have to show that we have learned our lesson.”
Wadephul gets asked about how to convince the electorate to spend more on defence, also in the context of the UK government’s internal discussions on that point.
He says you need to speak with the electorate and explain that Nato and supporting Ukraine “has the purpose of securing our freedom and security in Europe.”
He says "that is what Andy Burnham is also doing in the UK, as far as I ma able to follow it from here.”
When he eventually gets round to the question, Rutte says, erm, it’s not for him to comment on party politics.
“We have an alliance of 32 countries and whoever is elected is then the elected leadership of that country,” he says.
He acknowledges that politics is “rough” and “a contact sport,” but eventually does not address the underlying point anyway.
He gets pressed on that further, with a specific reference to France and Germany, and what would it mean for the alliance if far-right parties won power there.
But once again seeks to evade the question, as he effectivelly says “let’s see what happens.”
“I have every confidence that whoever is elected in whichever election will stay the course when it comes to the key elements of investing in defence, making sure Ukraine will not lose this war.”
Wadephul goes back to the Leipzig drone attack, stressing its hybrid character: both in terms of actual, physical damage, but also in terms of its influence on “hurting … social coherence in Germany” and potentially influencing regional elections in Germany.
He says “we have to be prepared for that, and we have to stand together” in a show of resilience against radical forces within the country.
Rutte doesn’t immediately answer a question on whether he is concerned by the rising support for far-right parties, but instead repeatedly praises Germany for its response to the Leipzig incident.
'We cannot be naive' about the threat posed by Russia, Nato's Rutte says
Wadephul talks about his recent experience of visiting Ukraine, and seeing “raid alerts not only by night, but also the whole day over.”
But he says, despite that, you could see high spirits from the Ukrainians who are ready to defiantly keep defending their country.
Rutte says Russia remains to pose long-term threat to Europe, with its entire economy focused on defence and war preparations.
He says “we cannot be naive” about Russia in what feels like a bit of a swipe at suggestions of peace talks with Moscow as he has no illusions:
“I know you will always have people telling you: oh, if you would only sit down with Putin and this and that… This is long-term. It is a threat. We cannot be naive.”
Nato's Europeans 'increasingly understand taking greater responsibility for our own security is not optional,' Rutte says
Rutte says “there was a belief that we could continue doing more with less, and that the United States would keep doing the heavy lifting for us,” but this has changed in the last few years.
“I see a real mindset shift. Europeans increasingly understand that taking greater responsibility for our own security is not optional. That rebuilding our armed forces is indeed essential … increasing our defence industrial base is not only good for our security, it is good for our economies too. And that security is not something the US should do for us, but with us.”
Russia's actions are 'reckless, dangerous and a threat to life,' Nato's Rutte warns, but says they only strengthen resolve to help Ukraine
In his speech, Rutte repeatedly praises Germany’s role within Nato, and then eventually gets to his stark assessment of the situation in Ukraine – and Europe.
He says:
“Russia’s brutal attacks against Ukraine are unrelenting. Russia is suffering enormous losses, now estimated at more than 40,000 killed or seriously wounded every month. Think about it for a moment. Over 40,000 every month.
Despite those heavy losses, Putin shows no willingness to bring the war to an end.
Instead, Russia repeatedly strikes Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, often targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and at the same time, the list of Russia’s malign hybrid activities across Europe grows longer and longer: cyber-attacks, sabotage, arson, airspace violations, drone incidents.
…
The latest hostile actions by Russia are reckless, dangerous and a threat to life. But we are not intimidated. We know these are the tactics of a desperate regime that is failing to meet its objectives in Ukraine. Putin thinks he can divide us, destabilise us and weaken our support for Ukraine. But he will fail. These malicious actions are having the opposite effect.”

Ukraine Knocks Out 17 Russian Air Defense Systems, Six Bridges and 20+ Depots in August
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck 17 Russian air defense systems, six bridges, more than 20 storage facilities, and over 30 command posts in August as part of a sustained campaign targeting Russia’s operational rear and military-economic capabilities, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on September 10.
According to the ministry, the strikes were carried out using middle-strike capabilities as Ukraine continues to expand attacks against Russian military targets at operational depth.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A major focus of the August operations was Russian air defense infrastructure. Ukrainian forces struck positions of S-400 Triumf systems in Gelendzhik and Russia’s Bryansk region, as well as Pantsir systems in Yeysk and Tor systems in the Rostov region. Buk-M3 and Strela-10 air defense systems were also targeted in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine’s Luhansk region, including near Kreminna.
Ukrainian forces also destroyed several Russian radar stations, according to the ministry. Among them were a long-range Nebo-U radar in temporarily occupied Sevastopol, as well as Nebo-SV, Kasta, and Podlet radar systems. Electronic warfare equipment was also targeted, including a Peresvet-M system in temporarily occupied Luhansk.
The ministry said degrading Russian radar, air defense, and electronic warfare capabilities is intended to create opportunities for Ukrainian weapons to penetrate deeper into Russia’s rear.
Alongside air defense systems, Ukrainian forces continued targeting Russian military logistics. Strikes hit railway bridges near Chonhar, Vladyslavivka, and Svitlodolynske, as well as road bridges across the Seym River in Russia’s Kursk region and the Molochna River in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region. A crossing over the Mokri Yaly River in the Donetsk region was also targeted.
More than 20 ammunition and logistics depots, as well as repair facilities, were struck in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories and Russian regions bordering Ukraine, according to the ministry. Such attacks are intended to disrupt supply routes and reduce the combat effectiveness of Russian units.
Ukraine also continued targeting infrastructure used for Russian unmanned systems and uncrewed maritime vessels. A base for uncrewed surface vessels in Russian-occupied Chornomorske, Crimea, was among the facilities struck during August.
More than 30 strikes were carried out against command posts, storage sites, and launch positions associated with Russian attack drones in the Bryansk and Donetsk regions and Russian-occupied Crimea. Ukrainian forces also disabled several ground-based relay stations used to control Geran and Gerbera attack drones, according to the ministry.
Middle-strike weapons were additionally used against Russian command facilities, including primary and reserve command posts in Russian-occupied Donetsk, an FSB unit in Shchaslyvtseve, and a drone training center in Russian-occupied Luhansk.
The middle-strike operations form part of Ukraine’s broader campaign to push attacks deeper into Russia’s rear. In August, Ukrainian long-range strikes reached targets more than 1,500 kilometers from the state border, hitting critical components of Russia’s military-industrial and energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Middle East on brink of World War III, warns Iranian lawmaker among escalating tensions - report
articles.body:
Iranian lawmaker Kamran Ghazanfari said that the region is “practically on the brink of World War III.”
The report of his comments appeared in Iran International. Ghazanfari has been known for some outlandish claims. For instance, he claimed in the past that Iran’s president Ebrahim Raisi was assassinated by Israel and its allies in 2024.
The Ghazanfari comments are interesting because they likely illustrate how some of Iran’s more extremist politicians and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) elites view the war. They see it as a regional and global conflict.
The Islamic Republic has worked with Russia and China and has hopes that it can challenge the US-led world order. Iran has long portrayed its Islamic Revolution as a unique event that would transform the region and the world.
This goes back to the fact that Iranian Islamists believed they were presenting a new path during the Cold War that was different from those of the American and Soviet blocs. That changed in the 1990s when the Soviet Union declined.
Iran positions itself on side of a new world order
While Iran has at times considered reconciliation with the United States, it has also sought to position itself alongside countries that want a new world order. Weakening the US and pushing it out of the Middle East is a key goal of Tehran.
Iran International noted on September 9: “Ghazanfari, a Tehran representative in the parliament, said that we are ‘practically on the brink of World War III’ and considered the expansion of the war between Russia and Ukraine and the increase in tension between world powers as grounds for the formation of a widespread conflict.”
The report noted that he made the comments in an interview with the official Iranian Labour News Agency (ILNA).
“Ghazanfari said that NATO’s support for Ukraine in its war with Russia - and Moscow’s tensions with Britain and Germany - have increased the possibility of the conflict spreading to other European countries. He also called the US-China dispute over Taiwan another area of widespread conflict in the world.”
In the interview, Ghazanfari also focused on Iran’s plan to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). “According to him, there is a possibility that this issue will be put on the parliament’s agenda again.”
In the past, he has critiqued the chances of a US deal. For instance, in June he criticized the memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US. At the time, it seemed America and Iran might be able to reach an agreement. Ghazanfari said that any deal with the US would lack legitimacy and not be binding.
At the time, Iran International reported that “Iranian lawmaker Kamran Ghazanfari” said in a “warning to the negotiating team” that they should not cross any of the supreme leader’s red lines.
US reportedly threatens Iran, members of negotiation team
“Ghazanfari added that the United States had repeatedly threatened Iran and members of its negotiating team during the two-month talks, saying any deal reached under such conditions would have no validity under international law,” Iran International said.
Ghazanfari has also warned in the past about American and Israeli plans for a broader military operation. He claimed that the US might seize Iranian islands.”
“Evidence and signs show that the United States and Israel are planning a large-scale operation. They probably intend to seize some of our islands in the south and have brought many forces and equipment into the region,” he said.
Iran’s regime is currently continuing attacks in the region. Its recent attacks on Jordan and threats to attack tankers indicate that it wants to show that it can respond in kind to any US strikes and is telegraphing that it will not back down.

articles.title: Satellite images confirm Ukraine’s strike on Russian warship
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Defense Forces struck Russia's Novorossiysk naval base overnight on September 8-9, hitting the frigate Admiral Essen and starting a fire on its superstructure.
- Ukraine's General Staff also reported hits on the frigate Admiral Makarov, the small missile ship Buyan-M and the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck Russia’s naval base at Novorossiysk overnight on September 8-9, hitting the Kalibr-missile frigate Admiral Essen and starting a fire on its deck superstructure, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence agency, known as HUR.
HUR said operators from its Active Operations Department carried out the strike as part of a joint deep-strike operation with other branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, targeting both port infrastructure and the Project 11356 frigate. Ukraine’s General Staff separately said the attack also hit a second Kalibr-capable frigate, the Admiral Makarov, the Project 21631 small missile ship Buyan-M, and the Project 22160 patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Robert Brovdi said the operation additionally destroyed several Russian missile boats in the port, a Su-33 fighter jet and a Mi-8 helicopter near Anapa, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) northwest of Novorossiysk, along with two air-defense radar systems near Gelendzhik. Ukraine has not disclosed how many drones or missiles took part in the operation.
Satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian OSINT monitoring group Exilenova+ shows fires and apparent damage at the port consistent with the reported strikes on the Admiral Essen, the Admiral Makarov and the Buyan-M. The same channel said the attack combined drones with at least one Ukrainian Neptune cruise missile, a detail that has not appeared in HUR’s or the General Staff’s own statements on the operation.
Both the Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov have been hit before. Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck both frigates in August 2026, along with the Vasily Bykov, in an earlier raid on the same base. Novorossiysk has served as the Black Sea Fleet’s main operating base since repeated Ukrainian strikes pushed Russian warships out of Sevastopol in occupied Crimea.
Russian officials in Novorossiysk said debris from intercepted drones struck a church, industrial sites and residential buildings, killing four people and injuring about 30. Moscow has not issued its own account of damage to the naval vessels named by Ukraine.
The extent of damage to the Admiral Essen, the Admiral Makarov, the Buyan-M and the Vasily Bykov has not been independently confirmed, and Ukraine’s General Staff said assessments of some of the reported strikes were still being finalized.

articles.title: Defense Forces use “middle strike” capabilities to hit 17 Russian air defense systems and 30 command posts in August
articles.body:
Defense Forces use “middle strike” capabilities to hit 17 Russian air defense systems and 30 command posts in August
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense.
Among the targets struck were 17 air defense systems, six bridges, more than 20 warehouses, and more than 30 command posts.
In accordance with the President’s directive, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and units of the Defense Forces are systematically working to intensify strikes deep into enemy territory.
Every destroyed radar station, air defense system, and electronic warfare system opens the way for strikes deep into the rear of the Russian Federation’s army. Destroyed bridges complicate logistics. Struck warehouses and command posts reduce the combat readiness of enemy units.
To ensure the unimpeded operation of Ukrainian weapons systems, the destruction of Russian air defense systems continued in August.
In particular, the following S-400 air defense systems were struck: “Triumf” (Gelendzhik and Bryansk Oblast, Russian Federation), “Pantsir” (Yeysk, Russian Federation), “Tor” (Rostov Oblast, Russian Federation), “Buk-M3” (Luhansk Oblast), and “Strela-10” (Kreminna, Luhansk Oblast).
A number of radar stations were also destroyed, including the long-range “Nebo-U” radar in the temporarily occupied Sevastopol, the “Nebo-SV” radar, the “Kasta” and “Podlyot” stations, as well as electronic warfare systems, notably the “Peresvet-M” in the temporarily occupied Luhansk.
The Ukrainian Defense Forces continued to systematically strike at the Russian Federation’s logistical arteries.
The “Syvash” railway bridges in the Chongar area, near Vladyslavivka and Svitlodolynske, as well as road bridges across the Seim River in the Kursk Oblast and the Molochna River in the Zaporizhzhia region, were targeted. A crossing over the Mokri Yaly River in the Donetsk region was also struck.
In addition to infrastructure facilities, the Defense Forces struck more than 20 warehouses containing logistical supplies and ammunition, as well as repair bases in the temporarily occupied territories and in the border regions of the Russian Federation.
In August, the systematic identification and destruction of Russian targets associated with the use of unmanned systems and naval vessels continued.
A base for unmanned naval craft in Chernomorsk (Crimea) was destroyed.
More than 30 strikes were also carried out against command centers, storage facilities, and launch sites for attack UAVs, particularly in the Bryansk region of the Russian Federation, the Donetsk region, and in the temporarily occupied Crimea.
A number of ground-based relay stations used to control “Geran/Gerbera”-type strike UAVs were disabled, weakening the enemy’s ability to coordinate drone attacks.
Russian military command posts were struck by “middle strike” weapons, including the main and backup command posts in the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk, an FSB unit in Shchaslyvtseve (Kherson region), and a UAV training center in the temporarily occupied city of Luhansk.
“The systematic use of ‘middle strike’ capabilities allows Ukraine to systematically reduce Russia’s military potential and disrupts the stability of the enemy army’s command and control system,” the Ministry of Defense noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, in July, the Ukrainian Defense Forces continued their systematic campaign to strike Russian operational rear areas and logistics routes using “middle strike” capabilities, focusing on disrupting supply lines in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions, as well as in the temporarily occupied Crimea.

articles.title: Ukrainian Navy: Russia's Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk hit by Neptune missile
articles.body:
Ukrainian Navy: Russia's Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk hit by Neptune missile
The Russian frigate Admiral Essen, which was struck on the night of 8-9 September, was hit by a Ukrainian-made Neptune missile.
Source: Ukrainian Navy; a Ukrainian OSINT project Exilenova+
Details: Ukrainian forces attacked the Russian warship with a missile during a combined strike by Ukraine's defence forces involving units of the Unmanned Systems Forces, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and other elements of the Ukrainian military.
Quote from the Navy: "Navy personnel used a Neptune missile to hit the Admiral Essen frigate, a carrier of Kalibr cruise missiles."
More details: OSINT project Exilenova+ posted a satellite image of the Russian base in the city of Novorossiysk following the overnight attack. DIU reported that the frigate's superstructure was hit.
For reference: The Admiral Essen is a Russian Project 11356R Burevestnik-class frigate, launched in 2014 and commissioned into Russia's Black Sea Fleet. The vessel took part in missile strikes on Syria in 2017 and has been involved in strikes on Ukraine since 2022. It is armed with 3M14 Kalibr cruise missiles, the Shtil-1 surface-to-air missile system and a 100mm A-190 gun.
The R-360 Neptune cruise missile is designed to destroy ships with a displacement of up to 5,000 tonnes and, like other missiles of its class, can be launched from land, surface and air platforms. In April 2022, a Neptune missile was used to sink the Russian cruiser Moskva.
In late 2025, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was also using the upgraded Long Neptune version. The Neptune-D system uses RK360L cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,000 km and a 260kg warhead. The missile is designed to strike both land and maritime targets.
Background: It was reported earlier that Ukraine's defence forces and the Unmanned Systems Forces struck a number of Russian military assets in Novorossiysk and Anapa on the night of 8-9 September. Confirmed hits included a Su-33 carrier-based fighter and an Mi-8 helicopter, two Russian radars – a Kasta-2E2 and a 92N6 radar from an S-300/S-400 air defence system – near Gelendzhik, as well as the Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.
