articles.title: SBI suspects SBU official of organizing ammunition storage in Mila village near Kyiv
articles.body:
Officers of the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) have notified a department head in charge of supply and logistics at the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) of suspicion for overseeing the arrangement and operation of an artillery ammunition depot in the village of Mila near Kyiv.
"It has been established that when deciding to locate the warehouse in a former vegetable storage facility, he failed to take all control measures regarding the security of storing explosives and ammunition. In addition, the warehouse was illegally located near residential buildings. The premises not only failed to meet requirements for weapons storage facilities, but its placement was not coordinated with relevant law enforcement structures and air defense units. The official also failed to take measures to minimize the risks of simultaneous destruction of a large quantity of ammunition by the enemy," the press service of the SBI reported.
Russian unmanned aerial vehicles launched a strike on the facility, triggering ammunition detonation and a fire that spread to neighboring premises.
As a result of the detonation, 35 people were killed. In addition, 191 private residential houses, 14 apartment buildings, a police station, garages, a restaurant, a nursing home, a shop, and a logistics center were damaged, as well as 24 vehicles, including a police service car and a fire truck.
The official has been notified of suspicion of inaction of military authority committed under martial law (Part 4 of Article 426 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
Pechersky District Court of Kyiv remanded him in custody as a preventive measure with an alternative of bail.
The article's sanction provides for punishment in the form of imprisonment for a term of up to 10 years.
His name and the specific department he headed have not been disclosed.
As reported by the Prosecutor General's Office of Ukraine on Thursday, after a similar tragedy in the city of Vyshneve (Kyiv region), measures were initiated to liquidate the depot and remove the ammunition, but as of August 28, when the occupiers attacked the storage facilities with drones, these measures had not been completed. It is emphasized that the depot was located less than 100 meters from residential buildings, and requirements regarding the permissible quantity of ammunition and its dispersal—intended to reduce the risk of simultaneous detonation and damage to surrounding facilities—were not observed.
"The investigation is also examining the circumstances of improper security control over the facility and the failure to take measures to strengthen its air defense cover. Forensic explosives and fire safety evaluations have been ordered in the proceedings... All circumstances are being established, as well as other individuals whose decisions, actions, or inaction may have affected the scale of the consequences of the Russian attack," the agency reported.
Earlier, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that such tragedies are unacceptable, especially after a similar event occurred in Vyshneve near Kyiv, calling it the result of "terrible negligence by those who stored explosives right next to people." He reported that criminal proceedings had been opened regarding the incident and called for a full investigation into all the facts of what transpired.

articles.title: Trump vows to hit ‘a lot more’ Iranian tankers
articles.body:
Trump vows to hit ‘a lot more’ Iranian tankers
President Donald Trump claims that the US has already taken out “about nine” Iranian oil tankers and threatened to attack “a lot more,” as the two countries trade strikes on commercial and military vessels around the Strait of Hormuz.
US Central Command has confirmed that it destroyed eight Iranian crude carriers in two recent operations – three on September 5 and another five on Tuesday – after accusing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of firing ballistic missiles at US warships.
“We’ve taken out about nine of their tankers,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. “You’re going to see a lot more.”
The president did not elaborate on potential targets or the timing of further attacks, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Iran would continue to lose tankers whenever it targets US naval vessels.
CENTCOM forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, Sept. 8, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and… pic.twitter.com/Gi8a2tloN1
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) September 8, 2026
“They lost five more last night. Four were damaged. One was sunk. So they’ll continue to pay a price for that,” Rubio said, adding that the US will continue to “strangle them economically.”
CENTCOM said the five vessels struck on Tuesday were the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1, and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and the Derya near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub. US forces ordered the crews to abandon the ships before they were attacked and “rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM said.
Iran has retaliated by claiming attacks on ten vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, including two US Navy ships and eight tankers. CENTCOM has denied that its warships were hit. Iran also launched ballistic missiles toward the Al-Azraq air base in Jordan, while the IRGC warned tanker crews near Bahrain and Kuwait to abandon their vessels ahead of potential attacks.
The renewed confrontation has driven Brent crude back above $100 a barrel amid concerns over further disruptions to one of the world’s most important energy corridors.
Trump, however, predicted that oil prices would stabilize and that the broader war with Iran would end “immediately after” the November 3 US midterm elections, claiming that Iran has already lost and is attempting to hold out long enough to influence the vote.
“I think the war will end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer.”
Asked about the prospect of renewed negotiations with Tehran, Trump said his administration is “not looking for it,” although he acknowledged that talks could still take place.
“There is a lot more than nuclear,” he said with regard to an agreement, adding that other issues will now have to be put on the table.

articles.title: US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video

US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
US-operated Patriot batteries may have fired roughly 60 interceptor missiles to counter an Iranian barrage of just 20 ballistic missiles over Jordan, highlighting the enormous ammunition demands involved in defending against sustained ballistic attacks, Defense Express reported on September 9.
Iran struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan overnight, a facility used by US forces. Jordanian authorities said air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming ballistic missiles, while two fell before reaching their intended targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage from the attack, however, provides an unusually revealing look at how intensely Patriot batteries were operating during the engagement.
Defense Express estimated from available videos that approximately 60 Patriot interceptors may have been launched during the defense. Claims circulating online that as many as 100 were fired appear exaggerated, the outlet noted.
Even the lower estimate would mean roughly three interceptors launched for every Iranian ballistic missile in the salvo, although the exact number of Patriot missiles fired has not been officially confirmed.
Defense Express described several Patriot batteries as effectively operating in a “machine-gun” mode as they attempted to defeat the incoming missiles.
Video from the attack also appears to show Iran using ballistic missiles carrying cluster submunitions, adding another layer of difficulty to the interception effort.
The scale of Patriot expenditure is particularly notable because the systems protecting the area are believed to be operated by US forces rather than Jordanian crews.
Jordan has never publicly declared Patriot systems as part of its own inventory. The United States, however, has deployed Patriot batteries in the country when necessary to defend US facilities and support Jordanian airspace protection.
That distinction matters, Defense Express noted.
Previous cases of unusually high Patriot interceptor consumption against Iranian ballistic attacks could potentially be explained by limited experience among foreign operators.
US air-defense personnel have already spent more than six months responding to repeated Iranian ballistic missile attacks against American military installations since the beginning of Operation Epic Fury on February 28.
The crews therefore have substantial practical experience with this particular threat environment.
If the estimate of roughly 60 Patriot interceptors is accurate, the September 9 engagement illustrates that high missile consumption may be an inherent feature of defending against modern ballistic salvos rather than simply a consequence of inexperienced operators.
For Ukraine, which relies heavily on Patriot to stop Russian ballistic missiles, the episode also underscores a familiar problem: successful air defense can consume enormous quantities of some of the world’s most expensive and difficult-to-produce interceptors in a matter of minutes.
As Defense Express noted, the question is therefore not only whether Patriot can stop ballistic missiles, but how many interceptors must be available when a sustained barrage arrives.
Earlier, reports emerged that US forces may have used as many as 96 to 128 PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a single night while defending military bases in Jordan from an Iranian ballistic missile attack—potentially consuming up to 17% of estimated US stocks.

articles.title: Battlegroup South infantry begins assault on Druzhkovka — Russian Defense Ministry
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Units of Russia’s Battlegroup South, supported by unmanned systems crews, have secured positions on the outskirts of Druzhkovka (in the Donetsk People’s Republic), and infantry troops are already carrying out successful operations to storm the city, deputy company commander of the battlegroup’s separate unmanned systems regiment with the call sign Artist, said in a video released by the Russian Defense Ministry.
"Our crews have secured positions on the outskirts of Druzhkovka. The infantry is already attempting to storm the city itself — and quite successfully," Artist said.
He noted that the units are operating according to a standard plan: cutting off the enemy’s logistics to prevent the delivery of ammunition and supplies, and making maximum use of drones. "Drones are currently the most important deterrent and the key factor enabling our valiant infantry to advance," the service member added.
According to the deputy company commander, the enemy is trying to create the "right media image" for its audience by dropping flags and sending troop groups into populated areas, but these groups do not return. "Konstantinovka is ours, and we have already advanced far beyond Konstantinovka," he emphasized.
Ukraine loses up to 35 soldiers in 'pocket' in Kharkov region over past day
Ukrainian units have lost up to 35 military personnel in the "pocket" in the Kharkov Region over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry has reported.
"Over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s losses have amounted to up to 35 military personnel, one armored fighting vehicle, two ATVs and four ground robotic systems," the ministry stated.
Russian Armed Forces strike power substation at Nikolayev port
Russian forces struck the Trikhaty power substation, which supports the operation of the port of Nikolayev, overnight, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Trikhaty power substation, which supports the operation of the Nikolayev port, has been struck," the ministry said in a statement.
Earlier, the Russian Defense Ministry also reported that last night, the Russian Armed Forces continued to carry out group strikes on military-industrial facilities, Ukrainian seaports and ships, as well as logistics centers supporting the Ukrainian armed forces.
Russian forces tightening encirclement of Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
Russian troops are tightening the inner ring of the encirclement around Ukrainian units in the Kharkov Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"In the Kharkov region, units of the Battlegroup North are tightening the inner ring of the encirclement around enemy forces," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces hit facility producing unmanned boats, drones in Kiev
Russian forces used precision-guided weapons to hit a warehouse of an enterprise producing unmanned boats, drones and components for them in Kiev overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of strikes by precision-guided ground-launched and air-launched weapons, as well as attack unmanned aerial vehicles, [Russian forces] hit a warehouse of an enterprise producing unmanned boats and fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as components for them, in the city of Kiev," the ministry said.
Russia delivers group strikes on military industry sites, Ukraine’s sea ports
The Russian Armed Forces continued to deliver group strikes on Ukraine’s military industrial sites and sea ports overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces continued to deliver group strikes on Ukraine’s military industrial sites, sea ports and vessels, as well as logistics centers used in the interests of the Ukrainian military," the statement said.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian military depots in Nikolayev Region
The Russian Armed Forces delivered an overnight high-precision weapons strike on Ukrainian military and fuel and lubricant storage depots in the Nikolayev Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of attacks by high-precision ground-based and air-based weapons and strike drones, [Russian servicemen] struck the following targets in the Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region: <…> the Nikolayev-2 logistics centers used to store military cargo and equipment for the Ukrainian military, the Elektrotechnika logistics center used to store and distribute drones and their spare parts, the Dimetra company warehouse terminal used to store Ukrainian military equipment, the Zhovtnevoye warehouse terminal used to store fuel, lubricants, and Ukrainian military equipment. [Russian forces] also destroyed six tanks with fuel and lubricants intended for the supply of the Ukrainian military and five warehouses with military cargo," the statement said.
Russia hits Ukrainian Starokazachye checkpoint used for military purposes
The Russian Armed Forces delivered a high-precision overnight strike on the Starokazachye automobile checkpoint facilities in the Odessa region that was used to transport military cargo for the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of attacks by high-precision ground-based and air-based weapons and strike drones, [Russian servicemen] struck the Starokazachye automobile checkpoint logistics sites, which were used to transport military cargo into Ukraine," the statement said.
Russian forces strike logistics, energy facilities used by Ukrainian army in Nikolayev
Last night, the Russian Armed Forces carried out strikes with precision weapons against warehouses, logistics facilities, and energy infrastructure used by the Ukrainian armed forces in the city of Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Ground-and air-based precision weapon and attack drone strikes hit the following targets: <…> in the city of Nikolayev and the Nikolayev Region: the Nika Terra cargo terminal used to store fuel, lubricants, and military equipment of the Ukrainian armed forces (three tanks containing fuel and lubricants intended to supply the Ukrainian army and three storage facilities with military cargo were destroyed), as well as an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production facility and storage warehouse located on the terminal’s grounds; the Metro logistics center, used to store Ukrainian military cargo and equipment," the ministry said in a statement.
The Defense Ministry added that strikes were also carried out against the ATP YUTK logistics center, used to store military cargo and property intended to support the Ukrainian armed forces, and the Nova Poshta logistics center, used for the delivery, distribution, and storage of military cargo and materiel for the armed forces of Ukraine.

articles.title: Polish FM Sees Little Hope for Ukraine Peace Talks as Putin Holds Out
articles.body:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said Wednesday he was not optimistic about the prospect of peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, adding that Moscow continues to reject ceasefire proposals and has not softened its aims.
Sikorski was speaking in Latvia, where he took part in a meeting with the foreign ministers of Latvia, Ireland, Finland and Hungary, with talks covering Ukraine, EU enlargement, Russian hybrid activity and the Middle East.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
His comments come days after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow and then Kyiv in a renewed peace push, meeting Vladimir Putin before holding talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The Moscow talks produced no breakthrough, while Kyiv said it was ready to resume trilateral negotiations with the US and Russia.
Speaking alongside Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže at the Ādaži military base on Wednesday, Sikorski said: “Putin still believes he has two cards to play—mobilization and a harsh winter.
“So we must ensure that Ukraine’s cards—its ability to strike refineries and its ability to hold the front line—continue to be strengthened.”
Sikorski added, “The bigger picture is that Russia does not understand the psychology of democracies. We are slow to mobilize. But once we do, we can mobilize enormous resources.”
He also said Poland and Latvia faced many of the same Russian threats, including airspace violations, migration pressure, and sabotage.
Russian Drone Strike on Sumy Shopping Center Kills 2, Injures at Least 20
‘We’re not going to sit idly by.’
“We do not want to escalate the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next move,” Sikorski said.
NATO has a brigade based in Ādaži comprising nearly 3,000 troops, including more than 235 Polish soldiers. Poland has kept a military contingent in Latvia since 2017 as part of NATO’s strengthened eastern-flank presence.

articles.title: The World's Best Companies of 2026
articles.body:
The economy built around AI has continued to boom even as experts and leaders work to hammer out the technology's execution problem and debate the guardrails that should be put around it. Demand for AI chips remains strong, as Nvidia holds its top spot in TIME and Statista’s 2026 statistical ranking of the World’s Best Companies, highlighting top performing companies around the globe based on evaluations of employee satisfaction, revenue growth, and sustainability transparency. But new companies are also entering the scene as the AI boom reaches down the supply chain.
Companies like Wistron (no. 16), Lenovo (no. 51) and Zurich Insurance Group (no. 70) are new additions to the 2026 list. Major Nvidia supplier Wistron reports that the demand for its AI servers continues to exceed supply. The Taiwan-based manufacturing company recently opened a plant in Texas to ramp up production. Chinese computer company Lenovo, known for being a maker of devices like PCs, smartphones and tablets, saw annual profits rise to record sales driven by the newer AI server part of their business. And the wave of growing demand for physical infrastructure to support AI has created an opportunity for firms like Zurich Insurance Group to cash in on selling more data center construction-related insurance. Zurich plans to expand its dedicated insurance and risk management solution for large-scale data center projects soon into Europe and Latin America. S&P Global puts total insurable values for each data center at up to $30 billion per location.
Beyond AI, European defense technology companies are seeing cashflow as a result of European NATO allies committing in 2025 to spend a projected €800 billion on defense readiness by 2030. “The increased defense spending in Europe is actually one of the largest demand signals we have seen in generations,” says Hugues Lavandier, senior partner in McKinsey’s Aerospace & Defense Practice. A good portion of that spending is still going outside of Europe, but Lavandier “won't be surprised that we increasingly see more of that spend going to Europe for sovereignty reasons.” The war in Ukraine among other recent geopolitical tensions has shown Europe that the art of war fighting and the equipment needed is also changing. “The share of that money being spent on equipment is actually going up,” Lavandier says, especially on new technologies like drones and unmanned vehicles, and addressing technical challenges like navigation, electronic warfare, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
Traditional companies in the space like French defense electronics maker Thales (no. 22; up from no. 224 in 2025) and Italian defense and aerospace company Leonardo (no. 25; up from a no. 126 in 2025) are seeing uptick in orders. At the same time, “non-traditional players are entering into the field, especially as suppliers,” Lavandier says. “In particular, a number of automotive players have entered into the fray…sometimes even selling plants, making capacity available.” Thales, for example, recently announced a sovereign drone partnership with French carmaker Renault (no. 42). A number of new startups are also taking this opportunity to translate the investment into innovations, sometimes as standalone products or in partnership with other companies, similar to Anduril’s ventures in the U.S. For example, German drone-maker Quantum Systems, which is currently supplying armed forces in Ukraine, announced significant investment from German telecomm giant Deutsche Telekom (no. 7), which owns the T-mobile brand, and also announced a new partnership with Rheinmetall (no. 287) to co-create an anti-drone shield.

articles.title: Zaluzhny: lack of technology, funding prevents Ukraine from seizing initiative from Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience, but state funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited, which is why private investment can and must become a mutually beneficial solution for both sides, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny notes.
"Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience. No other country can offer more relevant experience for developing new arms, modernization, and tactics for their application. However, the lack of technology and funding prevents seizing the initiative from Russia and its partners," Zaluzhnyi said during a speech at the Defence & Resilience Tech Scale Up Showcase in London, the text of which was published in his column on the Interfax-Ukraine agency's website on Thursday.
He called on Ukraine's partners to increase financial and technological investments in arms production in Ukraine, not only to reduce Russia's military potential, but also to strengthen their own defense capabilities.
"State funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited. Therefore, private investments can and must become a beneficial solution for both sides. Creating clear mechanisms for cooperation with Great Britain at the institutional level will help attract private capital, technologies, and ultimately create new markets and develop long-term cooperation between the defense industries of Ukraine and its partners," the diplomat said.
Zaluzhnyi stated that Ukraine has gained significant experience in drone production, but the component base, and especially its production, currently remains outside Ukraine, which precludes possibilities for scaling and modernization in the long term, "where marketing gives way to strategy and the outline of victory finally becomes visible." "Even now, these investments are vital in countering urgent threats such as ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones," the former Commander-in-Chief emphasized.
He noted that achieving victory or a dignified peace requires systemic impact on Russia's ability to continue the war, rather than isolated technological solutions.
"Systemic impact means implementing strategies to achieve the main goal: victory over the enemy. Naturally, building such a systemic impact is possible only with appropriate strategies. These strategies must be based on implementing financial and technological policies that enable producing today what is needed tomorrow, or better yet, the day after tomorrow. And what is needed today should be taken from storage facilities as something produced yesterday. Defense production must be part of a war strategy, not the other way around, where war is made to justify someone's promises and profits. Only in this way is it possible to seize the initiative, impose one's will on the enemy, and demand terms from them," Zaluzhny concluded.

articles.title: Iran will strike 20 targets for every two hits by enemy, IRGC warns
articles.body:
Iran will strike 20 targets for every two hits by enemy, IRGC warns
TEHRAN— Iran will respond to any attack with a significantly larger number of strikes, the spokesman for the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday, warning that Tehran would target as many as 20 enemy positions if two or three Iranian targets were attacked.
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi made the remarks while speaking to reporters about the IRGC Navy's reported capture of a US unmanned submarine in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Iran's control and management of the strategic waterway had become "realized, certain and demonstrable."
He said Iran would use 'its established capabilities' in the Strait to respond to any hostile action.
"Any vessel that intends to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without taking Iran's management of the waterway into consideration will definitely not be able to pass through," Mohebbi said.
His comments underline the strategic importance Tehran attaches to the Strait, one of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints and a major conduit for global energy shipments. Iran has repeatedly emphasized that its geographic position along the northern shore of the waterway
gives it substantial leverage in any military confrontation in the Persian Gulf.
US naval forces have withdrawn
Mohebbi also addressed the deployment of US naval forces in the Persian Gulf before the beginning of the "US-Israeli war of aggression" against Iran.
He said between 30 and 40 US vessels and warships had previously been deployed inside the Persian Gulf but revealed that none remained in the area.
"Today, not even a single one of them is present in this area, and US warships have withdrawn at least 400 kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
The IRGC spokesman also sought to underscore Iran's ability to conduct strikes at considerable distances, saying advances in missiles and other weapons had expanded the range of Tehran's retaliatory options.
"We also hit an aircraft carrier a few days ago at a distance of about 500 kilometers," Mohebbi said.
He then issued a broader warning about the scale of any potential Iranian retaliation. "We have reached a point where if the enemy hits two or three of our targets, we will respond strongly with 20 targets," he said.
"The Islamic Republic will use this power to respond to the enemy's aggression and make the enemy regret continuing its aggression," Mohebbi added.
Deterrence through asymmetric capabilities
The remarks reflect a central element of Iran's military doctrine: seeking to deter attacks by demonstrating an ability to impose costs beyond the immediate battlefield.
Rather than relying solely on conventional force projection, Iran has invested heavily in missiles, drones, fast attack craft, naval mines and other asymmetric capabilities. The IRGC Navy has in particular developed tactics intended to exploit the geography of the Persian Gulf and Strait of
Hormuz, where narrow waterways and dense commercial traffic can complicate the operations of larger naval forces.
The Strait of Hormuz is especially significant because of its role in international energy markets. Millions of barrels of crude oil, condensate, and petroleum products pass through the waterway each day, making any sustained disruption potentially consequential for global oil supplies and prices.
For Tehran, however, the strategic value of Hormuz extends beyond its economic importance. Iranian officials have repeatedly presented control of the waterway as a component of national deterrence, arguing that the ability to threaten or restrict maritime traffic can raise the costs of military action against Iran.
Mohebbi's warning therefore appears intended not only as a battlefield threat but also as a message of deterrence: any attack on Iranian territory or military assets, Tehran says, could trigger retaliation on a substantially larger scale.
Such statements remind one not 'an eye for an eye,' but 'two eyes for an eye'."

articles.title: Ukroboronprom Reveals Designation of Palianytsia Missile-Drone
articles.body:
Ukroboronprom has revealed the designation of the Ukrainian-made Palianytsia missile-drone, which Ukraine’s Defense Forces use to strike targets in Russia.
The weapon was displayed under the designation UAV-290 at MSPO 2026, an international defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
Previously, the missile-drone was displayed at various exhibitions and events, sometimes as Palianytsia and other times as UAV-290.
It has now been officially confirmed for the first time that the two names refer to the same weapon, developed and manufactured by the state-owned Luch Design Bureau.
UAV-290 Palianytsia is designed to autonomously strike various stationary ground targets at the enemy’s tactical depth.
The missile-drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that provides a cruising speed of up to 800 km/h.
Palianytsia is launched from a trailer or semitrailer using a solid-fuel booster.
After launch, it switches to autonomous flight using an integrated INS+GPS navigation system.
The UAV-290 carries a 100 kg warhead and weighs 350 kg. Its stated range is 650 km.
The missile-drone is 3.5 meters long, with a 1.7-meter wingspan.
The manufacturer states that navigation and terminal guidance are performed using a combination of an autonomous inertial navigation system, immune to electronic warfare, and satellite navigation to correct deviations.
In August 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had used, among other weapons, the UAV-290 to strike a Russian Navy base and port in Novorossiysk.

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence strikes Kalibr missile carrier Admiral Essen again: details of Novorossiysk attack
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has reported that on the night of 8-9 September, operators from its Active Operations Department, as part of a joint deep-strike operation with other components of Ukraine's defence forces, struck infrastructure at the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk, as well as the Russian Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Details: The DIU reported that the strikes caused a fire on the superstructure of the Admiral Essen.
The Admiral Essen is a carrier of Kalibr cruise missiles, which Russia regularly uses to attack civilian infrastructure in Ukraine.
Ukraine's defence forces have struck the missile carrier on several previous occasions.
The Security Service of Ukraine and Ukraine's defence forces struck the Russian frigate on the night of 1-2 March 2026. At the time, a Ukrainska Pravda source in the service said that the damaged vessel was unable to launch Kalibr missiles.
In August, Ukraine's Defence Intelligence and defence forces also struck the Russian missile carriers Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov, as well as the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.

- On the night of 8-9 September, monitoring Telegram channels reported that drones had attacked Novorossiysk, causing a fire at a fuel oil terminal.
- The mayor of Novorossiysk confirmed that a fire had broken out but claimed it had been caused by falling debris. He did not name the facility that had been attacked or provide details about the extent of the damage or possible casualties.
- OSINT analysts reported that facilities at the port complex had been struck, damaging at least one tank at the Novorossiysk fuel oil terminal.
- The terminal is one of the key facilities of the Novorossiysk transport hub and forms part of the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, Russia's largest port by cargo turnover.

articles.title: Who should be in charge of the war?
articles.body:
Who should be in charge of the war?
This article is based upon my experiences in MOD UK and Army and Joint staff during the first Gulf War, Bosnia and with NATO in Kosovo.
I turned for support to my US defence academic friend and author Dr Thomas Durell Young a former member of staff at the US war college, and a former Policy Director in MOD Bulgaria Retired Colonel Vladimir Milenski. We all worked variously together with MOD Ukraine in 2014 and 2015 and between us on reform in over 15 other countries worldwide.
I apologize in advance to my female military friends for using he throughout this article, but it reflects simplicity of writing before translation not denigration of your amazing contribution to the national war effort.
Introduction: War Does Not Suspend Democratic Defence Governance, it severely tests it
In a democratic state at war, the defence system must be able to fight effectively while remaining politically controlled, legally accountable, strategically coherent and operationally agile.
War increases pressure on institutions, but the defence system must not become insular or a power on its own. War does not remove the need for clear authority, lawful responsibility and public accountability. On the contrary, the greater the stakes, the more important it is to know who governs defence, who advises government, who generates forces, who plans strategy and campaigns, who commands operations, and who answers for results. Today this is not totally clear in Ukraine.
The institutional question is therefore not primarily one of terminology. Different democratic states use different titles for organisations and posts.
What matters is whether these offices form a coherent system in which authority, responsibility, military advice, operational command, force generation, political control and accountability are clearly separated where necessary and integrated where useful – and most importantly society can see who is in charge and responsible for each task.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork. The fastest and best process is always two friends working together with a common purpose. Lack of trust, institutional arrogance, poor teamwork, bureaucracy or unclear tasks lead to delay – and delay kills.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition.
I have been lucky to work in a combined MOD/General Staff in UK with teams of officers and civil servants serving together. Meetings contained staff from all relevant HQs from MOD to units and many key decisions could be made and implemented immediately without need for bureaucracy. The civilian component came with different, less narrow thinking and skills, and added to achieving results hugely. Sharing work openly is vastly better than strict ownership.
In Ukraine, the main headquarters are the MOD and the General Staff (GS) (Most countries would call this HQ, Defence Staff as it is more than just army). We suggest a third strand is needed as Joint Staff, which should manage the fighting. UK and many NATO countries have an operational Joint Staff HQ and US have the regional combatant commands (COCOMS) reflecting their world view. Together, these three HQs would form a leadership triangle with clear and separate tasks. I have worked variously at all three levels. Depending on the issue in need of resolution, one headquarters leads the staff work, while the others support it.
The next day the task and leadership requirement may be totally different. States that inherit command structures from the Soviet military tradition and then introduce institutions associated with modern democratic and NATO ways of defence management are always challenged in who does what, how and when.
The problem is not that one idea, or vocabulary is "Eastern" and another "Western." The problem is that mixed systems often create parallel chains of authority, overlapping staff, unclear responsibility and commanders who are held accountable for outcomes without being given the authority or resources to achieve them. The current Ukrainian Joint Staff is a case in hand. It was given a role on the battlefield for which it was not intended. And in truth, it was never Joint either.
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the central principle should be simple: responsibility must follow authority. No institution or part of an institution should be able to use power without accountability, and no commander should be given responsibility without sufficient authority and resources to complete the task.
The Ministry of Defence: Civilian Authority, Policy, Resources and Accountability
The Ministry of Defence is the civilian political–administrative authority responsible for governing and enabling defence. In a democratic state, MOD is an arm of government and not an operational headquarters. It should not function as a parallel military command. Its legitimacy comes from constitutional authority, ministerial responsibility, parliamentary oversight and the rule of law.
In wartime, the responsibilities of the Minister remain the same, but he must do them faster and with more focus. He not only has to lead the whole defence system but also be a hands–on manager for MOD encouraging the staff to be proactive, supportive, innovative, and fast working. His ministry must also be operational 24/7, ready and able to react to emergencies. And the strong political role of this post is why a civilian, preferably an experienced politician, should always be appointed.
Military ministers may think and understand well the fighting task but are unused to the political and civil signals. They rarely understand the requirements for political briefing, networking and consensus building to get the best overall defence result.
The ministry task is complex. It must translate national political objectives into defence policy and strategic guidance; managing resources, the budget, procurement, mobilisation policy, personnel policy, international assistance, defence industry and sustainment. It must coordinate with government, parliament, other ministries, allies and civil emergency structures; and at the same time ensure legality, transparency, democratic oversight and anti–corruption controls.
The minister must also personally keep the defence committee constantly briefed about problems with any of the above tasks and especially the possible requirements for new or changed laws. Some Ministers in Ukraine have seen working with Parliament as the enemy instead of a vital and fundamental part of the defence system. The failure to pass many vitally needed laws in 12 years of war highlights this mistake exactly.
The ministry must also hold the military leadership accountable for readiness, plans, performance and use of resources. This does not mean political micromanagement of operations. It means that civilian authority as part of government sets objectives, provides means, defines limits, demands professional advice, evaluates performance and accounts to the democratic state. Its role is not to be military but to brief government and parliament, set strategic direction, provide the maximum resources available, oversee performance and carry political–administrative responsibility.
There is no doubt that to achieve a well–oiled, well–managed system the key requirement is outstanding teamwork across the whole system. I learned this well in MOD, but I also learned that we military are poor at arguing and getting our point across. Too often we use emotions and military arrogance to make our point where our civilian colleagues want hard logical arguments and facts. I learnt the hard way with papers and briefs returned covered in red ink and questions like "Why?" and "where is the proof?" spread all over them.
In this regard the Minister and senior commanders, MOD, General Staff (GS) and Joint Staff (JS) must function as a single organism, working closely together not in opposition. To do this, however, they all need common and high–quality briefings from the staff. They usually only know what the staff presents to them; they are not deity. Honesty is everything. Where there is a combined MOD/GS with teams of officers and civil servants working in tandem such as in UK or the Pentagon, most decisions can be made and implemented immediately.
In Ukraine with a separate MOD and General Staff the leadership must constantly look for new processes and better ways to design coordinated and collective team work to get the fastest and most coordinated results. The NATO or Continental Staff system for the military is arguably the best method for this, but it must be used in all its concepts and methods not just a renaming of the old methods. Ukrainian staff still have not grasped the essence of this tool. But this needs another article.
The Chief of Defence / Commander–in–Chief: Strategic Military Leadership and Professional Advice
The Chief of Defence, or Commander–in–Chief (CinC) of the Armed Forces is the senior professional military authority of the state. The title may vary, but the function must be totally clear. This officer is the principal military adviser to the President, government, Minister of Defence and national security bodies, and is responsible for the strategic military leadership of the armed forces as an institution. All three authors agree they have seen more Commanders–in–Chief fail than succeed.
The main reason is failing to grasp that they are not there to run defence like a CEO, and they are not just king of the castle as too many want to be. They must be the expert conduit between society and government, and the military system, ensuring that information and activity flows both ways smoothly and correctly.
The role requires translating political objectives into military strategic options; advising honestly on risk, feasibility, costs and consequences; directing the development of campaign–level plans through the staff system; ensuring jointness and equality across every aspect of the defence system; maintaining morale, readiness, discipline, professional standards and strategic coherence. The list and scope is enormous in its breadth and importance. This is why the Commander–in–Chief should not be the fighting commander. When he takes this role to himself the other key defence tasks that need his time suffer from neglect of proper command attention – and then like the TCC and mobilisation, the whole system degrades.
A further key role for any Commander–in–Chief is to select and provide advice to the President on which officers of all services, not just army, are suitable for high ranks, especially for operational command. Equally, the Commander must advise the President about senior officers who must be moved for failing to achieve results because of lack of ability, staleness or physical tiredness.
Accountability for the Commander–in–Chief flows upward to the civilian leadership through lawful oversight mechanisms like briefing President, Minister and Parliament regularly.
The Commander–in–Chief is responsible for the professional quality of this personal military advice, which means that those below him must also brief him honestly with trust that even when giving bad news they will not be judged or punished for this as has happened too often in the past. He is also responsible for the strategic employment of the armed forces, the integrity of the command system and the readiness and morale of the force.
The Commander–in Chief should be strong enough to lead the military institution through good and bad, but he must always remain subordinate to democratic authority.
The Chief of Staff: Staff Authority, Not Independent Command
The role of Chief of Staff is often the most sensitive in a mixed system. Chief of Staff is subordinate to the Commander–in–Chief and in Ukraine should be the daily manager of the defence system on his behalf by managing the General Staff. He is responsible for staff processes and quality at all levels, planning quality, coordination, staff discipline and ensuring military options developed inside the Joint Staff are fully supported by the system. This officer may be powerful in practice because good staff work shapes strategic decisions, but the authority should be exercised under the Commander–in–Chief and not as an independent command function.
If the Chief of General Staff issues orders, those orders should be staff orders issued under the authority of the Commander–in–Chief not personal command directives. The guiding formula is straightforward: the Chief of General Staff should be powerful as a staff coordinator and the lead manager of the armed forces, but not independent as a commander.
The General Staff: Strategic Staff, The Engine Room of Change and Creating a Stronger Future.
The General Staff, or Defence Staff as named in many contemporary systems, should be understood as the strategic staff that serves the Commander–in–Chief. Its purpose is to convert political direction and strategic military guidance into business plans, force development, mobilisation arrangements, readiness systems, doctrine, training policy, logistic priorities and strategic assessments. With these activities General Staff has a simple three–fold role.
First is supporting the Joint Force Commander with the resources he needs to conduct the fight.
Second is to create new and innovative military resources for the future, and third is to ensure that the whole defence system in the rear is focused upon supporting war as efficiently as possible. This means creating tight processes and effective organisations everywhere with no waste or delays.
Thus, the General Staff is the military brain of the institution and must remain focused upon the future. It should not become a rival command chain and should not be involved in the daily direction of the war or pull tasks to itself that are proper tasks of the subordinate services and agencies like the army or air force.
This distinction is especially important in countries shaped by the Soviet military inheritance. In Soviet–derived systems, the General Staff often accumulated planning, force management, mobilisation, operational direction, intelligence and direct command functions. That model reflected a different political–military logic: centralised control, vertical authority, limited civilian policy capacity, staff–driven command and secrecy over accountability.
In a contemporary democratic system, such concentration of functions creates serious risks: duplication of authority, unclear responsibility, staff interference in command, excessive centralization, extremely slow decision cycles, weakened joint command and poor accountability for operational outcomes. The more intense the war becomes, the more damaging these frictions and disfunctions become to the fighting force.
The General Staff should therefore not directly command operational formations and be involved in warfighting. When they are the staff risk being busy with the wrong tasks, slowing decision–making, weakening operational commanders and destroying the clear link between authority and responsibility. They also lose the focus of their own key tasks and create delays that slow the others they deal with.
The Joint Force Commander: Commander of all Current Joint Warfighting Operations
The Joint Force Commander should be the operational commander responsible for the conduct of assigned campaigns and operations. His task is to win the war. This role is essential because modern war is Joint by nature. Every single capability including civil–military cooperation cannot be managed as separate single service efforts. They must all be integrated under an operational commander with real authority over assigned forces.
The Joint Force Commander's responsibilities should include commanding assigned forces in the operational area; planning and executing campaigns and major operations; identifying needed resources for the upcoming operations, integrating service and functional components; allocating operational priorities; synchronizing effects; reporting progress, risk, losses, needs and opportunities; and adapting operations within the strategic guidance received. He must also highlight operational gaps and weaknesses.
The key is that the title must be matched by authority. If every significant tactical or operational decision is controlled by the General Staff or the political center, the appointment becomes hollow and accountability disappears. A Joint Force Commander who is responsible for operational outcomes must have the authority to command assigned forces, set operational priorities and make timely decisions within strategic guidance.
The Joint Force Commander should be accountable to the Commander–in–Chief for his military performance, and through that chain to civilian authority. This accountability should be based on mission, resources, constraints and delegated authority. It should not be reduced to blame after failure or praise after success; it should be continuous discipline of reporting, assessment, adaptation and lawful command.
Joint Staff: The Operational Warfighting Machinery of Joint Integration
The Joint Staff should manage and coordinate the war fighting organization. It should focus on fighting the war through Joint operational and intelligence integration, translating and directing strategy to subordinate formations and then supporting their operations. It is the staff mechanism through which the armed forces integrate all possible capabilities into a coherent and coordinated war fighting system focused on a single warfighting strategy. When a state has both a General Staff and a Joint Staff, the distinction between them must be precise and with no overlap of cause for misunderstanding.
A well–designed Joint Staff enables the Joint Force Commander to plan, coordinate, assess and adjust joint operations on behalf of the country. His staff support operational–level planning both for close, medium and deep operations with a key aim to both focus battlefield effect and to direct resources where the strategic and operational needs demand. The staff prepare orders and directives for joint operations, work closely with MOD and the General Staff on resource requirements, maintain the recognized operational picture, coordinate with allied headquarters and link national military strategy with campaign execution.
There is always a danger that a Joint Staff can become either redundant if the General Staff take too much operational power, or too weak to integrate the services effectively if the legal authorities are not strong enough. Either outcome is deeply harmful for the war effort. Equally if the Joint Staff try to duplicate the General Staff, they add bureaucracy without authority. When the staff lack influence and real authority, joint operations remain dominated by service and agency interests or by improvised ad–hoc coordination. The result is operations that lack focus, coherence and coordination. Operations and ammunition are wasted on activities that do not have the desired cumulative effect of defeating the enemy. The Joint Staff must therefore have a defined role and clear access to the Commander–in–Chief. It is also vital that the Joint Commander and Chief of Staff have common purposes, are like minded with shared experiences, and even better, are good friends.
The Central Democratic Principle: Responsibility Must Follow Authority
The principle that responsibility must follow authority is the normative heart of democratic wartime defence governance. It protects the state from two equally dangerous failures: institutions that exercise power without accountability, and commanders who are blamed for outcomes they were not empowered or resourced to influence.
In such a system, accountability should be distributed as follows:
- Political leadership is accountable for political objectives, war aims, mobilisation of society, alliances, national resilience, and acceptable risk.
- The MOD is accountable for defence policy, resources, institutions, procurement, personnel, sustainment, and oversight.
- The Commander–in–Chief is accountable for professional military advice, strategic military leadership, readiness, and use of the armed forces.
- The General Staff is accountable for the quality of development plans and R&D, assessments, readiness systems, mobilisation, force development, and staff work.
- The Joint Staff is accountable for war fighting, joint integration and operational planning.
- The Joint Force Commander is accountable for the conduct of assigned operations.
- Armed forces (army/navy etc.) are responsible for delivering trained forces ready and equipped for combat
This distribution of accountability does not fragment command; it clarifies it. Political leaders remain responsible for political aims and national risk. Civilian defence authorities remain responsible for policy, resources and oversight. Senior military leaders remain responsible for professional advice, readiness and strategic coherence. Operational commanders remain responsible for the conduct of assigned operations. The system works when each level has enough authority to discharge its responsibility and enough oversight to prevent abuse.
Each principal defence office should therefore have a statutory duty list that answers five questions: what decision or product the office must deliver; by when it must be delivered; to whom it must be submitted; what authority is granted to deliver it; and what evidence will be used to assess compliance. Legal accountability should include periodic reporting to the Minister of Defence, government, President or parliament; written records of military advice and decisions; deadlines for operational assessments and readiness reports; audit trails for resources; and explicit consequences for failure to perform lawful duties.
Conclusion: Clarity Is a Strategic Capability and Battle Winner
For a democratic state at war in 2026, the decisive institutional test is not the number of headquarters, staff or command titles, but the clarity of authority, responsibility and accountability among them. A state may have a Ministry of Defence, a Chief of Defence or Commander–in–Chief, a General Staff, a Joint Staff, a Chief of General Staff and a Joint Force Commander. But unless their roles are clearly distinguished, the result may be duplication and weakness rather than strength.
Ukraine's challenge is especially demanding because it must fight a high–intensity war while transforming inherited command structures. The aim should not be cosmetic adoption of Western terminology, nor rejection of every inherited practice simply because of its origin. The aim should be a genuinely democratic and joint wartime defence system: civilian–led, professionally advised, operationally effective, legally accountable and clear enough that every major decision and action has an identifiable owner.
Institutional clarity is not an administrative luxury. It is a strategic capability. It shortens decision cycles, strengthens trust between civilian and military leaders, improves the use of resources, enables joint operations, reduces politicisation and makes accountability possible. In war, these are not secondary virtues. They are the key conditions for endurance, adaptation and victory.
Glen Grant

articles.title: At least three killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine while Zelenskyy is in Canada for talks
articles.body:
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said they had carried out their deepest strike inside Russia, with drones travelling 3,000 km to target two gas condensate plants, the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky plants, located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, one of Russia's key oil and gas regions.
As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives in Canada for talks with leader Mark Carney, Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire.
At least three people were killed in Russian overnight attacks. Ukraine's Armed Forces reported that Moscow attacked Ukraine with 149 drones overnight from Wednesday into Thursday, 128 of which were intercepted. The statement added that they had been launched from Russian cities including Kursk, Millerovo and from the temporarily occupied region of Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea, striking 13 locations.
A late Russian attack on a shopping center car park in Sumy killed at least three people and injured 14 including a teenager, on Wednesday, Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Sumy Oblast Military Administration said on Telegram.
Attacks on the eastern city of Kharkiv have left at least two people injured, after a residential buildings were damaged by drones, according to the city's mayor Ihor Terekhov.
Another large scale attack hitting residential building in the central city of Kryvyi Rih left two people in critical condition, its Head of Kryvyi Rih Defence Council, Oleksandr Vilkul said on Telegram.
Four firefighters have been hospitalised after responding to a blaze on a market in the Western city of Khmelnytskyi, sparked by fallen debris from a Russian drone attack. The firefighters were injured in a secondary explosion, officials reported.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said that they had managed their deepest strike inside Russia, as their drones travelled 3,000 km to strike two gas condensate plants, the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky, located in one of Russia's key oil and gas regions; the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region.
Ukrainian media reported that Russian Telegram media channels had said Ukraine launched a drone attack on the Republic of Dagestan.
The southern coastal city of Sochi also reportedly came under attack by Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels sparking multiple fires, according to Russian authorities. Russian media said residents also reported explosions on the port Caspian sea city of Makhachkala, it is known for its handling of dry and liquid cargo, residents also reported a lack of air raid warnings.
Zelenskyy travels to Canada
As Russia and Ukraine trade fire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy travelled to Canada on Wednesday to hold talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney as he hopes to build a closer relationship with his allies.
According to a statement by Carney, Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic, and energy cooperation."
Carney added:"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," and that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defence, recovery, and reconstruction."
Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are scheduled to stay in Canada until Friday, with events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay on the agenda, as well as a meeting with Cabinet members in Banff, Alberta.

articles.title: 3,200 km Into Russia: Ukraine Hits 2 Major Gas Facilities in Record-Breaking Strike
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) say they struck two major Russian gas-condensate plants in the Yamalo-Nenets region on Sept. 9, sending drones more than 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles) deep into Russia in what they called a record strike.
Initial reports emerged Wednesday evening on monitoring Telegram channels that Ukraine had reportedly attacked the Novy Urengoy condensate preparation plant in the city of Novy Urengoy about 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from Ukrainian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian outlet Astra reported that Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) attacked Yamal for the first time, and that a fire broke out at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy.
Yamalo-Nenets Governor Dmitry Artyukhov confirmed that a drone attack had taken place.
“Today, a drone attack on one of the industrial facilities in Novy Urengoy was repelled. As a result of the fall of UAV debris, a fire broke out. Emergency services specialists are working at the scene,” he wrote.
According to Artyukhov, there were no deaths or injuries. The extent and nature of the damage are being established. The governor did not specify which facility was targeted.
Meanwhile, monitoring Telegram channels, including Exilenova+, identified the Novy Urengoy condensate preparation plant as the likely target.
The Ukrainian company Fire Point also appeared to hint at its involvement, saying its drones had traveled more than 3,300 kilometers and successfully hit a target in Novy Urengoy.
‘Carthage’: The Scandal Behind Kravchenko’s Sudden Resignation
“Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target,” the company wrote.
Later, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) confirmed their involvement in the attack.
“For the first time! Record defeat for the entire time of the war: SSO hit critical Russian plants 3,000 km away,” the report released Wednesday evening reads.
The Special Ops clarified that SSO Deep Strike units hit two major Russian gas-condensate facilities – the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky plants. Both facilities are located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, one of Russia’s key oil and gas-producing regions.
“The SSO drones traveled more than 3,000 kilometers to the target. Until today, this was considered a completely safe rear for the aggressor,” the report added.
The Special Ops said that the facilities are critically important to Russia’s gas-condensate industry. The plants process significant volumes of gas condensate extracted from deposits in the Yamal region.
The Novy Urengoy condensate preparation plant has a design capacity of 19.5 million tons of raw materials per year, while the Purovsky gas-condensate processing plant processed 13.4 million tons of gas condensate in 2025.
“The SSO continue to successfully implement Ukraine’s long-range sanctions against Russia, reducing its ability to wage a war of aggression,” the report added.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also said in his morning address Thursday, Sept. 10 that Ukrainian forces had struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities “that are working for war” during the previous day. He listed a refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region among the facilities hit.
“Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a fair response. Thank you to every soldier, to everyone who ensures our long-range strikes and accuracy,” Zelensky added.
UAV threat reported in another oil region nearly 2,500 km from border
Drone threats were also issued Wednesday for the Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug for the first time.
The region is about 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from the Ukrainian border and accounts for around 40% of Russia’s oil production. Residents were advised not to go outside, approach windows or leave safe locations until the warning was lifted.
Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsia, reported the temporary suspension of operations at six airports: Khanty-Mansiysk, Surgut, Sovetsky, Igrim, Nyagan and Urai.
Authorities also warned of disruptions to communications and mobile internet. Students attending second-shift classes at educational institutions were moved to remote learning.
A local teacher told NeMoskva outlet that the region initially introduced an “Unmanned Danger” warning, indicating the approach of drones toward the region. About an hour later, authorities issued the “Threat of UAV Attack” warning, indicating an imminent threat.
Before this, drones had not directly targeted cities and industrial facilities in the district. However, authorities declared a missile threat in the region for the first time on May 5.
The region is home to two major industrial facilities: Nyagangazpererabotka and the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant.
In summer 2026, Ukraine struck nearly all Russian refineries within range. Ukraine’s military said in July that the attacks had knocked 43% of Russia’s refining capacity offline, contributing to a nationwide fuel shortage and export restrictions.
Despite the loss of refining capacity, think tank analysis found Russia’s overall oil exports remained relatively stable between June and July, with higher crude exports and energy prices partly offsetting revenue losses.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has acknowledged the impact while arguing that, amid Russia’s fuel crisis, it is more “profitable to export crude oil than to process it domestically.”
