articles.title: Kremlin reveals new details of Putin-Trump call
articles.body:
Kremlin reveals new details of Putin-Trump call
Washington could help bring the Ukraine conflict to an end sooner by stopping all assistance to Kiev, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said, commenting on the latest phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump.
The two leaders spoke by phone on Tuesday in the wake of a new round of shuttle diplomacy that saw Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visit Moscow and Kiev over the weekend.
The issue came up as the two presidents discussed ways to reach a settlement of the conflict, Ushakov told journalist Pavel Zarubin on Wednesday. Asked what Washington could do to bring the hostilities to an end sooner, the Kremlin aide said that “first and foremost, [it could] probably stop providing any assistance to Kiev.”
The official acknowledged that US assistance to Ukraine had already “declined significantly” since Trump returned to the White House, compared with the previous administration, when military aid “was provided on a massive scale.”
The two presidents also discussed resuming talks with the Ukrainian side, including in trilateral format that would include the US mediators, Ushakov added.
Trump said he had a “great” conversation with Putin, adding that the Russian president did want “to make a deal.” If Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky “is wanting to make a deal, that’d be very nice,” he told reporters on Wednesday before boarding Air Force One en route to Dallas for the GOP National Convention.
Moscow has repeatedly said it is ready to settle the Ukraine conflict as long as its root causes are addressed and the realities on the ground are taken into account.
Russia’s demands include Ukraine abandoning its plans to join NATO and adopting neutral status, accepting restrictions on its armed forces, and formally recognizing Crimea and four other former Ukrainian regions as Russian territory. Crimea voted to join Russia shortly after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev. Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporozhye and Kherson regions held similar referendums in September 2022.
Kiev has consistently rejected Moscow’s demands on territorial and security issues, insisting on restoring control over all territories it lays claim to and joining NATO.
Moscow has repeatedly cited Kiev’s aggressive posture, as well as the position of its European backers as major obstacles to a peace settlement.
On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that the several European leaders calling for a ceasefire were actually seeking to preserve an “openly Russophobic and aggressive neo-Nazi regime” in Kiev, adding that the Russian people would never accept this outcome.

articles.title: Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm elections, threatens to attack Pickaxe Mountain
articles.body:
Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm vote, Houthis close in on key Strait, sources say
CAIRO/WASHINGTON/DUBAI, Sept 10 - President Donald Trump said he expected the war with Iran to end after the November U.S. midterm elections and threatened again to attack a site associated with the Islamic Republic's nuclear programme after the two sides launched their biggest wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the six-month-old war.
Tensions in the region were high, with Saudi civil defence authorities on Thursday issuing emergency alerts in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours, as clashes flared with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
The Houthis were edging closer on Thursday to gaining more leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world's most important routes for shipping, four Yemeni government military sources said.
Brent crude prices hovered above $100 a barrel as supply routes through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted.
Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the waterway on Wednesday after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, the latest in a series of tit-for-tat strikes that have signalled scant chance of an imminent end to hostilities.
DEADLINES TO END WAR
The war and subsequent increase in fuel prices have helped drive Trump's popularity to record lows. The president said Tehran was trying to influence the November U.S. midterm elections, which will determine whether his Republican Party retains control of Congress.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
Trump has previously set deadlines for the war to end.
The Wall Street Journal reported later that top White House advisers, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have privately warned Trump that the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency, which ends in January 2029. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Trump also said the U.S. may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes near Iran's damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
"We notice there's a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard," Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention. Trump has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.
The U.S. and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February partly due to concerns over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Iran says its nuclear activities are for peaceful purposes.
In recent weeks Washington had cited increasing success guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global oil supplies before the war. But a resumption of fighting this month appears to have set back any such gradual reopening. Just seven vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, half the 10-day average, preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Thursday.
RED SEA CLASHES
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen has also escalated in the past few days, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.
Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha and are launching attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish, the Yemeni sources told Reuters on Thursday.
Government forces and their allies are relocating south to Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait, across from the island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said.
Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most populous areas and much of the north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal or the SUMED pipeline on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
Blocking the narrow passage would isolate Gulf oil-producing countries such as energy superpower Saudi Arabia from their main shipping routes after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — the primary maritime energy artery between Asia and Europe.
Earlier this week, at least 73 people were wounded in four southern Saudi cities, including Khamis Mushait, in recent Houthi strikes on the world's largest oil exporter.
The militant group said it attacked an air base in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Saudi civil defence authorities issued an all-clear on Thursday following another emergency alert declared in Khamis Mushait. REUTERS

articles.title: Trump predicts Iran war end, says Putin ready for Ukraine deal
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the war with Iran could end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while signaling possible diplomatic openings on both Tehran and the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters before traveling to Dallas, Texas, for the Republican Party's first midterm convention, Trump claimed Iran was seeking to influence the elections and could not sustain the conflict much longer.
"I think the war will end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said.
Asked about the possibility of renewed nuclear negotiations with Tehran, Trump said his administration was not actively pursuing talks but did not rule them out.
"We're not looking for it. Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it's not something we're looking at," he said.
Trump said any potential agreement with Tehran would extend beyond its nuclear program, suggesting other issues would also be included in negotiations.
"There is a lot more than nuclear," he said.
He also said recent U.S. strikes in the Strait of Hormuz had incapacitated about nine Iranian tankers and suggested further military action could follow.
Trump separately struck an optimistic tone on efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the Russian leader was "wanting to make a deal."
Trump described his conversation with Putin as "good" and said a trilateral meeting involving Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "could happen."
"If Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump said.
His comments followed visits to Moscow and Kyiv last weekend by U.S. mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, though no significant breakthrough toward ending the war has been announced.
The Kremlin said Putin told Trump that Moscow had no "aggressive plans" toward Europe and provided the U.S. president with an assessment of developments on the battlefield.
Putin also outlined what he believed Washington could do to help bring the fighting to an end, according to Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Washington has stepped up mediation efforts since Trump's return to the White House, including a meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska last year.

articles.title: Middle East live: Trump warns Iran over activity at Pickaxe Mountain fortified site
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday and were advancing towards the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Yemeni government and military sources said. The vital waterway serves as a key shipping lane linking Europe to Asia. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
European Central Bank raises key interest rate to 2.5 percent as war fuels inflation fears
The European Central Bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.5 percent on Thursday as the Middle East war pushes up energy costs and threatens to send prices higher.
"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," said the central bank.
Iran's government opposes parliamentary bill to expand definition of 'enemy infiltration'
Iran's government opposes a parliamentary bill that would impose tougher criminal penalties for activities deemed to constitute foreign influence or infiltration, state news agency IRNA reported on Thursday.
The bill, backed by parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, would restrict contacts with foreign media and institutions, the sharing of information, scientific cooperation and other activities that authorities deem to facilitate foreign influence.
The elected government's opposition to the measure appears to signal pushback towards hardliners, who have supported enacting tougher security laws during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Iran suspends freight charge on foreign vessels carrying energy products to or from Iran, Fars news reports
Iran has suspended a 10 percent charge on freight fees for foreign vessels carrying imported or exported oil, gas and liquid petroleum products to and from Iran, the semi-official Fars news agency reported.
A US naval blockade has sharply disrupted the country's seaborne oil exports.
Pakistan says no military response discussed under Mecca pact over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Pakistan said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia, but added that Pakistan will "act" when the "time comes".
The comments by Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesperson came in response to a question on how Islamabad plans to fulfill its obligations under a joint defence accord it signed with Turkey and Saudi Arabia.
The joint defence agreement signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them.
"There is no such thing under discussion right now ... When time comes (we) will act under the agreement," foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at a weekly media briefing.
Iran-backed Houthis take control of Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha, sources say
The Iran-backed Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha, closing in on the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, three Yemeni government sources told Reuters.
Pakistan insists Mecca alliance is 'defensive'
The Mecca agreement, signed between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia last month, is a "defensive alliance" and there are no plans to expand it at the moment, Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesperson said.
The statement came in response to a question at a weekly briefing on how Pakistan plans to fulfill its obligations under the accord after Saudi Arabia was attacked by the Houthis.
Yemen's Houthis report about 40 strikes in fresh Saudi attack
Yemen's Houthi rebels reported about 40 airstrikes launched by Saudi forces on Thursday in a fresh salvo following attacks by the Iran-backed group against the kingdom.
"The Saudi enemy's air force conducted around 40 strikes in recent hours in the governorates of Taiz, Hodeida, Al-Jawf and Marib," Houthi news agency Saba said.
Israeli strike in Gaza kills family of four, hospital and Palestinian security officials report
An Israeli strike in Gaza on killed a family of four including two children, Palestinian hospital and security sources said.
"The bodies of four members of the Ahmad family were recovered in pieces after an Israeli strike hit a house in the Beit Lahia Project area in the northern Gaza Strip," an official at Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City said, identifying the children as aged 12 and eight.
The Israeli military told AFP it was checking the reports.
A Palestinian security source in Gaza, which is under the control of Hamas, said that Israeli warplanes struck after midnight in Beit Lahia and separately in the heart of the Jabalia refugee camp, with Israeli forces also firing on tents of displaced people and ambulances.
Hormuz shipping traffic appears to fall to single digits
Vessel transits at the Strait of Hormuz fell slightly on Wednesday to seven, compared with the previous day's 12, preliminary shiptracking data showed on Thursday, with levels also lower than the 10-day average of 14.
Out of these seven, four vessels exited and three entered, according to the data.
Some vessels could be sailing through the waterway with their transponders turned off and these are not considered in the counts.
Trump says oil prices may not fall until after midterm elections
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after US midterm elections.
Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3 percent, pushing international Brent crude past the $100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the US and Iran escalated.
“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”
US military aircraft damaged in strikes on Jordan air base
Multiple American military aircraft suffered damage in strikes overnight on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, CBS reporter Jennifer Jacobs said on Wednesday on X.
One A-10 Thunderbolt, known as the Warthog, was struck and left with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were placed back into service, she added.
Trump warns Iran against activity at Pickaxe Mountain fortified site
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the United States may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, urging Tehran to be cautious.
"We notice there's a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard," Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention.
Pickaxe Mountain, located near Iran's heavily damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility, is a fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes.
Trump has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.
The rise in oil and gas prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began in February, has become a major issue for Trump and his Republican Party in the lead-up to the midterm US elections in November.

Israel told the British consulate in east Jerusalem that it must close and that diplomats assigned there would lose their accreditation within 30 days in a reprisal for London-led Western sanctions over settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
The US military denied reports of Iranian strikes on its warships.

articles.title: Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed two, injured three
articles.body:
Moldovan President Sandu condemns Russian drone strike on border crossing point that killed 2, injured 3
Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned an overnight Russian drone strike on the Starokozache international border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, in a Sept. 9 statement on X.
Russia struck the Starokozache border crossing overnight with drones, killing two civilians and injuring three others, Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper said. Rescuers evacuated another 16 people from a bus, according to Kiper.
Sandu also said that a Russian drone forced Moldova to close its airspace temporarily, warning that the Russian advance in Ukraine is moving further west.
"I urge more air defense support for Ukraine," Sandu said.
Earlier in the day, referring to Russian attacks on the border crossing, among others, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X that "there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes."
The Southern Regional Directorate of Ukraine's State Border Guard Service announced in a Facebook post on Sept. 9 that border operations had resumed.
"The operation of this border crossing point will help to avoid congestion and traffic build-up on other routes along the border with Moldova. At the same time, security measures for citizens crossing the border will continue to be implemented in response to any (Russian) attempts to attack border infrastructure," the statement reads.
Russia most likely wants to disrupt logistics with its attacks on border crossings, Andriy Demchenko, the spokesman for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said during the national telethon, Suspilne reported.
The attack was the fourth one on a border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine, Demchenko added.
A Russian Shahed-type drone strike overnight on Aug. 25 damaged the Vynohradivka border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in Odesa Oblast, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at the time.
In a post on X, Sybiha called on the international community to "condemn Russia's systematic targeting of civilian transport corridors and critical border infrastructure."
Moldova's Foreign Ministry reported on Aug. 27 that five drones violated Moldovan airspace on the night prior.
"We have repeatedly warned about the unacceptable risks posed by Russia's war against Ukraine," the ministry wrote.
A suspected Russian Shahed-type drone violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace on Sept. 8, forcing airspace closures, emergency alerts and the scrambling of NATO fighter jets.
The Moldovan military detected an "unmanned aerial vehicle" at 4:20 p.m. local time on Sept. 8, the Moldovan Defense Ministry said in a statement, identifying it as a "Shahed-type" drone that entered the country's airspace from the "direction of … Ukraine."
Spanish F/A-18 fighter jets, deployed as part of a NATO air-policing mission, were scrambled from Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base in Romania as the drone entered Romanian airspace.

articles.title: How the US post-9/11 overreaction built today's illiberal world
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How the US post-9/11 overreaction built today's illiberal world
There are events that happen within history, and there are events that change its direction. The attacks of 11 September 2001 unquestionably belonged to the latter.
Twenty-five years ago, Al-Qaeda's attacks on New York and Washington killed almost 3,000 people, traumatised the US and produced images that became instantly seared into global consciousness.
But 9/11 was more than an atrocity. It altered the course of an era.
Barely a decade after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the US stood as the world's sole superpower and liberal democracy appeared to have no serious ideological rival. Francis Fukuyama's famous declaration of the "end of history" captured the extraordinary confidence of the age.
Liberal democracy, globalisation and an international system supposedly governed by universal rules appeared not merely ascendant, but inevitable.
Then the planes hit.
A quarter of a century later, that world seems almost unrecognisable. Liberal democracy is in retreat, the far right is ascendant across much of the West, most notably in the US, Russia is waging a war of territorial conquest in Europe, and the international rules supposedly restraining state power appear increasingly conditional.
This week provided another remarkable marker of how far we have travelled. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, its greatest electoral result to date, bringing a party once considered beyond the limits of respectable German politics tantalisingly close to governing a German state.
None of this can be solely blamed on 9/11. But nor can the world of 2026 be understood without examining what the US and its allies did in response to it.
The Global War on Terror (GWOT) transformed more than US foreign policy. It changed the relationship between security and liberty and helped normalise the idea that extraordinary threats demanded extraordinary powers.
The Patriot Act vastly expanded surveillance. Guantanamo Bay became a legal black hole in which alleged "enemy combatants" could be detained indefinitely without charge. The CIA abducted suspects and transferred them through an extraordinary rendition programme to states where torture was routine. The invasion of Iraq showed that even the world's leading liberal democracy was willing to bypass the international order it claimed to defend.
The Bush administration was not pursuing an explicitly illiberal project. Quite the opposite: it believed US power could protect and ultimately spread liberal democracy.
But it pursued liberal ends using profoundly illiberal means.
That distinction matters. Donald Trump is not simply George W. Bush with the mask removed, nor did the Patriot Act somehow inevitably produce the AfD. But the GWOT created a political world in which exceptional measures became increasingly normal and showed how easily restraints on state power could be discarded once "security" was invoked.
I have previously called what followed the "procession of illiberalism": ideas and machinery created for the War on Terror being taken up and repurposed by movements with very different, explicitly illiberal goals.
The Western front
Orban's Hungary became perhaps the clearest European example.
During his 16 years in power, Orban openly set about building what he called an "illiberal state". His governments expanded Hungary's counterterrorism apparatus while increasingly depicting Muslim migrants as an existential threat to Hungary and Christian Europe.
The terrorist became the extremist; the extremist became the Muslim migrant; those helping migrants became accomplices; and eventually multiculturalism, LGBT rights, liberal civil society and "globalism" itself were portrayed as threats to the survival of the nation.
Orban may have lost power this year, but the politics he helped pioneer travelled far beyond Hungary.
The AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt cannot be reduced to this history. Economic stagnation, anger at Germany's established parties and the particular history of eastern Germany all matter.
But today's European far right operates on political terrain profoundly shaped by the post-9/11 era. Borders become front lines and migration becomes invasion. Muslims are treated as a civilisational danger, while multicultural liberal democracy itself is presented as something weakening the nation from within.
In Trump's US, the process has become almost absurdly literal.
Guantanamo, perhaps the ultimate physical symbol of the GWOT's suspension of normal rules, has been repurposed for the detention of migrants. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), itself created by the Bush administration during the War on Terror, has become the frontline institution of Trump's mass-deportation programme.
The machinery and language built to confront foreign terrorists have turned inwards.
The targets have changed, but the logic is familiar. Identify an existential enemy, strip away normal protections and invoke security to justify extraordinary state power.
The War on Terror never left the Middle East
If the GWOT has turned inward in the West, in the Middle East its original logic never really disappeared.
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza made this explicit. Israeli leaders repeatedly invoked 9/11 and presented the war as part of the same civilisational struggle against terrorism. Benjamin Netanyahu described 7 October as Israel's own 9/11 and compared Israeli military action beyond its borders to what the US did after the attacks.
The comparison is revealing.
Once again, an appalling terrorist attack became the justification for an overriding security imperative. Once again, exceptional violence was presented as necessary because the threat was existential. And once again, international law was treated as secondary to the state's claimed need to destroy its enemy.
The results in Gaza have been catastrophic - the enclave devastated, tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and most of its population displaced, while the US supplied the military and diplomatic support that allows the genocide to continue.
Gaza is not simply another version of the GWOT. But the political logic is recognisable. Terrorism becomes more than a crime or military threat. It becomes a condition under which normal restraints can be suspended - even one under which genocide can be justified in the language of security.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived another defining feature of the post-9/11 era, namely the crime of preventive war.
In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran amid under the guise of negotiations over its nuclear programme, wiping out its entire leadership, bombing civilian targets, most deplorably a girls school, and civil infrastructure. The war has since spread across the region, with Iran attacking US bases and neighbouring pro-US Arab states and fighting engulfing the economically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Once again, the language is strikingly familiar - nuclear danger, terrorism, national survival and a threat that cannot be allowed to materialise.
This was one of the central ideas behind the GWOT, namely that waiting for a threat to become imminent could itself be too dangerous.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the War on Terror has therefore taken two different paths. In the West, its security politics have increasingly been redirected from terrorists towards migrants and other supposed internal enemies. In the Middle East, many of its original assumptions about preventive war, existential threats and exceptional violence remain alive.
When the rules stop being universal
Vladimir Putin shows how the same era also helped weaken the international order from another direction.
Putin initially enthusiastically embraced the GWOT. Russia was already waging a brutal war in Chechnya when 9/11 occurred, and he rapidly recast Moscow's campaign as another front in the global struggle against terrorism. Bush, in turn, described Putin as a partner in that struggle.
But by Putin's 2007 Munich Security Conference speech, Russia was openly attacking the US-led order and accusing Washington of violating international law.
The War on Terror had given Putin both an opportunity and, later, an alibi. Russia borrowed its language of existential security while pointing to Iraq and US exceptionalism as proof that the liberal international order was hypocritical.
That does not mean Iraq justifies Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It does mean the US weakened the very principles needed to condemn such aggression consistently.
Gaza has deepened that crisis further. When Western governments invoke sovereignty, international law and civilian protection in Ukraine while giving Israel the means to devastate Gaza, the damage goes beyond charges of hypocrisy.
If the rules depend on who is breaking them and against whom, they stop being universal rules at all.
Before 9/11, the US emerged from the Cold War claiming to lead a liberal world order grounded, however imperfectly, in international law, human rights and democratic government.
The GWOT did not destroy that order. It fractured it.
Its deeper tragedy is that the Bush administration believed US power could be used not simply to defeat terrorism, but to preserve and spread liberal democracy. Torture, rendition, indefinite detention and illegal war were justified by supposedly liberal ends.
Twenty-five years later, even the ends have changed.
The ascendant illiberals of our age do not promise to improve the liberal order. They promise to replace it: universalism with ethno-nationalism, international law with raw sovereign power, multiculturalism with civilisational identity, and the restraints of liberal democracy with the permanent demands of "security".
Nor is this solely the work of those who openly seek liberalism's destruction. As during the GWOT, the rise of illiberalism has also been made easier by governments that defend international law selectively, tolerate its violation by allies and then wonder why appeals to the "rules-based order" carry less and less weight.
Modern illiberalism would almost certainly have emerged without 9/11. But the response to those attacks hastened its rise, furnished it with powerful political tools and helped knock the world off its liberal democratic axis.
Perhaps the most enduring legacy of 9/11 and the War on Terror is therefore neither Afghanistan nor Iraq, but the spread of its central proposition: when the threat is grave enough, the rules no longer apply.
Twenty-five years after the towers fell, the state of exception has escaped the emergency that created it.
The enemies have multiplied, the exceptions are becoming the rule, and the world that once proclaimed the inevitable triumph of liberal democracy increasingly resembles an age of monsters.
Sam Hamad is a writer and History PhD student at the University of Glasgow, focusing on totalitarian ideologies.

articles.title: IAEA exposes North Korea's secret nuclear enrichment facility, expansion of weapon infrastructure
articles.body:
North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report that the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations.
In the report, dated August 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang's nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009.
It identified a new two-story building at Yongbyon as the site's second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building's construction.
Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs.
Expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material
The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024.
The IAEA said the developments in North Korea's nuclear program violated UN Security Council resolutions.
"The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern," IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The report accompanied Grossi's statement.
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency's authority. North Korea's mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had "no legal right… to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT," referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

articles.title: Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes
articles.body:
Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports.
The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods.
Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis.
Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday.
The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing.
The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”.
A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks.
Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas.
The US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days.
Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data.
The back-and-forth strikes signalled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told reporters.
Iran said it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time.
The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh.
Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea.
The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil.

articles.title: Iranian troops struck US aircraft carrier at 500-km range
articles.body:
Highlighting the IRGC’s naval capabilities, General Mohebbi stated that Iran was demonstrating its power by preventing unauthorized vessel transits and blocking enemy naval weaponry.
He noted that prior to Operation “Ramadan,” approximately 30 to 40 US warships had been present in the Persian Gulf, but he claimed that not a single warship remained in the region today. He added that all U.S. vessels had pulled back at least 400 kilometers from Iran’s coastline.
The spokesman attributed this retreat to Iran’s deployment of new weaponry and advanced missiles, asserting that Iranian forces retained the capacity to strike targets at distances exceeding 400 kilometers. He further stated that Iranian forces had recently targeted a US aircraft carrier located 500 kilometers away, maintaining that the Strait of Hormuz remained a center of Iranian military strength to deter foreign aggression.
Referring to earlier remarks by Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Expediency Discernment Council, concerning a new exclusion zone, General Mohebbi clarified that the designated area extended from near Chabahar across portions of the Sea of Oman and the Persian Gulf leading toward the Strait of Hormuz.
He explained that while military actions had previously focused strictly on the Strait of Hormuz, a broader security zone had now been established, with exact coordinates scheduled for official publication.
Elaborating on the mechanism of “maritime sanctions,” the spokesman warned that any unauthorized commercial or military vessel entering the defined zone would be denied insurance, legal, and support services, and would be prohibited from navigating through the Strait of Hormuz.
Regarding countermeasures against potential naval blockades, General Mohebbi observed that maritime blockades could extend throughout the Sea of Oman and into international ocean waters. However, he maintained that the IRGC possessed undisclosed operational strategies to neutralize such measures.
He further claimed that U.S. forces were suffering from severe physical and operational attrition, asserting that the USS Abraham Lincoln had required hull repairs and repainting due to severe rusting, and that its crew was experiencing low morale under continuous sea operations.
Reaffirming Iran’s military readiness, General Mohebbi emphasized that regional maritime dynamics had shifted in Iran’s favor due to smart strategies and modern armaments. He warned that any miscalculation by the United States or its allies would bring a decisive response from Tehran.

articles.title: Government again commits not to extend Dreadnought sub life
articles.body:
The Government has confirmed that it has accepted a Strategic Defence Review recommendation not to extend the service lives of the Royal Navy’s Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines beyond their intended end-of-service dates from the mid-2050s.
The position was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked whether ministers had committed to Recommendation 34 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard replied: “The Government accepted this 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommendation and is in the process of implementing it.”
Recommendation 34 explicitly calls on the Government to avoid repeating the costs associated with extending ageing submarine fleets and to begin planning for the system that will eventually replace Dreadnought.
The Strategic Defence Review stated: “To avoid the costs of the past, the Government must commit to not extending the life of the Dreadnought class submarines beyond their intended end-of-service dates from the mid-2050s. It should start to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought nuclear deterrent within this Parliament.”
The Government has also confirmed separately that work to define Dreadnought’s eventual successor is beginning as part of wider investment in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise.
In a written answer in July, Obese-Jecty asked what plans the MOD had to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought strategic deterrent.
Pollard said: “As announced in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government will invest over £20 billion more in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise over the next four years than the previous four years to modernise and sustain our nuclear deterrent, the cornerstone of our national security.”
He added: “This will fund our new deterrent submarines and warheads, establish a nuclear fuels programme, start defining the Dreadnought successor, and upgrade our infrastructure across the defence nuclear estate.”
Pollard said this would allow the Government to meet its commitment to begin defining the future system during the current Parliament, stating: “This will allow us to meet the Government’s commitment to start to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought strategic deterrent within this Parliament.”
The Dreadnought class is being built to replace the Royal Navy’s existing Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines and will carry the UK’s strategic nuclear deterrent through much of the middle of the century.
The Strategic Defence Review recommendation is intended to avoid the additional cost and complexity that can arise when major platforms remain in service significantly beyond their originally planned lives. Rather than relying on a later life-extension programme for Dreadnought, the review calls for work on its eventual successor to begin decades in advance, with the requirement-definition process now being funded through the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise programme.

articles.title: Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
Iran's capture of a US military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril.
The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter.
After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design.
More recently, the U.S. military moved swiftly to prevent Iranian forces from taking possession of uncrewed maritime technology. In 2022, a US Navy patrol ship and MH-60S Seahawk helicopter were deployed after an Iranian naval vessel attempted to tow away a Saildrone surface vessel in the Gulf, according to the Navy.
Analysts say Iran is unlikely to gain a decisive military advantage from the captured drone, but the episode nonetheless represents a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington's efforts to project technological superiority.
Iranian embassies mock US
Iranian embassies around the world have mocked the US for losing its drone. Iran's embassy in Ghana, in a post on X, boasted about picking the submersible up in "a strait controlled by people who can hear a shrimp sneeze," adding that, "Our guys picked it up like a plastic bottle in a fishing net. Fully intact. Still blinking like an idiot. Condolences to whoever was holding the joystick."
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins of US Central Command said the "defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment." Anduril did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"Of course Iran will take every opportunity as a propaganda win," said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. "It can help the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) make better versions of their own designs."
Iran will almost certainly try to pry open the drone's hardware, but the drone's software carries built-in defenses, said Bryan Clark, a senior fellow and director of the Center for Defense Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute. Iranian engineers "could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems," he said, pointing to Tehran's track record with captured American aircraft.
"Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!" Iran's embassy in Hyderabad wrote on X.
The incident has also highlighted a disconnect between the messaging of Anduril and its customer, the US Navy.
Navy officials said the Dive-LD was an older-model vehicle that suffered a malfunction and was recovered by Iranian forces after being left "dead in the water."
Anduril has promoted the Dive-LD as "the most reliable and flexible" large autonomous underwater vehicle available, saying it is capable of operating for up to 10 days in demanding conditions. In addition to its use by the US Navy, the Dive-LD was the testbed vehicle for the development of Australia's new Ghost Shark large underwater drone.
"This is something that Iran has proven very adept at exploiting for its own benefit in terms of seeking to frame the narrative as one of US, in this case, ineptitude and their ability to sort of retain control over the Strait of Hormuz," said Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

articles.title: Germany pledges more missiles and shells for Ukraine
articles.body:
Germany will transfer additional Patriot and AIM-9 missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine while financing tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has announced.
Speaking at the opening of the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Pistorius said Berlin would urgently provide PAC-2 Patriot interceptor missiles and called on other countries to examine whether they could release weapons from their own inventories ahead of the winter.
Pistorius acknowledged the tension between maintaining national reserves and supplying Ukraine, but told participants: “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine. But please, if in doubt, decide in favor for Ukraine.”
Germany will also increase deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks, with Pistorius saying the weapons were already being supplied to Ukraine. The additional missiles form part of a wider effort to strengthen Ukrainian air defences before temperatures fall, with the German minister warning that Russian attacks against power stations, ports and other infrastructure could increase during the winter.
Germany is also continuing deliveries of IRIS-T air defence systems and missiles. Pistorius said Ukraine was preparing to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles using funding from the EU-Ukraine Defence Loan.
According to Pistorius, the size of that procurement will allow industry to expand production by establishing another missile production line. He said the order represented an example of how support for Ukraine could also increase European defence manufacturing capacity, allowing production to serve both Ukrainian requirements and wider European rearmament.
Pistorius also referred to the City Dome project, through which Germany is supporting the establishment of additional defences for Ukrainian cities against missile and drone attacks. Beyond air defence, Germany will finance several tens of thousands of long-range artillery rounds for Ukraine. The ammunition will be procured through the British Artillery and Air Defence Consortium before being transferred to Ukrainian forces.
Pistorius thanked UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and his team for helping arrange the procurement, describing it as an example of cooperation between countries participating in the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
Germany will also continue deliveries of drones and long-range ammunition as part of its support for Ukrainian forces operating on the front. The commitments were announced as members of the contact group focused heavily on preparing Ukraine for another winter of Russian air attacks, with air defence missiles identified by Kyiv as its most immediate requirement.

articles.title: US-Israel strikes against Iran have systematically undermined human rights
articles.body:
US-Israel strikes against Iran have systematically undermined human rights
In February 2026, the US and Israel launched large-scale joint military strikes against Iran. This blatant military operation, conducted without authorization from the UN Security Council, drew strong condemnation from the international community.
The fighting has ebbed and flowed, and negotiations have been fraught with setbacks. After more than half a year of conflict, reportedly over 3,750 Iranian civilians have been killed and more than 33,000 wounded; regional countries have also suffered collateral damage, and strategic corridors have been repeatedly blocked. UN Secretary-General António Guterres lamented that the war is inflicting immense human suffering.
One may well ask: How can the US - which has long styled itself as a "beacon of human rights" and frequently used human rights as a pretext to criticize other nations - so flagrantly trample on the human rights of the Iranian people? Here are some shocking facts.
Attacking civilians, killing women and children - violations of the right to life. Women and children are the most vulnerable in war, and they pay the heaviest price. UN data show that among Iranian civilian casualties, approximately 500 are women and over 2,500 are children. Just recently, a heavy bomb dropped by US forces on July 30 over a civilian residential area in southern Iran hit a family of five, instantly killing a couple and their two-year-old child. On the very day the US-Israel forces started their airstrikes, a missile struck a girls' elementary school, killing all 168 students - a tragedy that shocked the world.
Carrying out assassinations and attempting regime change - violations of the right to self-determination. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government. A nation's future and destiny can only be decided by that nation itself; bombs and threats can never replace the choice of the people. The US and Israel have carried out successive "decapitation" strikes against Iran's supreme leader and other senior political and military officials. This is a classic case of extrajudicial execution. Even UN human rights experts, who have long been critical of Iran's human rights record, have clearly stated that international law does not accept extrajudicial "justice," and have urged the US to respect the Iranian people's right to self-determination.
Destroying homes and turning people into refugees - violations of economic, social and cultural rights, and the right to development. According to reports, the US-Israel military operations have so far destroyed over 125,000 civilian facilities in Iran, including 339 hospitals, 857 schools and 32 universities. Since the latest escalation of the Middle East crisis, over 4.1 million people in countries such as Iran and Lebanon have become displaced, and about 117,000 have fled to other countries seeking asylum. War is tearing families apart and creating an unprecedented humanitarian crisis. Homes may be rebuilt, but lost lives, shattered childhoods, and missed educational opportunities cannot be recovered.
Poisoning the air and cutting off water supplies - violations of environmental and health rights. As multiple oil depots in Iran were hit and set ablaze, toxic pollutants were released into the air, even causing toxic rain in some places. This has led to breathing difficulties and illness or disability among local residents. In a separate incident, US forces struck a desalination plant on Qeshm Island, affecting the water supply to 30 villages. The World Health Organization has issued warnings that "black rain" and acid rain pose a real danger to the Iranian people. The environmental damage caused by just a few months of war may take decades to repair.
Damaging cultural heritage and desecrating religious sites - violations of freedom of belief and cultural rights. Persian civilization is a shared treasure of humanity.
However, US and Israeli bombing has already damaged at least 149 historical landmarks and museums across 20 Iranian provinces, including five UNESCO World Heritage sites. UNESCO has expressed deep concern and called for all necessary measures to protect both people and cultural heritage sites. As Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi pointed out, "Iran's cultural heritage is not merely the national asset of Iranians; it is part of the shared memory of humanity." Destroying cultural heritage means destroying the collective memory of humankind - it is cultural genocide.
The use of force by the US and Israel against Iran shows the world that the international rule of law is taking the heaviest blow, that human rights and humanitarian principles are being most deeply trampled on, and that the moral decay of US "neo-imperialism" is being most starkly exposed. The military operations have not only ruthlessly stripped the Iranian people of their basic human rights, but also pushed the entire Middle East toward a humanitarian abyss, shaking the very foundation of world peace. Every bomb dropped on schools, hospitals, residential neighborhoods, and millennia‑old monuments is a heavy blow to human rights values and the bottom line of humanity.
Without peace, human rights are just empty words. Only by upholding peaceful dialogue and abandoning the obsession with the use of force, by adhering to multilateralism and rejecting unilateralism and hegemonism, can we save lives from the terror of war and prevent civilization from being swallowed by the flames of conflict. This is the enduring pursuit of the international human rights cause and the deepest aspiration of humanity as we work to build a community with a shared future.
The author is a commentator on international affairs.

articles.title: Australia declares its new air defense missile system combat ready
articles.body:
- Australia's Army declared Final Operational Capability for NASAMS on September 9, 2026, with 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery as the first operational unit.
- The system, built under the SRGBAD project with Raytheon Australia and Norway's Kongsberg, uses Australian CEA Technologies radar and Hawkei-mounted launchers.
Australia’s Army has declared Final Operational Capability for its National Advanced Surface to Air Missile System, confirming the ground-based air defense system is ready to support Australian Defence Force operations. Defence announced the milestone on September 9, 2026.
NASAMS is built to detect, track and destroy cruise missiles, aircraft, helicopters and drones. The system was delivered under the Short Range Ground Based Air Defense project, known as SRGBAD, part of a broader air and missile defense setup that also draws on ships and fighter aircraft to protect ADF personnel and infrastructure.
Soldiers from Adelaide’s 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery, are the first operational unit to field the system. The regiment, based at Woodside in South Australia, ran live-fire trials and qualification training as part of the phased rollout that led to this week’s declaration.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability for NASAMS marks a significant milestone in strengthening Australia’s integrated air and missile defence capability,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles. “NASAMS provides Army with a modern, highly capable air defence system that enhances our ability to protect Australian Defence Force personnel, critical assets and infrastructure from a range of airborne threats.”
Raytheon Australia is the prime contractor on SRGBAD, running under the Army’s long-standing LAND 19 Phase 7B program. NASAMS itself was co-developed by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, and Kongsberg Defence Australia built the system’s Fire Distribution Centres locally before handing final units to Raytheon Australia last year. The SRGBAD program is valued at roughly A$2.5 billion.
The Australian version pairs the Norwegian NASAMS design with locally built CEA Technologies radar, the CEATAC and CEAOPS active electronically scanned array systems, mounted alongside launchers on Hawkei protected mobility vehicles. Raytheon’s AN/AAS-52 Multispectral Targeting System adds day and night optical tracking. The setup replaces the Army’s older RBS-70 man-portable air defense missiles.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability delivers a world-leading capability for Defence and provides a major boost to Australia’s integrated air and missile defence,” said Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy. “Australian-designed radar technology is a key part of this capability, highlighting the important contribution local industry makes to Australia’s national security.”
NASAMS is in service with, or on order for, more than a dozen countries. Ukraine has used the system in combat against Russian cruise missiles and drones since 2022, giving the design an operational record beyond Australia’s own trials. Defence has not disclosed how many NASAMS batteries or launchers 16th Regiment will ultimately operate; the regiment is expected to field two batteries once full capability is reached.
Each NASAMS troop is built around a Fire Distribution Centre, a CEATAC radar, an optronic sensor vehicle and several launchers, with the Hawkei launchers and canisters carried on MAN/Rheinmetall HX77 trucks. The missile load is a mix of AIM-120 AMRAAM and Sidewinder missiles, the same interceptors used on Australian and allied fighter jets.
Sustainment of the system will run primarily through Australian-based support contracts already in place with CEA Technologies and Raytheon Australia.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits 8 Russian War Sites From Arctic to Caspian
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities supporting Moscow’s war effort in a sweeping campaign stretching from the Arctic to the Caspian Sea, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, Sept. 10.
In a Telegram post, Zelensky said the targets included an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Russia’s Republic of Dagestan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions also came under attack, according to the president.
“Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a just response,” Zelensky said.
Shahed supply route hit on the Caspian
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones attacked the Makhachkala port, which Russia allegedly used to receive Iranian-made Shahed attack drones transported across the Caspian Sea.
A strike and subsequent fire were recorded within the port, RBC-Ukraine reported, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
The Makhachkala facility is Russia’s only ice-free deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It operates throughout the year and connects Russia with other countries in the region, including Iran.
Shahed drones delivered through the port were reportedly transported onward to deployment areas before being launched against Ukraine.
During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons (3.2 million tons) of cargo, including over 2.08 million tons of oil.
Russia Hits Same Dnipro Plant Twice, Killing 2
Eight targets across six Russian regions
Along with the Makhachkala port, Zelensky confirmed that a refinery had been hit in the Yamalo-Nenets region of Russia’s Arctic. He did not identify the facility or describe the damage there, but the reported attacks covered six Russian federal subjects.
The president did not provide details about the sites attacked in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries, ports, logistics hubs, and other infrastructure Kyiv says supplies Moscow’s military or generates revenue used to finance Russia’s invasion.
Zelensky thanked the Ukrainian personnel involved in the latest operations and those supporting the country’s ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russia.
“I thank every warrior and everyone who ensures our long-range capability and precision,” he said.

articles.title: Europe is playing a dangerous game with Russia
articles.body:
Europe is playing a dangerous game with Russia
History doesn’t repeat itself, not even as farce, and thus the latest chapter in the centuries-long confrontation between Russia and Europe will look different from those that came before it.
Today, the German authorities are closing Russian cultural and diplomatic institutions on flimsy pretexts and Norway is seizing Russian research vessels – and while the methods are new, the underlying impulse is familiar. Europe has sought to constrain Russia’s independence since at least the late 15th century.
For now, however, European governments aren’t seeking direct military confrontation, but this should not be mistaken for pacifism in Berlin, Brussels, Paris, or London – nor should we take seriously their ritual declarations about dialogue and a new regional security architecture, given there are more practical reasons for their restraint.
First, Western Europe’s largest states lack the human and material resources for a war with Russia, and although their position is somewhat better when it comes to weapons, much of that capacity is already being directed toward Ukraine, whose population is being asked to make enormous sacrifices in pursuit of European objectives.
However, the European people show little appetite for these sacrifices, mainly because living standards haven’t deteriorated nearly enough to persuade ordinary Germans, Italians, French, and British people to march into a conflict with Russia. Nor should anyone place much faith in Poland or the rest of Eastern Europe because Warsaw’s increasingly belligerent rhetoric disguises a much weaker willingness to actually fight.
Second, the Europeans understand that their American patrons have no desire to become embroiled in a potentially fatal confrontation with Moscow. The supposed American nuclear umbrella over Europe has always contained an element of mythology, and the region’s leaders understood this even during the Cold War.
France’s development of an independent nuclear deterrent was itself an acknowledgement that Europe could not assume that the US would risk its own destruction on their behalf. Charles de Gaulle and his successors didn’t build this arsenal because they were confident of American guarantees.
Nobody in Europe, therefore, seriously believes that Russia can be easily defeated in a war, because if they did, the temptation to attempt it would be much greater.
Yet these rational calculations run up against a more subjective danger, and we shouldn’t overestimate the European elite’s instinct for self-preservation.
Unlike Russia or China, Western Europe has experienced no comparable replacement of its ruling elites over the past 150 years, meaning today’s political establishments are, in an important sense, descendants of those that led Europe into the First and Second World Wars.
Western European politicians, particularly German and British, have historically displayed a tendency towards adventurism. Indeed, George Kennan, an astute observer of political cultures, drew a revealing contrast in his 1946 Long Telegram where Russian foreign policy, he wrote, “is neither schematic nor adventurist” and “doesn’t take unnecessary risks,” but the same cannot always be said of Europe.
The US, for all its willingness to use military force, generally prefers overwhelming odds, which is why its habit is to attack when it is confident that the opponent can’t inflict unacceptable damage in return. This makes the Americans, in a certain sense, more predictable and therefore more amenable to diplomacy. Even at the height of American unipolar power, Washington harbored few illusions about what a direct war with Russia would entail.
Europe has a more troubling historical record and its powers have repeatedly created dangerous situations that ultimately escaped their control, with World War II as the supreme example. Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and Germany’s invasion more than a century later were also enormous gambles, courses of action that appeared reckless even to many contemporaries.
For the moment, Europe is conducting its struggle against Russia primarily through indirect means because it lacks the resources for something more ambitious and retains enough sound judgment to recognize the dangers of escalation – but it would be reckless for Moscow to assume this restraint will last forever.
With every new stage of confrontation, European governments are burning bridges that might have otherwise supported a more balanced system of coexistence. Seen in this context, Russia’s decision to close the Goethe Institutes isn’t merely a symmetrical response to German measures, but also makes sense in the long term.
Whether we like it or not, cultural and humanitarian cooperation has increasingly become an instrument of state policy, though exceptions remain. Russian and French museum professionals, for example, continue to work together on some projects, as do academics and cultural figures in other fields, but these relationships have become increasingly subordinate to the logic of soft power.
Even seemingly innocuous forms of international cooperation are now expected to serve national objectives, and this is regrettable – but it reflects the expansion of modern foreign policy far beyond traditional diplomacy. Governments can use funding and institutions to influence almost every sphere of international contact.
Russia isn’t entirely different in this respect. We too often judge educational and cultural cooperation by its political consequences, and governments and the public naturally ask why money should be spent on international projects if they produce no discernible benefit for the country that funds them.
But in Western countries, these demands are particularly pronounced, so institutions such as the Goethe-Institut cannot realistically be separated from Germany’s broader foreign-policy objectives, and German officials inevitably expect publicly supported cultural organizations to influence attitudes towards Germany and advance the country’s interests.
The result is paradoxical: The political burden placed upon cultural institutions eventually undermines the very value of the relationships they were created to foster.
Perhaps the erosion of these old forms of cooperation is therefore unavoidable and it may even prove necessary if future cultural and academic contacts are to become less dependent on the political climate in European capitals.
For now, however, Russia faces a more immediate problem, in which European leaders remain afraid of direct confrontation, yet their own decisions are steadily pulling them deeper into a spiral of confrontation.
Their caution is real, but history gives Russia little reason to assume that caution will always prevail over adventurism – and that requires vigilance from Moscow and the resolve to act accordingly.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis amid Yemen conflict
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pakistan warns Iran to rein in Houthis amid renewed Yemen conflict
Pakistan has delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Yemeni Houthi allies after they stepped up attacks on the kingdom, in a coordinated effort to prevent the crisis from spiralling, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said.
The Houthis struck an airbase in Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities on Tuesday, wounding 73 people, in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Wednesday that Saudi warplanes carried out 54 airstrikes across various Yemeni provinces over the past 12 hours, adding that they would "not go unanswered and unpunished".
The escalating conflict, which represents a second theatre of war threatening global energy supplies, comes as Iran and the United States wage their biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping in the Gulf region since their war began.
Pakistan's warning to Iran carries significant weight because of its recently signed Mecca Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey.
While officials in Islamabad stressed any military role would be confined to defending Saudi territory, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said attacks spilling into the kingdom could trigger a joint security arrangement involving Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad.
"An aggression on one country will be considered an aggression on all three countries," Asif said on Pakistani TV.
"There is no ambiguity or doubt... Unprovoked aggression or spillover... into Saudi Arabia will definitely make this agreement operational."
The Pakistani defence ministry, foreign ministry and the military did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Fears of regional conflict
Pakistan’s intervention, after years of balancing ties with Saudi Arabia and Iran, has underscored the seriousness of the Houthi attacks. The message to Tehran is clear: rein in the Houthis or risk turning a proxy conflict into a broader regional security crisis, the sources said.
A senior regional diplomat said Pakistan had conveyed the message to Iran over the past 24 hours, urging Tehran to use its influence to halt Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message to Tehran on Tuesday and Tehran's response was that "Iran does not control the Houthis".
However, two Iranian sources said Tehran had told the Houthis last week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia. Tehran promised additional funding and weapons, they said, while several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks.
The regional diplomat said Islamabad was seeking to restrain the Houthis before the escalation reached a point where Riyadh could press Pakistan to play a more active role in defending it.
"Pakistan has an agreement with Saudi Arabia, but I am hopeful the situation will not reach the point where Pakistan has to practically step in," the diplomat told Reuters. "It will pursue a diplomatic solution for now."
Pakistani support for Saudis
The Pakistani source said Saudi officials had met senior Pakistani and Turkish military representatives in Riyadh to coordinate their response. The three countries agreed that their troops would not enter Yemen and that any response would be launched from Saudi territory, the source added.
A second Pakistani source said no decision had been made to join retaliatory strikes, stressing that its military pact with Riyadh was defensive and limited to protecting Saudi territory. Pakistani forces could provide military, technical, ground or air support within Saudi Arabia, but would not take part in combat operations on foreign soil, the source said.
The pressure campaign waged by Iran and the Houthis could have the opposite effect to that intended by Tehran, the regional diplomat said.
By targeting Gulf security in a bid to pressure Washington over its blockade of Iranian ports, Tehran risks driving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and other U.S.-aligned states into closer security coordination rather than fracturing their ties.
Trump's blockade of Iran set to continue
Regional officials also see little sign that Washington is prepared to relent.
President Donald Trump appears committed to maintaining the US.blockade until Iran reaches an agreement with Washington, the diplomat said, while Qatar is quietly exploring new proposals aimed at bringing both sides back to negotiations.
Another regional source said Saudi Arabia's military response would remain focused on the Houthis rather than Iran itself. Nor do Saudi officials believe Houthi attacks will achieve Tehran's broader objective of ending the U.S. blockade.
Riyadh is not expected to press Washington to lift the blockade, that source said, stressing that Trump believes sustained economic coercion is the most effective pathway to negotiations.
"The question is how much pain Iran can absorb, and for how long," the source said. "Trump does not want a military solution. He wants to squeeze them through the blockade."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was nearly hit by a drone during takeoff from Moldova as he was traveling to Oslo, Norway, for the funeral of King Harald.
The aircraft safely arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening, where Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre met with the Ukrainian leader the following morning, as reported by Reuters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Støre emphasized the severity of the situation during the discussions, describing the current circumstances in Ukraine by noting, "It is a very dramatic situation."
He added that the continuous aerial threats and operational demands leave "a deep impression" on those witnessing the ongoing defense effort.
In addition to his meeting with Støre, Zelenskyy met with Norwegian Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide shortly after landing in Oslo on Tuesday evening.
The recent near-miss in Moldova is not the first time aerial threats have targeted the Ukrainian president's travels abroad.

Four unidentified military-grade drones tracked the flight path of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska during their official visit to Ireland.

articles.title: SSU foils FSB plot to assassinate public activist in Kyiv region, arrests suspect
articles.body:
SSU foils FSB plot to assassinate public activist in Kyiv region, arrests suspect
As reported by Ukrinform, the SSU said this.
The special operation was carried out under the personal coordination of SSU Head Major General Oleksandr Poklad.
The investigation established that the suspect planned to shoot the activist during his morning walk with his dog in a forest.
To do so, the agent had been tracking the potential victim’s daily schedule and movements for an extended period. He also received coordinates from the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) to a cache, where he retrieved a pistol with ammunition and a suppressor.
Following instructions from the Russian intelligence service, the young man was then supposed to spend the night in the forest near the public figure’s home and kill him with several shots from an ambush.
SSU officers uncovered the enemy plot in advance and arrested the suspect in an ambush while he was preparing the assassination attempt.
According to the case materials, the FSB’s order was carried out by a recruited 19-year-old resident of Mykolaiv. Russian agents took notice of him because of his activity on social media. In particular, the suspect had published posts supporting fascist and Nazi ideology.
After recruiting him, the Russian intelligence service sent the suspect to Kyiv to carry out the killing.
During searches of the suspect’s belongings, investigators seized three pistols with suppressors and ammunition, as well as smartphones containing evidence of his work for the FSB.
SSU investigators served him with a notice of suspicion under several articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
The suspect is in custody. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
In turn, Gennadiy Druzenko, co-founder and president of the Mykola Pirogov First Volunteer Mobile Hospital, chairman of the board of the Center for Constitutional Modeling, a participant in the Revolution of Dignity and a veteran of the Russian-Ukrainian war, wrote on Facebook that the assassination attempt had been planned against him.
According to Druzenko, on the same day that an assassination attempt against Ihor Obolenskyi, commander of the Khartia Corps, was foiled, Russian intelligence services also sent a hitman to his home.
“The recruited hitman, who had specifically come from another city, carefully studied my daily routine, knew my routes, had my photograph, and was preparing to shoot me with a pistol fitted with a suppressor during my morning walk with my dog in the forest. The Security Service of Ukraine and its Counterintelligence Department did an excellent job. The criminal was arrested in the act,” Druzenko said.
As reported by Ukrinform, on July 31, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced an attempted assassination of Khartia commander Ihor Obolenskyi. The attacker and his accomplice were arrested.
